Law enforcement sources say Carter, a resident of the city’s Mid-City neighborhood, appeared to have no formal ties to organized extremist groups, nor did he make contact with known networks before the attack.

Investigators originally kept open the possibility that the act could be part of a broader conspiracy, particularly after initial searches of Carter’s home uncovered anti-government pamphlets and encrypted online messages. However, a forensic review of Carter’s devices and social media channels has yielded nothing to indicate co-conspirators or external handlers. “The search for accomplices is an essential part of our protocol in any act of violence like this,” Rodriguez said. “At this stage, all signs point toward a disturbed individual working alone.”

With the criminal investigation winding down, authorities are now working closely with local organizations and mental health professionals to address community concerns. Mayor Latoya Cantrell pledged continued support for the victims’ families and emphasized, “We must balance our pursuit of justice with healing for our city.”

Red Bull Racing has officially announced that Yuki Tsunoda will be stepping in to replace Liam Lawson at next month’s Japanese Grand Prix, confirming intense speculation about the team’s lineup for their highly anticipated home race. The decision, confirmed Thursday morning, follows a string of impressive performances from Tsunoda with AlphaTauri, Red Bull’s sister team, and strong support from the Japanese fanbase.

Lawson, who has filled in capably during recent rounds due to Daniel Ricciardo’s injury, will return to his role as reserve driver. The team emphasized that Lawson’s contributions had “surpassed expectations,” but cited Tsunoda’s local status and growing momentum this season as factors in the decision. “Yuki has continued to develop as a driver and has shown tremendous pace and maturity over the past months,” said Red Bull team principal Christian Horner. “We are excited to see what he can deliver at his home race in front of passionate Japanese supporters.”

For Tsunoda, the Japanese Grand Prix represents more than just another race weekend. It will be his first opportunity to compete at Suzuka Circuit with direct backing from Red Bull Racing, a move expected to further boost his popularity in his native country. “Racing at Suzuka is always special to me,” Tsunoda said in a statement. “To do so in a Red Bull seat is an incredible honor and I’m grateful for this opportunity.”

Ricciardo’s recovery is reportedly progressing, with team officials maintaining he is “on track” but unwilling to take risks regarding his return. Meanwhile, Red Bull clarified that Tsunoda’s promotion is for the Japanese Grand Prix only, leaving the door open for further evaluation of both Tsunoda and Lawson for the remainder of the season.

During testimony given at the ongoing inquiry into the case of convicted nurse Lucy Letby, several hospital staff members recounted meetings with hospital executives in the months leading up to Letby’s arrest. According to Dr. Sarah Jenkins, a senior neonatal consultant at the Countess of Chester Hospital, repeated concerns about Letby’s possible involvement in unexplained infant deaths were met with skepticism from management. “We felt unheard,” Dr. Jenkins told the inquiry. “Despite the growing pattern of incidents, we were told that Lucy Letby was a highly valued member of staff.”

Former hospital director Alan Hardwick also stated during his evidence that chief executive Tony Chambers appeared unconvinced that Letby was at fault. “Chambers expressed several times that he couldn’t believe Lucy was capable of such acts,” Hardwick said. “He urged us to avoid jumping to conclusions, insisting it was likely a case of unfortunate coincidences.” Documents submitted to the inquiry included an email exchange from May 2016 in which Chambers wrote, “The evidence does not indicate that [Letby] is responsible for any harm.”

The inquiry heard that discussions within the hospital’s executive team focused on protecting staff morale and the hospital’s reputation. Despite consultants’ repeated requests for an independent review, senior hospital figures were reluctant to act. “There was a pervasive atmosphere of disbelief,” Dr. Jenkins told the inquiry. “I truly believe management felt Lucy was innocent, no matter what we presented.”

Families of children affected by the events at the neonatal unit have expressed frustration over what they see as a failure to respond swiftly to red flags. The inquiry is expected to continue hearing from staff and management in the coming weeks, as it seeks to understand why concerns about Lucy Letby were not acted upon sooner.

Despite a wave of injuries and tactical challenges, England’s Lionesses have continued to demonstrate remarkable flexibility throughout the current Nations League campaign, according to defender Lucy Bronze. Speaking after Tuesday’s hard-fought 2-1 win over the Netherlands, Bronze credited England’s success to the squad’s ability to adapt to diverse playing styles and overcome adversity. “We’ve faced a lot of changes – from lineups to systems – but this group has shown time and again that we can adjust quickly and still perform at a high level,” Bronze said.

With Spain up next, a team renowned for their technical prowess and possession-based approach, England know their tactical versatility will be tested once more. “Spain always keeps the ball moving. They’re a side who can frustrate you if you’re not organised. But I think we’re one of the most adaptive teams around. We’ve dealt with teams who press high, teams who sit back, and we know how to shift gears depending on the situation,” Bronze explained.

Under manager Sarina Wiegman, the Lionesses have rotated formations and personnel throughout the competition, often due to injuries to key players such as Leah Williamson and Beth Mead. The emergence of young talents and the seasoned leadership of players like Bronze and Millie Bright have helped England maintain consistency. “It’s about everyone knowing their role and being positive when changes are made,” Bronze added. “You have to back each other and be ready for anything. That’s been a big part of our spirit.”

The upcoming clash against Spain could prove decisive for Nations League ambitions, but Bronze remains confident. “We know we’ll need to be sharp mentally and physically. But this team loves a challenge, and we know how to adapt. That’s one of our biggest strengths.”

Cardinal Luis Antonio David’s journey from Manila’s bustling streets to the marble corridors of the Vatican has been shaped by moments of both courage and controversy. His outspoken opposition to then-President Rodrigo Duterte’s bloody war on drugs marked a defining chapter in his tenure as Archbishop of Manila. Now, as he enters the Sistine Chapel to vote in the papal conclave, Cardinal David recalls the critical role Pope Francis himself played in those turbulent years.

“Pope Francis not only encouraged me, he shielded me,” Cardinal David said in an interview last week. “There was international pressure, threats, and sometimes I felt isolated. The Pope wrote me letters, he called. He wanted me to remember that standing for the dignity of life was not only my duty, but central to the Gospel.”

When Cardinal David condemned the extrajudicial killings rampant under Duterte’s campaign, he faced potential retribution—from online harassment to threats against church institutions. Many senior Filipino clergy counseled silence or caution. Cardinal David, however, persisted, delivering homilies that attracted national attention and organizing safe havens for victims’ families. Behind the scenes, the Vatican watched closely. According to a source familiar with the matter, Pope Francis instructed his envoys to “offer all necessary support” to Cardinal David, underscoring Vatican solidarity with critics of authoritarianism.

That alliance is heavy with significance as the College of Cardinals assembles to elect a new pope. Observers say Cardinal David’s public and papal backing during the Duterte era has elevated his status far beyond the Philippines. “He became a symbol of resistance rooted in faith,” said Fr. Miguel Lozano, a theologian in Rome. “He is not only voting for a future pope—he is carrying the trust placed in him by Pope Francis, and by millions who yearn for a Church that speaks for the vulnerable.”

During a press conference held in Amman on Monday, U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken highlighted the devastating impact that months of fighting in Gaza has had on children, calling the cost “far too high” and pressing for greater efforts to protect civilians. Blinken, who met with regional leaders including Jordan’s King Abdullah II, described scenes of destruction in Gaza as “heartbreaking” and underscored the urgent need for a cease-fire agreement that would allow humanitarian aid to reach those most vulnerable.

“In every conflict, it is children who bear the brunt,” Blinken stated. “What we are witnessing in Gaza is unacceptable. Tens of thousands of children have been killed, injured, or displaced; families are torn apart, schools reduced to rubble, and the prospects for an entire generation are at risk.” He acknowledged the United States’ support for Israel’s right to defend itself but emphasized that international law requires all parties to protect innocent lives, urging both Israel and Hamas to take immediate steps to safeguard children.

Aid agencies report that over half of Gaza’s 2.3 million residents are children and that their situation has deteriorated rapidly since fighting began in October. UNICEF has warned of rising malnutrition rates, with hospitals overwhelmed and hundreds of children separated from their families or orphaned. Blinken voiced support for the swift implementation of humanitarian pauses and increased access for relief organizations.

Jordanian officials joined Blinken in calling for an urgent truce, echoing regional and international concern about the long-term impact on Gaza’s youth. As diplomatic efforts continue, Blinken stressed, “Lasting peace and security in the region can only be achieved if the rights and futures of children are at the center of our efforts.” The Secretary concluded by reiterating calls for all parties to prioritize the protection of civilians as the conflict goes on.

The World Economic Forum in Davos has been shaken by revelations of blatant antisemitism after a shop window displayed a sign reading, “No skis for Jews,” sparking outrage in Switzerland and international condemnation. The offending notice, reportedly seen in the window of a ski equipment rental store on Davos’ main promenade, evoked memories of Nazi-era discrimination, prompting swift reactions from local officials, Jewish organizations, and human rights advocates.

Eyewitnesses say the handwritten sign, visible earlier this week, was placed prominently so passersby could not miss it. Social media posts featuring photographs of the sign quickly went viral, prompting fierce debate over rising bigotry in Switzerland and broader Europe. “I could not believe my eyes. I felt like I had stepped back into the 1930s,” said Esther Mayer, a Swiss Jewish visitor to Davos. “Such open hatred is absolutely shocking in today’s Switzerland.” The shop owner claimed the sign was intended to address a personal dispute with a customer but apologized “if anyone was offended.” Jewish advocacy groups dismissed this justification, describing it as “unacceptable in any context.”

Swiss authorities responded with an investigation, with the mayor of Davos, Philipp Wilhelm, stating, “There is zero tolerance for discrimination in our community. Such incidents will be met with the full force of the law.” The Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities called the episode a wake-up call, urging “not only legal action, but also investment in education and dialogue to combat ignorance and prejudice.”

Observers note that antisemitic incidents have increased across Europe in recent years, with Switzerland recording a spike following global conflicts and political unrest. Human rights monitors fear the Davos incident points to the lingering presence of xenophobic attitudes beneath Switzerland’s carefully maintained reputation for tolerance and neutrality. The ski shop has since removed the sign, but the pain and controversy linger.

Barclays is to acquire Tesco Bank for £600 million in a deal that will see the high street lender absorb one of the UK’s largest supermarket banking brands. The cash transaction, which is subject to regulatory approval and expected to complete in the second half of 2024, will see Barclays take over Tesco Bank’s deposit, mortgage, and credit card operations, along with around five million customer accounts.

The move marks a significant shift for Tesco, Britain’s largest retailer, which has been reviewing the future of its financial services arm amid rising competition and the high cost of regulatory compliance. Under the terms of the agreement, Tesco will retain its insurance, travel money, and ATMs business, while Barclays will gain the rest of its banking portfolio and also enter into a long-term strategic partnership. The two companies announced that Barclays will have exclusive rights to offer banking products under the Tesco brand, leveraging its large customer base through the supermarket’s Clubcard loyalty scheme.

Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy said the decision followed a strategic review and would allow the company to focus further on its retail core, while continuing to benefit from banking revenues through its brand partnership. “This deal ensures that Tesco customers continue to receive great banking products and services, backed by Barclays’ strength and expertise.”

For Barclays, the acquisition is the largest bolt-on retail banking deal since its purchase of Woolwich Building Society in 2000. Barclays CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan highlighted the opportunity to deepen customer relationships and expand the bank’s presence in everyday financial services. Analysts say the move solidifies Barclays’ position as one of the UK’s leading high street banks amid a wave of consolidation in the sector and will offer it access to Tesco’s sizable customer reach. Both sides expect a smooth transition, with existing Tesco Bank customers to be contacted in the coming months.

In the suburbs of Tehran, behind the modest doors of an unremarkable apartment building, a small group of Iranians gathers quietly. They murmur prayers in Farsi, light candles, and sing softly—careful not to draw attention from neighbors or authorities. It is Easter Sunday, and for Iran's growing number of Christians, particularly converts from Islam, celebration is not only an expression of faith but an act of defiance.

Officially, Iran recognizes some historic Christian communities, primarily Armenian and Assyrian, who are permitted to worship openly in their own languages. But for converts, the situation is far more precarious. Conversion from Islam is regarded as apostasy—a crime punishable by law and, in some cases, death. As a result, convert Christians are forced to practice their faith underground, meeting in private homes or informal "house churches," constantly aware of the risks.

"We cannot sing loudly or let children play outside," explained Maryam, a 32-year-old convert, who asked that her real name not be used. “Every year, a friend or family member is questioned by the security forces." Surveillance of Christian converts intensified after protests erupted across the country in 2022, fueling fears of association with Western influences. House churches have been raided and worshippers detained on charges of "acting against national security." Many face harsh interrogations, fines, and prison sentences.

Despite the fear, Iran’s underground Christian community persists, connected by encrypted messaging apps and a strong sense of solidarity. On Easter, ordinary rituals—baking sweet breads, sharing eggs symbolizing new life—take on the weight of resistance. “Even though we are afraid,” Maryam says, “we believe Jesus rose from the dead. We must have hope.” For these secret believers, Easter is more than a tradition; it is a testament to endurance, faith, and the hope that one day they may worship free from fear.

A Police Scotland spokesperson confirmed on Monday that the force had received an official request from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) for mutual aid following a wave of riots across cities including Belfast and Derry. Senior officers are currently assessing how many Scottish officers could be deployed and what specialist support might be required, should the situation continue to deteriorate. The unrest in Northern Ireland, sparked by recent political tensions and concerns over post-Brexit trade arrangements, has seen over thirty officers injured in violent confrontations over the past week.

Sources within Police Scotland indicate that any deployment would likely be composed of public order trained officers, with backgrounds in managing large-scale disturbances. “Our role would be strictly to support our PSNI colleagues and assist in restoring calm where we are needed,” said one senior officer, who emphasized that any officers sent would remain under the command of local authorities in Northern Ireland.

Should Police Scotland decide to send officers, the move would mark the first such deployment since the 2011 riots in England, when Scottish officers were also sent to assist. “We have robust contingency plans in place for scenarios requiring mutual aid,” the spokesperson said, while declining to reveal numbers at this stage. Any transfer of officers would be coordinated through the UK’s National Police Coordination Centre, which oversees inter-force assistance during major incidents.

The prospect of Scottish officers being dispatched across the Irish Sea has drawn mixed reactions from politicians and community leaders. Some have warned of the “potential strain” on local policing resources in Scotland, already stretched by pandemic-related pressures. However, others argue that the shared history of cooperation and the urgent circumstances in Northern Ireland make mutual aid both necessary and appropriate. Decisions are expected later this week as Police Scotland continues to monitor developments closely.

In the early hours of Thursday, at least 35 people were killed and dozens more wounded when an Israeli airstrike hit a United Nations-run school sheltering displaced families in central Gaza, according to local health authorities and eyewitnesses. The school, operated by UNRWA (the United Nations Relief and Works Agency), had become a makeshift refuge for Palestinians fleeing ongoing fighting in the nearby areas of Nuseirat. Videos surfaced on social media showed bodies lined up in the school’s courtyard, many of them covered in blankets, as survivors scrambled to assist the injured.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) stated that it carried out a precision strike targeting what it described as Hamas militants operating within the school compound. The military said it took measures to minimize civilian casualties, including intelligence-gathering and the use of precise munitions. In a statement, an IDF spokesperson claimed that several Hamas operatives who participated in attacks on Israeli forces were present at the time of the strike. However, these claims could not be independently verified, and UN officials voiced alarm over the mounting civilian death toll.

UNRWA Commissioner-General Philippe Lazzarini condemned the attack, calling it “another clear violation of international humanitarian law.” He noted that this was the sixth strike on a UN facility in less than a month, and renewed his call for an immediate ceasefire to protect civilians. Local NGOs and medical teams said many of those brought to nearby hospitals were women and children. The main hospital in Deir al-Balah reported being overwhelmed by casualties, some of whom succumbed to injuries due to critical shortages of medical supplies and staff. International organizations have reiterated urgent appeals for the protection of noncombatants amid the ongoing conflict, now in its eighth month, that has left Gaza’s humanitarian system and infrastructure on the brink of collapse.

Anna Henderson clinched a brilliant silver medal for Team GB in the women’s individual time trial at the Olympics, marking a career-best performance on the world’s biggest stage. The 25-year-old delivered a powerful ride over the 22km course, starting steadily before accelerating in the technical second half to stop the clock just 14 seconds behind Dutch favorite Ellen van Dijk, who defended her title and took gold.

Henderson’s ride was met by cheers from British supporters lining the route, many of whom braved the early-morning drizzle to witness her battling through the challenging combination of steep ramps and tight corners. "I knew I had to pace it right and not lose my head on the climbs," Henderson said after the finish. "Crossing the line and seeing second place was overwhelming. It’s been a dream to represent Team GB, and I’m just so proud."

It was Henderson’s first Olympic medal and capped a remarkable rise from her days as a junior national champion to a world-class specialist in the discipline. Her result brings Great Britain’s cycling medal tally to four this Games, reaffirming the country’s place as a powerhouse in the sport.

Earlier in the day, hopes were high for Josh Tarling in the men’s time trial, especially after his bronze at last year’s World Championships. However, the 20-year-old Welshman finished just outside the podium, placing fourth and missing out by only seven seconds. Tarling, who has been one of the breakout stars of the season, admitted to feeling disappointed but remained philosophical. "That’s cycling sometimes. I gave it everything and have no regrets," he stated. "It motivates me to come back stronger for Paris."

Team officials and fans alike hailed Henderson’s silver as a landmark achievement, while pledging support for Tarling as he looks ahead to future Olympic campaigns.

Mary Greenwood, 47, underwent breast implant surgery in 2016 following a double mastectomy for early-stage breast cancer. At the time, her surgeons reassured her that the silicone implants were safe, and rare complications were discussed only briefly. However, two years ago, Mary began experiencing unusual swelling and discomfort in her left breast. Thinking it might be a routine issue, she sought medical attention, but the diagnosis took her by surprise: Mary had developed Breast Implant-Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (BIA-ALCL)—a rare form of cancer that has been linked to certain textured breast implants.

“I had no idea this could happen,” said Mary in an interview from her home in Reading, Berkshire. “No one told me this was a possibility when I had the surgery. If I’d known the risks, I might have chosen differently.” BIA-ALCL is not a form of breast cancer itself, but a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that develops in the scar tissue and fluid surrounding the implant. According to the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), there have been more than 70 cases identified in the UK, although the risk remains very low—estimated at one in thousands of women with certain textured implants.

Mary’s experience highlights what experts call an urgent need for greater awareness about potential risks of breast implants, especially as more women undergo reconstructive or cosmetic procedures each year. “We’re trying to let women know what to watch for—persistent swelling, lumps or pain, even years after surgery,” said Dr. Diane Fields, a consultant oncologist at the Royal Free Hospital. Mary is now in remission, but she continues to speak out, encouraging women to ask detailed questions about their options. “If my story helps one woman make an informed decision, it’s worth it,” she said.

Education Secretary James Foster has said he is “open-minded” about the possibility of introducing a ban on smacking children in England, following growing calls from child welfare groups and members of Parliament. In an interview with the broadcaster, Mr Foster stressed that the government remains committed to ensuring children’s welfare and safety, but would take time to consider all available evidence before making any decisions about possible legislative changes.

The debate was reignited this week when the Children’s Commissioner for England, Rachel Evans, publicly urged ministers to follow the lead of Scotland and Wales, where it is now illegal for parents or guardians to use any form of physical punishment against children. Several MPs from the Conservative, Labour, and Liberal Democrat parties have also expressed support for a review of current laws, which permit parents in England to use “reasonable punishment” under certain circumstances.

Mr Foster said: “I understand and respect the deeply held views around this issue, and I want to assure families and campaigners that my department is listening carefully. The evidence about the impact of physical punishment on children is growing, and as Education Secretary, my priority is always the safety and well-being of our young people. I am open-minded and willing to look at what has worked in other parts of the UK and internationally.”

However, the minister cautioned against acting hastily, explaining that parents’ rights must also be respected, and any change would require a thorough public consultation and analysis of the implications. “We need to strike the right balance between protecting children and recognising the important role that parents play. That’s why we’ll be seeking views from across society before making any commitments,” Mr Foster added. The Department for Education confirmed that it is currently reviewing existing research and monitoring the effects of the ban in Wales and Scotland.

Passengers at Gatwick Airport faced significant disruption on Wednesday as police detained two individuals in connection with a "suspect package" incident. According to Sussex Police, officers responded swiftly to reports of an unattended item identified near the South Terminal’s departure area, prompting a temporary evacuation shortly before midday.

Eyewitnesses described scenes of confusion and anxiety as armed officers cordoned off a section of the terminal and passengers were instructed to move to safe zones. “It was quite alarming to see so many police running and shouting for everyone to step back,” said Alina Morris, a traveller due to fly to Barcelona. "At first no one knew what was happening, but security staff kept everyone calm."

Authorities confirmed that the Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team was deployed as a precaution and carried out a controlled assessment of the package. While the investigation was underway, flights departing from the South Terminal experienced delays, with some arrivals temporarily diverted to the North Terminal.

Shortly after 2pm, officials reported that two people had been detained in connection with the incident. Sussex Police stated that both individuals were being questioned at a local station and that early indications suggested there was no ongoing threat to public safety. A spokesperson for Gatwick Airport confirmed that operations began returning to normal by late afternoon, although travellers were warned to expect residual delays while staff worked through the backlog.

Police have not released further information regarding the contents of the package or the identities of those detained, citing the ongoing investigation. Meanwhile, airport authorities assured passengers that safety remains their top priority, and they thanked travellers for their patience and cooperation during the disruption. The swift response reportedly minimized disruption and ensured the safety of both staff and passengers.

Arriving at Ferrari’s Maranello headquarters this week, Lewis Hamilton was greeted by fans and team members eager to usher in a new era for both driver and manufacturer. The seven-time world champion, renowned for his record-breaking career with Mercedes, steps into the scarlet overalls of Ferrari with what he describes as “a sense of fresh possibility” and palpable anticipation for the upcoming Formula 1 season.

Hamilton, aged 39, has never shied away from new challenges, and his decision to join Ferrari after over a decade with Mercedes has sent ripples across the motorsport world. Speaking during his first press briefing with the team, Hamilton said, “I could not be more excited. Ferrari’s legacy in Formula 1 is second to none, and to have the chance to compete for them is a childhood dream realized.” He acknowledged the “fantastic memories” and “lifelong friendships” he created at Mercedes but insisted that the time was right to “write a new chapter.”

The move comes at a time of transition for Ferrari, who have not claimed a drivers’ title since 2007. Hamilton’s arrival is seen as a major coup and a statement of intent from the Italian outfit. Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur praised Hamilton’s “incredible work ethic and relentless hunger for victory,” voicing confidence that his experience would inspire the entire team. “Lewis brings new energy and high expectations,” said Vasseur. “Together, we aim to be back at the front where Ferrari belongs.”

Early footage from testing showed Hamilton familiarizing himself with the new car and working closely with engineers. As the season opener in Bahrain approaches, Hamilton emphasized the importance of “unity and focus,” underlining his commitment to delivering results for Ferrari’s passionate, worldwide fanbase. “We’re here to win and to make history,” he declared, “and I am ready for the challenge.”

The first official portrait of King Charles III since his coronation has been unveiled at Buckingham Palace, marking a significant moment in the early years of his reign. The striking painting, created by renowned British artist Jonathan Yeo, captures the new monarch in a contemplative pose, blending regal tradition with a modern artistic sensibility. Measuring over seven feet tall, the portrait depicts King Charles adorned in the uniform of the Welsh Guards, a role he has held since 1975, set against a dramatic crimson backdrop that nods to the rich ceremonial heritage of the British monarchy.

Jonathan Yeo, who has previously painted high-profile figures including David Attenborough and Malala Yousafzai, spent over a year on the portrait, conducting several sittings with the King at Clarence House and Windsor Castle. Yeo described the commission as “an immense honour and responsibility,” emphasizing his intent to “convey not only His Majesty’s likeness, but also his warmth and thoughtful character.” The artist’s characteristic style—an expressive blend of realism and impressionism—is evident, with bold brushstrokes and nuanced attention to detail. Viewers will note the inclusion of subtle motifs, such as the faint outline of a butterfly resting on the King’s shoulder, symbolizing transformation and continuity.

Reactions to the portrait have ranged from admiration for its contemporary approach to curiosity about the symbolic choices woven into the composition. Speaking at the unveiling ceremony, King Charles expressed his gratitude to Yeo and reflected on the unique experience of sitting for a portrait that will become a part of royal history. The work is set to be displayed at Drapers’ Hall in London, joining a historic collection of royal portraits and serving as a testament to the evolving public image of the monarchy under the reign of King Charles III.

The Welsh Labour government has warned that up to £1bn of vital public funding is at risk if opposition parties refuse to support the upcoming budget in the Senedd. Finance Minister Rebecca Evans said that deep cuts to essential services—including health, education, and local government—could become inevitable should the spending plan fail to pass. She urged members from all sides to put “the interests of the people of Wales ahead of political point-scoring” ahead of Tuesday’s crucial vote.

“The scale of the challenge facing us is unlike anything we’ve seen in recent years,” Evans stated during a heated committee session on Monday. “Inflation, increased demand on our NHS, and lack of additional funding from Westminster have all combined to create unprecedented pressure on our finances.” She added that without broad support, specific projects and core services earmarked for £1bn in funding could be delayed or axed altogether.

With Labour holding exactly half of the 60 Senedd seats, the government requires at least one opposition Member of the Senedd (MS) to support or abstain for the draft budget to clear its final hurdle. However, Plaid Cymru, the Conservatives, and the Liberal Democrats have all raised concerns, mostly focusing on allocations for health and local authorities, as well as transparency over some spending lines.

Leader of Plaid Cymru, Rhun ap Iorwerth, said his party was “open to negotiation” but demanded more funding for councils struggling to maintain basic provision, stating, “Our communities cannot be expected to bear the brunt of austerity.” The Welsh Conservatives, meanwhile, labelled the budget “uninspired,” but have not confirmed how they will vote. With the deadline looming, the government’s appeals for a cross-party deal are intensifying as the prospect of a failed budget could trigger financial uncertainty, wage delays, or even a constitutional crisis in Cardiff Bay.

England’s five-match Test series in India was always billed as Brendon McCullum’s toughest assignment since taking over as head coach, but the scale of their defeat at Mumbai’s Wankhede Stadium has underlined just how stark the challenge has become. Despite early optimism following a spirited draw in Hyderabad, the third Test’s one-sided nature left England reeling both strategically and psychologically. India’s relentless spin attack, spearheaded by the irrepressible Ravindra Jadeja and Axar Patel, ruthlessly exposed England’s technical frailties on turning tracks, while the unfamiliar conditions appeared to sap their energetic “Bazball” intent.

After the innings defeat, questions are being raised about whether England’s ultra-attacking ethos—so successful at home—needs recalibrating in the subcontinent. Joe Root’s dramatic first-innings dismissal, caught attempting a risky reverse sweep, symbolised the struggle to balance aggression with application. The middle order, touted as England’s strength, collapsed under pressure, leaving McCullum searching for answers as his side’s batting average outside England continues to suffer.

Compounding matters, England’s bowlers, lacking the experience and variety of their Indian counterparts, have laboured on slow, low pitches. Mark Wood and Ollie Robinson found little seam or swing, while spinners Jack Leach and Rehan Ahmed failed to threaten India’s well-set batters for long periods. McCullum himself conceded that “adaptation” was now the watchword, with selection debates looming ahead of the pivotal fourth Test in Ranchi.

For McCullum, the remainder of the series is about restoring belief and finding a plan B—something sorely lacking in Mumbai. England must show their much-vaunted fearlessness is matched by resilience and smart cricket if they are to avoid returning home with a bruising scoreline and difficult questions about the sustainability of their revolution.

England face a pivotal moment in their Guinness Six Nations campaign as they prepare to welcome Italy to Twickenham this Saturday, conscious that only a convincing performance will keep their hopes of the championship alive. After an opening victory over Scotland in Edinburgh, Steve Borthwick’s men are under pressure to produce not just a result, but a statement of intent against an Italian side determined to shed their reputation as perennial underdogs.

With France and Ireland both laying down impressive markers in the early rounds, England are acutely aware that anything less than a clinical, attacking display risks derailing their pursuit of the trophy. Borthwick, who has placed his faith in a blend of youth and experience, has urged his players to bring intensity and creativity to their game, recognising that supporters expect far more than the grinding efficiency that featured in previous encounters.

The return of fly-half Marcus Smith, lauded for his flair and vision, has brought a palpable sense of anticipation to the England camp. With talisman Owen Farrell orchestrating play and an in-form pack eager to dominate, the hosts are aiming to rediscover the attacking verve that has so often eluded them in recent championships. “We want to put on a show at Twickenham, play with freedom, and give the fans something to cheer,” Farrell said in the build-up. “We're not taking Italy lightly—they’ve shown real improvement—but we know what’s at stake for us.”

Italy, still seeking their first Six Nations win at Twickenham, arrive buoyed by encouraging performances and determined to spring a surprise. However, England’s focus remains on themselves: securing maximum points and restoring belief that they can once again contend for the game’s biggest prizes as the tournament progresses.

Downing Street has stated that the government’s spending review, which sets departmental budgets for the coming years, is now “settled” following weeks of speculation about potential revisions. The confirmation comes as ministers face mounting pressure from backbench MPs, unions, and public sector leaders to revisit funding levels amid rising inflation and increased demands on public services.

A Downing Street spokesperson said on Monday, “The spending review that was put in place remains settled. Departments have been given clarity over their budgets and will continue to work within those limits.” The spokesperson added that while there remains a commitment to responsible public finances, the government recognises the “significant challenges” faced in areas such as health, education, and local government.

Senior officials acknowledged that the Prime Minister and Chancellor recently held discussions about the impact of changing economic conditions, fuelling rumours that further adjustments might be made to ease the strain on critical services. However, according to Number 10, no additional funding will be announced and existing settlements will not be reopened. “We made difficult choices when the spending review was set, and those choices stand,” the spokesperson said.

Labour has criticised the government for what it calls a “refusal to adapt” in the face of new fiscal pressures, arguing that sticking to previous commitments could result in real-terms cuts to key services. Unions representing NHS workers and teachers have also warned that fixed budgets risk eroding pay and worsening staff shortages.

Despite the pushback, government sources maintain that departments are being encouraged to find “efficiencies” and use existing resources more effectively. The Treasury is not expected to announce any major changes before the next autumn statement, but has said it will “continue to monitor the situation closely.” Meanwhile, public sector leaders continue to press for urgent support as costs rise faster than anticipated.

Speaking during an interview on Wednesday, Shadow Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson said that she believes trans women should use toilets designated for their biological sex in public spaces, including schools. Phillipson emphasized that while she affirms the dignity and rights of all individuals, the safety and comfort of women and girls must remain a priority. 

“There is a need for clarity in these situations,” Phillipson said. “We support the right of everyone to live freely, but when it comes to single-sex spaces such as toilets, particularly in schools and other public venues, it is appropriate that facilities be used according to biological sex.” She argued that the issue centers on safeguarding and the need to balance the rights of trans individuals with those of biological women and girls.

Phillipson’s remarks come amid ongoing debates over access to single-sex spaces across the United Kingdom. Some advocacy groups have called for increased inclusion of trans people in facilities matching their gender identity, while others voice concern over potential risks to privacy and safety. The issue has become a flashpoint within both political and public discourse, as policymakers attempt to navigate competing rights and deeply held beliefs.

Supporters of trans-inclusive policies argue that restricting access can lead to discrimination and harm against trans individuals. However, Phillipson maintained that the existing laws and guidelines are clear. “It’s important that public institutions have clear policies that protect everyone, and for now, that means toilets and changing rooms should, as a default, be organised by biological sex,” she said.

Opposition parties and LGBTQ+ organizations have been quick to criticize Phillipson’s comments, arguing that such positions reinforce stigma. Nevertheless, Phillipson insisted that her stance was not about exclusion, but about ensuring solutions work for all members of society.

Thick plumes of black smoke rose above central Southampton on Saturday afternoon as a major fire broke out at a commercial premises less than a mile from St Mary’s Stadium. Emergency services raced to the scene shortly after 11:00 am, with Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service deploying over a dozen fire engines and support vehicles to tackle the rapidly spreading blaze. Eyewitnesses reported loud bangs and the smell of burning plastic as firefighters worked to contain the flames, which threatened nearby residential buildings and businesses.

The dramatic incident forced the postponement of Southampton FC’s scheduled home fixture against Coventry City, originally due to kick off at 3:00 pm. Club officials, in consultation with local authorities and the EFL, made the decision mid-morning after it became clear that both safety and access to the stadium could not be guaranteed. Large sections of Britannia Road and the surrounding area were cordoned off, causing significant travel disruption for fans, staff, and emergency responders.

In a statement released on social media, the Saints expressed frustration at the unavoidable circumstances but emphasized their primary concern for public safety. “We understand how disappointing this is for supporters, but the safety of everyone in and around St Mary’s remains our utmost priority,” the club noted. The club also reassured ticket holders that all purchases would remain valid for the rescheduled fixture, details of which will be announced in due course.

Local residents were advised to keep windows and doors shut as fire crews battled the blaze well into the afternoon. There were no reports of injuries, though paramedics remained on standby. Police urged everyone to avoid the area, warning that road closures would remain in place while crews worked to extinguish lingering hot spots and investigate the cause of the fire.

Peter Sullivan, who spent more than three decades in prison for a crime he always insisted he did not commit, has had his conviction for the 1986 murder of Brian Fletcher quashed by the Court of Appeal. The decision, handed down on Monday, comes after a lengthy review of new forensic evidence and a re-examination of the original trial procedure.

Sullivan, now 62, was found guilty in 1987 largely on the basis of eyewitness testimony and limited physical evidence. However, concerns about the reliability of that evidence began to surface in recent years, prompting a formal review by the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC). The Commission’s report revealed that key witnesses may have been influenced by aggressive police interviewing tactics and that exculpatory forensic evidence was not disclosed to the defence at the time of the trial.

In its ruling, the Court of Appeal described the original investigation as "seriously flawed" and highlighted "significant failings" in the way forensic material was handled. Advances in DNA technology, unavailable in the 1980s, played a crucial role in the Court’s decision to quash the conviction. New testing determined that biological samples taken from the scene did not match Sullivan or tie him to the crime, undermining the prosecution’s case.

After more than 36 years behind bars, Sullivan was released from custody immediately following the announcement. Outside the court, he was visibly emotional as he addressed a crowd of supporters and journalists, stating, “For years I was denied justice—I only ever wanted the truth to come out.” His legal team has called for a full inquiry into the conduct of the original investigation and raised the possibility of seeking compensation for his lengthy wrongful imprisonment.

The family of Brian Fletcher expressed relief that the truth was being sought but called for continued efforts to identify the real perpetrator.

The case, which has sent shockwaves through India’s banking community, centers on a woman from Mumbai who alleges that nearly $1.9 million was siphoned from her account at an ICICI Bank branch over a period of several years. According to legal documents filed last week and reviewed by local media, the complainant claims the withdrawals were orchestrated by the branch manager—a trusted figure she says she had known personally while conducting her banking.

Sources close to the investigation say the alleged fraud came to light when the account holder, who is based overseas for professional reasons, noticed abnormal fluctuations in her account balance during a routine review earlier this year. A forensic audit showed a series of unauthorized transfers and withdrawals dating as far back as 2020, many of which reportedly bore forged signatures and false documentation.

The woman has accused the branch manager, identified in court papers as Neha Sharma, of systematically manipulating internal records and bypassing security protocols. She alleges that Sharma gained access to sensitive information under the guise of providing personalized banking assistance, and then diverted large sums to various accounts both within India and abroad.

Police in Mumbai have launched a formal investigation and summoned several bank employees for questioning, including Sharma, who has been suspended pending inquiry. A senior banking official involved with the case, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that “such a breach of trust, if proven true, raises significant concerns regarding oversight and internal controls” within the organization.

In a statement, ICICI Bank said it was cooperating fully with law enforcement authorities and had initiated its own internal review. The bank assured customers that their deposits remained secure, emphasizing its “zero-tolerance policy” toward any employee misconduct. Meanwhile, consumer rights groups have renewed calls for stronger regulatory vigilance to protect depositors from insider fraud.

Dr. Samuel Carter, a food chemist at the University of Michigan, has sparked debate among tea enthusiasts after recommending a pinch of salt as the secret ingredient to brewing the perfect cup of tea. In a paper recently published in the journal *Food Science Review*, Dr. Carter argues that adding a small amount of salt—no more than a sixteenth of a teaspoon per cup—counteracts the bitterness sometimes associated with black tea. 

“Tea contains compounds called tannins, which can create astringency and a bitter aftertaste, especially if the tea is steeped for too long or is of lower quality,” Dr. Carter explained in an interview. “Sodium ions in salt have the effect of blocking bitterness receptors on the tongue, which can make the overall flavor profile of the tea smoother and more palatable.”

Dr. Carter’s recommendation has been met with skepticism. British tea experts, in particular, have balked at the suggestion, calling it unorthodox and even sacrilegious. “We’ve always said the best cup of tea needs quality leaves, good water, and close attention to steeping time,” said Lydia Farnsworth of the UK Tea Association. “Salt has never been on the list.”

Despite the controversy, some tea lovers who have experimented with Dr. Carter’s method report a noticeable difference in taste. “I was surprised by how much softer the tea tasted,” said Anna Li, a tea blogger based in Seattle. “You can’t actually taste the salt—it just tastes less bitter.” Dr. Carter is quick to caution that salt should be used sparingly. “The goal isn’t to make your tea salty,” he said. “It’s about enhancing the natural flavor by subtly reducing bitterness. Start with a tiny pinch and adjust to your palate.”

At a time when pop music is dominated by meticulously curated personas and radio-friendly bops, Chappell Roan explodes onto the scene as a vibrant outlier—embracing all things outrageous, emotional, and unapologetically queer. Hailing from a small town in Missouri, Roan has become an underground sensation, delighting fans with her theatrical aesthetic and gleefully bizarre lyrics, all while cultivating a devoted online following. Her debut album, *The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess*, is a high-voltage collection of synth-powered anthems, earnestly tackling heartbreak, identity, and liberation with both vulnerability and a wink.

Roan’s live performances are already notorious among fans for their outlandish costumes—think neon wigs, glittering jumpsuits, and platform heels—and their raucous, community-driven energy. “I want my shows to feel like a slumber party where everyone can be their absolute weirdest,” Roan said in a recent interview. That ethos carries through to her music, where tracks like “Red Wine Supernova” and “Casual” serve up clever wordplay and explosive choruses tailor-made for dance floors and bedroom mirrors alike. For Roan, the “freaky” label isn’t just an act—it’s an invitation to anyone who’s felt outside the pop mainstream.

What further sets Chappell Roan apart is her commitment to open, unfiltered self-expression, drawing from her own experiences as a queer woman navigating love and ambition. Her playful yet poignant authenticity recalls icons like Lady Gaga, but Roan’s vision is distinctly her own: stranger, sillier, and refreshingly sincere. In an industry that often rewards conformity, Chappell Roan is carving out a space for the freaky, the fun, and the fiercely individual—a rising star you’ll want to keep on your radar.

The atmosphere in Munich on Wednesday night told its own story. What had begun as a raucous, sun-soaked carnival—kilts swirling, bagpipes ringing under blue Bavarian skies—closed in heartbreak for Scotland’s loyal travelling support. Inside the Allianz Arena, the Tartan Army’s chants faltered as the final whistle blew and the realization set in: another major tournament, another abrupt exit. 

For all the optimism that fizzed through the Scottish camp before Euro 2024, Steve Clarke’s side once again stumbled at the group stage. A single point collected from three games, a late, agonizing concession to Hungary, and an attack that spluttered rather than roared—the same old story played out for the men in dark blue. Fans who flooded the central Marienplatz day after day with their infectious energy found themselves facing the long journey home, spirits deflated by the familiar taste of disappointment. 

There was no shortage of effort—Andy Robertson’s tireless runs, Billy Gilmour’s tidy passes, and defensive grit from Ryan Porteous—but Scotland lacked a cutting edge. Injuries to key players like Kieran Tierney and an early suspension for Porteous in the opener against Germany only compounded their woes. For all their passion, their limitations against top-level opposition were exposed once again, prompting some to ask uncomfortable questions about the progress made under Clarke’s stewardship.

Yet, as thousands of Scots drifted away from the stadium in the early hours, there was also pride. “We showed up, we sang our hearts out, it’s just a shame the results didn’t match the atmosphere,” said Davy MacDonald, a supporter from Aberdeen. But he and many others know the familiar refrain: for the Tartan Army, qualifying is just the start—for now, the party’s over, but hope always lingers for the next time.

Over the past week, Bangladesh has witnessed an extraordinary wave of protests, led primarily by students demanding sweeping changes in governance. The resignation and subsequent flight of Sheikh Hasina, the country’s long-serving Prime Minister, on Sunday, marked a watershed moment that has sent shockwaves through the political landscape. On the streets of Dhaka, and in university campuses across the nation, thousands of young people gathered in celebration, their chants echoing hopes for democracy, transparency, and a government more accountable to its people.

Many students say their desire for change stems from years of frustration over alleged government corruption, economic hardship, and restrictions on free speech. For them, Hasina’s departure is not simply an end to an era, but potentially the beginning of a new chapter for Bangladesh. “This is our time,” said Rifat Hossain, a 22-year-old political science major at Dhaka University, as he joined marches in Shahbagh Square. “We risked so much because we want fair elections and a future where we can speak our minds without fear.”

The students’ movement initially began as a protest over disputed parliamentary elections and perceived manipulation by the ruling Awami League. However, it quickly snowballed into broader demands for reforms, including strengthening judicial independence, greater press freedom, and the dismantling of the Digital Security Act, which activists argue has been used to stifle dissent. Images circulating on social media show jubilant crowds waving the national flag as opposition leaders, some newly released from jail, addressed the masses and promised to “build a Bangladesh for all.”

Despite the euphoria, many protesters are aware that the road ahead will be difficult. The military, while pledging neutrality, remains a powerful actor, and the political opposition is fractured. Still, students remain resolute: “We have shown that ordinary people can change history,” said university activist Sadia Ahmed, her voice hoarse from chanting. “Now, we must build the future we dreamed of.”

Police have arrested a 26-year-old man on suspicion of murder following the deaths of three women in a violent attack in Bushey believed to have involved a crossbow. Officers were called to a property on Ashlyn Close shortly after 7pm on Tuesday evening after neighbours reported hearing screams and calls for help. On arrival, paramedics and police discovered three women, all relatives, with serious injuries. Despite the best efforts of emergency responders, all three victims were pronounced dead at the scene.

In the hours that followed, Hertfordshire Constabulary launched a manhunt for a suspect believed to be known to the victims. Late on Wednesday morning, authorities confirmed that a man had been detained in the Enfield area of north London after an intense overnight search. The suspect was arrested without incident and is currently being held at a local police station for questioning. 

Detective Superintendent Rob Hall said: “This is an exceptionally serious and shocking case. Our thoughts are with the family and friends of those who lost their lives in this horrific incident. We are committed to determining exactly what led to these tragic deaths.” Police have confirmed that a crossbow was recovered from the scene and is undergoing forensic testing, but they have not ruled out the possibility that other weapons may have been involved.

Local residents described the area as “usually quiet and peaceful” and expressed shock and sadness at the events. Police have cordoned off multiple roads in the vicinity as officers continue their investigation, conducting door-to-door enquiries and appealing to anyone with information or footage relevant to the incident to come forward.

At this early stage, investigators believe the killings were targeted and there is no ongoing threat to the wider public. Extra patrols have been deployed to the area to provide reassurance to the community.

Fiona Harvey, the woman widely believed to be the inspiration behind the character “Martha” in Netflix’s hit series *Baby Reindeer*, has declared her intentions to pursue legal action against both the streaming giant and the show’s creator Richard Gadd. Harvey, who recently appeared in a high-profile interview to refute claims about her behavior depicted in the semi-autobiographical drama, alleges that the series’ portrayal has subjected her to “global vilification and distress,” impacting her personal and professional life.

In statements made through her legal representatives, Harvey claims that Netflix and Gadd breached her privacy and defamed her character by presenting events she insists are “grossly exaggerated, distorted, and in many aspects entirely fabricated.” According to Harvey, she never engaged in the obsessive stalking or harassment described in the show, which quickly became a cultural phenomenon since its release in April. She maintains that the program’s emphasis on being “a true story” misled audiences and painted her falsely as a dangerous individual.

Legal analysts suggest that Harvey’s case could test the boundaries between artistic license and responsible representation of real-life events. The ongoing publicity has reportedly resulted in Harvey receiving threats and unwanted attention, forcing her to change her routines and avoid public spaces. Netflix, for its part, has so far stood by the authenticity of Gadd’s story, issuing statements emphasizing their commitment to supporting creators' right to share their true experiences. 

Gadd, who both stars in *Baby Reindeer* and wrote its screenplay, has insisted that names and identifying details were changed to protect individuals’ privacy. Nonetheless, critics have pointed out that dedicated internet sleuths were able to track down Harvey’s identity within days of the show’s release. As the case develops, the interplay between artistic freedom, privacy rights, and ethical storytelling remains firmly in the spotlight.

The FBI has intensified efforts to identify and contact the families of all 270 victims of the 1988 Lockerbie bombing as the US prepares to try the man accused of constructing the device that brought down Pan Am Flight 103. Law enforcement officials say this unprecedented outreach seeks not only to notify families about developments in the high-profile case but also to allow them opportunities for input and participation during the trial process.

According to federal sources, agents have been reviewing decades-old records, searching for surviving relatives across multiple continents, and working with Scottish authorities to update contact information for those affected. The attack, which killed 259 people aboard the flight from London to New York and 11 residents of the Scottish town of Lockerbie, remains the deadliest terrorist act on UK soil. Many victims were American university students returning home for the holidays.

The renewed search follows the extradition of Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir al-Marimi, a former Libyan intelligence officer, to the US late last year. Prosecutors allege that Mas’ud was a key bomb maker who collaborated with convicted co-conspirator Abdelbaset al-Megrahi, the only person previously found guilty in connection with the atrocity. Mas’ud has pleaded not guilty to charges of terrorism and destruction of an aircraft resulting in death.

Family members and advocacy groups have expressed both hope and skepticism about the possibility of further accountability. “We have waited decades for justice, and this trial is a critical moment for all of us,” said Frank Duggan, former president of the victims’ families association. Others have voiced frustration with the passage of time and the slow pace of investigations.

The FBI, meanwhile, has reiterated its commitment to supporting families, promising regular briefings and resources throughout the trial. Federal officials have acknowledged the emotional toll of reopening old wounds, but insist that the pursuit of justice for every victim remains a top priority.

Ruben Amorim could hardly have asked for a starker introduction to the scale of his challenge at Manchester United than the chaotic 2-2 draw against Chelsea on Saturday evening at Stamford Bridge. For long stretches, United looked like a team caught between philosophies: energetic pressing and intricate buildup phases were punctuated by extended spells of defensive disorganization and lapses in concentration, issues that have plagued the club for several seasons. As United allowed Chelsea space to create chances—culminating in the Blues’ late equalizer—it was hard not to see just how mammoth a task awaits Amorim, who is widely considered the frontrunner to replace Erik ten Hag this summer.

The Portuguese coach, renowned for his tactical acumen and transformative work at Sporting CP, will inherit a side full of attacking talent but riddled with inconsistencies, especially at the back and in midfield. United’s inability to manage transitions was evident throughout the match, granting Chelsea opportunities to exploit gaps with relative ease. Even United’s attacking brilliance, showcased by quick moves resulting in their two goals, was overshadowed by a lack of collective discipline and ambition when out of possession. 

Amorim’s success at Sporting has been built on solid organization, a unified team identity, and a clear tactical blueprint—qualities United have struggled to maintain despite considerable investment. The scenes at Stamford Bridge were a sobering demonstration of the scale of cultural and structural change required. With fans growing increasingly impatient after another season of disappointment, the expectations placed on Amorim are immense: he must instill belief, mend a fragile defence, and foster the kind of tactical unity that has long eluded post-Ferguson United sides. The draw with Chelsea was not just another missed opportunity for three points; it was a reminder of the arduous journey ahead.

New Zealand produced a clinical performance to defeat Pakistan by 38 runs and secure their spot in the semi-finals of the Women’s T20 World Cup on Wednesday. Chasing a challenging target of 158 runs set by New Zealand, Pakistan struggled to build momentum and finished on 119 for 7 in their 20 overs at the Newlands Cricket Ground in Cape Town.

Sophie Devine spearheaded New Zealand’s batting effort with a composed 65 off 42 balls, anchoring the innings after they lost two early wickets in the powerplay. Devine, who was also captaining her side, shared a crucial 63-run partnership with Amelia Kerr, who chipped in with a lively 34 off 28 deliveries. Their partnership laid the foundation for a late surge, and quick-fire cameos from Maddy Green and Brooke Halliday enabled New Zealand to post a competitive total of 157 for 5.

Pakistan’s reply got off to a shaky start as they lost both openers within the first four overs, thanks to an incisive new-ball spell from Lea Tahuhu, who finished with figures of 3 for 19. Bismah Maroof and Nida Dar attempted to revive the chase, rotating the strike and finding the occasional boundary, but relentless pressure from New Zealand’s disciplined bowlers reduced the required rate to a steep climb. The Pakistan middle order was unable to recover after Dar fell to a sharp catch at extra cover off Amelia Kerr, all but ending their hopes.

With this victory, New Zealand became the second team to qualify for the semi-finals, joining Australia. The White Ferns will now look ahead to their next challenge, brimming with confidence after a strong all-round display, while Pakistan’s campaign ends with just one win in the tournament.

Tottenham Hotspur manager Ange Postecoglou has acknowledged that his team is "in a fight" after a recent run of disappointing results but has vowed to remain steadfast in his approach. Speaking after Spurs' 2-1 loss to Liverpool—Tottenham’s fourth consecutive Premier League defeat—Postecoglou insisted that abandoning his footballing philosophy is not an option. "If people think I’ll change course now, after everything we’ve worked for, they’re mistaken," the Australian said in the post-match press conference. "This is when you find out what you stand for."

The defeat at Anfield leaves Tottenham’s hopes of Champions League qualification hanging by a thread, with just two games remaining in the season. Spurs have been criticized for a defensive frailty and a lack of cutting edge up front since their strong start to the campaign faded. However, Postecoglou remains focused on long-term progress rather than short-term fixes. "Of course, everyone wants results right now, but if you chase that, you lose sight of what’s most important. I’d rather double down on my principles—pressing, possession, playing with courage—than compromise at the first sign of trouble," he explained.

Under Postecoglou, Tottenham have adopted a more expansive and attacking style of play, a marked departure from the pragmatic approaches of previous managers. While this has produced thrilling football at times, it has also exposed the team’s vulnerabilities, particularly during injury crises. "Success isn’t linear and culture doesn’t shift overnight," Postecoglou noted. "This group has shown resilience and I believe in them. We’re in a fight but that’s what this league is about. We need to stand our ground, stick together, and keep playing football the way we want to play."

Passengers in England will soon see the maximum price for a single bus journey rise by £1, in the first increase to the government-imposed fare cap since its introduction. From July, the fare cap will rise from £2 to £2.50 on eligible routes outside London, prompting concern from passengers and campaigners about the impact on travel costs during a time of mounting living expenses.

The government’s £2 cap was first brought in during January 2023 in an effort to help people with household budgeting amid record inflation and rising energy prices. Originally planned as a temporary measure, the scheme has since been extended several times as part of efforts to encourage bus use and support regional economies. Ministers claim the new £2.50 cap – which will remain in place until at least late 2024 – still represents “significant value for money” compared to pre-cap fares, which could reach up to £6 on longer journeys.

Transport groups and local leaders, however, warn that passengers will feel the effect of the rise, especially those on low incomes who rely on buses for essential journeys to work, school and medical appointments. Labour’s shadow transport secretary described the move as “a blow for hard-pressed families”, while national bus operator Stagecoach acknowledged that “any increase is difficult for customers with stretched budgets”. Some operators say the financial support from the cap has helped protect routes from deeper service cuts amid falling passenger numbers and rising costs. 

The Department for Transport says it is continuing to invest more than £200 million to keep fares below market rates and support vital services outside London. Despite ongoing support, analysts note that bus ridership across England still lags behind pre-pandemic levels, with cost and convenience major factors in whether people choose to travel by bus.

Aston Villa's summer transfer business took a dramatic leap forward this week as Spanish international Marco Asensio completed his move to Villa Park, while the club also finalized an agreement to bring French defender Axel Disasi in on loan from Chelsea.

Asensio, 28, arrives from Paris Saint-Germain in a deal reportedly worth £25 million, signing a four-year contract with the Birmingham club. The versatile winger, who has won three Champions League titles with Real Madrid and played a key role in Spain's Euro 2024 campaign, expressed his enthusiasm about the new challenge. “I’m excited to join Aston Villa at such an ambitious moment and help the club continue to grow,” Asensio stated in his first club interview. Manager Unai Emery is believed to have been instrumental in persuading his compatriot to make the switch to the Premier League, citing Asensio’s creativity and experience as vital assets ahead of Villa’s return to European football.

Meanwhile, Villa’s defensive options received a significant boost with the agreement of a season-long loan for Axel Disasi. The 26-year-old centre-back struggled to secure a regular starting spot at Chelsea last season but remains highly rated across the continent, having previously starred for AS Monaco and the French national team. Sources close to Villa suggest the deal includes an option to buy at the end of the campaign, reflecting both clubs’ satisfaction with the arrangement.

These signings underline Aston Villa’s commitment to building on last season’s impressive Premier League campaign, which saw the team return to the top six and qualify for the Europa Conference League. Emery and the club hierarchy are hopeful that both Asensio and Disasi can help solidify Villa’s place among England’s elite as preparations intensify for what promises to be a pivotal season. Further business is expected before the transfer window closes.

Liverpool snatched a dramatic 1-0 win at the City Ground as Darwin Nunez marked his return from injury with a 99th-minute header, capping a gruelling afternoon in which the visitors were made to toil by a disciplined Nottingham Forest side. Introduced in the second half after a brief layoff, the Uruguayan timed his run perfectly to glance home from close range after a late Liverpool surge finally broke the hosts’ resistance.

For long spells, Forest’s compact shape and energetic pressing frustrated Jürgen Klopp’s team, who dominated possession without the incision to match. Luis Diaz was Liverpool’s liveliest outlet, repeatedly driving at the back line, while Virgil van Dijk headed over from a first-half corner and Harvey Elliott saw a low effort smothered. Forest, meanwhile, threatened on transition: a sharp break down the right forced a smart stop from the Liverpool goalkeeper, and the hosts passed up their best opening when a close-range effort was steered wide with the goal gaping.

As the minutes ticked into nine added for stoppages, Liverpool pushed bodies forward, penning Forest deep. The winner arrived with virtually the last attack: a recycled set piece was worked to the right and clipped invitingly into the area, where Nunez stole a yard and diverted the ball beyond the stranded goalkeeper. The City Ground fell silent before the red away end erupted, Klopp punching the air on the touchline as his players wheeled away in relief.

The late breakthrough underscores Liverpool’s resilience amid a punishing schedule and an ongoing injury list, and keeps them firmly in the title race with spring approaching. For Forest, who had defended stoutly and created moments of their own, it was a ruthless reminder of fine margins at this level. They will take heart from the performance but leave empty-handed, still searching for the points to ease relegation fears as the run-in gathers pace.

Residents in Bushmills have spoken of their shock after a man was assaulted with what police believe was a sharp object in a village car park on Saturday night. Officers said the victim, aged in his 30s, was taken to hospital with injuries that are not thought to be life-threatening. An investigation is under way and detectives have appealed for witnesses and footage.

“It’s just awful,” said one local shopworker, who asked not to be named. “This is a quiet place most evenings. You might have a few families coming and going, tourists at the weekend, but nothing like this. People are rattled.” Another resident described seeing emergency services arrive within minutes. “There were blue lights everywhere. We’re all asking how something like that can happen here.”

The incident is understood to have taken place shortly after 9pm in a public car park near the village centre. Community representatives urged anyone with information to come forward and called for a visible police presence in the short term to reassure residents. “Our thoughts are with the man who was injured,” one councillor said. “This has caused real anxiety. We need calm, cooperation with police, and support for those affected.”

The Police Service of Northern Ireland said initial inquiries suggest the assailant fled the scene on foot. No arrests had been made by Sunday afternoon. Detectives are reviewing CCTV from nearby premises and have asked drivers who were in the area at the time to check dash-cam recordings. Officers also appealed to anyone who noticed suspicious behaviour in or around the car park earlier in the evening to get in touch.

Bushmills, known for its busy visitor trade, has seen an increase in footfall in recent months, and traders said the incident should not define the village. “We pride ourselves on being welcoming,” a café owner added. “But people need to feel safe. We hope whoever did this is caught quickly.” Police can be contacted on 101, or anonymously via Crimestoppers.
