David Lammy is expected to make an early visit to India in a bid to reset relations and inject momentum into a partnership that both sides see as strategically and economically vital. Officials said the trip, one of his first overseas engagements as foreign secretary, is intended to signal continuity on the UK’s Indo-Pacific focus while recalibrating tone and priorities under the new government.

Trade will dominate the agenda. Negotiations on a free-trade agreement have inched forward over multiple rounds but remain stuck on market access for goods such as cars and spirits, rules on digital trade and data flows, and provisions around services and professional mobility. British officials believe an intensified political push could narrow differences and unlock a package that boosts investment and supply-chain resilience, though they caution that substance will take precedence over speed.

Migration and skills policy is also likely to feature, with both governments weighing how to balance talent pipelines, student flows and return pathways against domestic pressures. London wants to expand collaboration in clean energy, critical minerals and life sciences, and to deepen ties between the City and India’s fast-growing fintech ecosystem. Climate finance and just-transition projects are being prepared as potential deliverables.

Security discussions will cover maritime cooperation in the Indian Ocean, counter-terrorism and technology safeguards. While London and New Delhi have not always aligned on responses to Russia’s war in Ukraine, officials say the UK will emphasise continued coordination where interests overlap and transparent dialogue where they do not, including on the challenges posed by China.

The outreach carries political significance at home. Labour figures have sought to rebuild trust with British Indian communities and with New Delhi after past frictions, reiterating support for India’s rise and for pragmatic, respectful engagement. Business groups on both sides are urging a clear timetable for the trade talks, streamlined visas for specialists and a sharper focus on investment barriers to convert warm rhetoric into outcomes.

Novak Djokovic and Roger Federer led an outpouring of tributes on Thursday, hours after Rafael Nadal announced he will retire at the end of the season, closing a chapter that defined men’s tennis for nearly two decades. Djokovic, Nadal’s most frequent opponent, hailed the Spaniard’s relentless competitiveness and resilience, noting that their rivalry across an astonishing 59 matches pushed both men to unprecedented heights. Federer, who shared some of the sport’s most iconic stages with Nadal, reflected on a bond forged through epic contests and mutual respect, recalling their classic 2008 Wimbledon final and the image of the pair in tears at the Laver Cup when Federer bade farewell in 2022.

Messages flooded in from across the tennis world and beyond. Carlos Alcaraz, the reigning standard-bearer for Spanish tennis, called Nadal his guiding light, while Andy Murray and Stan Wawrinka praised his ability to summon courage in the tensest moments. Iga Swiatek, who has cited Nadal as a model throughout her rise, thanked him for “showing how to fight with grace.” Roland Garros organizers saluted the 14-time champion, saying the tournament’s clay “will always remember every step of his left foot.” The Spanish Tennis Federation and LaLiga clubs posted tributes, and fans gathered outside the Rafa Nadal Academy in Manacor, leaving scarves and handwritten notes.

Nadal departs with 22 Grand Slam singles titles, 14 in Paris, 92 tour-level trophies and 209 weeks as world No 1, achievements compiled with a ferocious topspin forehand, exacting standards and a reputation for humility. His career, hampered in recent seasons by injuries but punctuated by stirring comebacks, helped shape a golden era with Federer and Djokovic that redefined what longevity and excellence could look like.

Tournament directors said plans are being discussed to honor Nadal at key stops on tour, with players expecting emotional scenes wherever he appears. “Tennis won’t be the same,” one veteran coach said, “but it will always carry his imprint.”

Astrobotic’s Peregrine lunar lander broke apart in Earth’s atmosphere above the Pacific on Friday, ending the first mission under NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative after a propellant leak made a Moon landing impossible. The Pittsburgh-based contractor confirmed the vehicle re-entered over a remote stretch of ocean and largely burned up, with any surviving fragments expected to fall harmlessly into the sea. There were no reports of damage or injuries.

Peregrine launched on 8 January atop United Launch Alliance’s new Vulcan rocket, a debut flight that placed the lander on the proper trajectory. Hours after separation, however, engineers detected a critical malfunction in the propulsion system traced to a faulty valve that caused a tank rupture and fuel loss. The leak crippled the lander’s ability to conduct course corrections and a braking burn at the Moon. Mission controllers stabilized the spacecraft’s attitude and attempted science operations in deep space while planning a safe disposal back to Earth.

The mission carried five NASA instruments aimed at studying the lunar surface environment, along with university and commercial payloads, including a small rover demonstration. It also hosted memorial capsules with human cremated remains, a feature that had prompted objections from Navajo Nation leaders in the weeks before liftoff. Astrobotic said it coordinated with U.S. government agencies on the re-entry corridor to minimize risk and comply with space safety guidelines.

Although the loss is a setback for Astrobotic, NASA officials have emphasized that CLPS is designed to buy frequent, relatively low-cost deliveries to the Moon from multiple providers, accepting higher risk to accelerate lunar science. The agency said data gathered during Peregrine’s nine days of operations will inform future flights, including troubleshooting for propulsion systems and thermal control. Astrobotic’s next mission, the larger Griffin lander slated to carry NASA’s VIPER rover, remains in development, while other CLPS partners prepare their own attempts to reach the lunar surface.

Mobile network EE is urging parents to hold off on giving smartphones to children in primary school, arguing that most under-11s are not ready for unrestricted internet access and social media. The company said it will shift the way its shops and website advise families, steering those who want to stay in touch toward basic handsets or children’s smartwatches that allow calls and location sharing but block apps and browsers by default. EE added it will expand its free online safety resources for families and make its default safety settings clearer when new child lines are activated.

The move lands amid intensifying debate about screen time, bullying and exposure to harmful content among pre-teens. Government guidance encourages schools to restrict phone use during the day, and Ofcom research suggests more than half of 8- to 11-year-olds now own a smartphone. Child-safety campaigners say parental controls often fail to keep pace with fast-evolving platforms and that phones intended for communication can quickly turn into portals for adult content, anonymous messaging and in-app spending.

EE said its recommendation is not a ban but a practical baseline to help parents resist peer pressure. “If a child needs to contact home, there are safer ways to do it,” a spokesperson said, pointing to devices that enable calls, GPS and approved contacts only. The company is also training retail staff to discuss readiness and the trade-offs of early smartphone ownership with families.

Some parents and headteachers welcomed the stance, saying it could make it easier to set consistent boundaries across a class. Others argued smartphones are vital for children with long commutes, split households or additional needs, and called for stronger age checks and default platform settings rather than relying on individual families to say no. EE said it is in talks with charities and other operators about common standards to reduce online harms while preserving connectivity for young users.

Manchester United have opted to keep Erik ten Hag in charge following a comprehensive end‑of‑season review, drawing a line under weeks of uncertainty and reaffirming their commitment to the Dutchman’s long‑term project. The decision reflects what senior figures describe as a belief that the team’s underlying trajectory, despite a turbulent campaign, remains upward, with evidence of progress in player development and tactical cohesion offsetting inconsistency in results.

Ten Hag is expected to lead a targeted reset over the summer, focusing on recruitment aligned to a clearer playing identity and on reducing the squad’s susceptibility to injuries that disrupted selection throughout the year. Club executives are understood to have emphasised tighter coordination between coaching, analytics and scouting, with an emphasis on athleticism, availability and decision‑making in key areas of the pitch. The manager will also be tasked with accelerating the pathway for several academy graduates who featured sporadically but impressed when called upon.

While acknowledging missed targets and uneven performances—particularly in Europe—the club view the season’s late resilience and improved defensive structure as indicators that the framework Ten Hag envisaged is starting to take hold. The review also highlighted the team’s capacity to manage high‑pressure moments domestically, a trait United hope to convert into greater consistency against compact, mid‑table opponents who often frustrated them.

Ten Hag’s immediate priorities include trimming a bloated wage bill, resolving the futures of fringe players and integrating early arrivals before the pre‑season tour. Fitness staff and medical protocols will be scrutinised, with a push for individualized workloads intended to curb soft‑tissue setbacks. Internally, there is a recognition that patience must be balanced with accountability: performance benchmarks and style‑of‑play metrics have been set, and the decision to retain the manager comes with the expectation of visible strides by the autumn.

Supporter reaction has been mixed but largely pragmatic. Many fans argue stability offers United their best chance of sustained improvement after years of churn; others insist that continuity must now be matched by clear, measurable progress on the pitch.

Tearful mourners lined the banks of the Waikato River as the casket of the Kīngitanga leader was carried onto Tūrangawaewae marae at first light, the sound of karanga rising through a winter haze. By afternoon, after a private burial attended by whānau and elders, his daughter was formally acknowledged as Māori queen, closing days of tangihanga with the rare spectacle of sorrow and succession in a single day.

Under grey skies, the proceedings moved with deliberate dignity. Pallbearers led the tūpāpaku from the wharenui for final farewells before the hearse wound toward the urupā. Returning to the marae ātea, senior rangatira and kaumatua encircled the new monarch, cloaking her in a korowai and offering karakia. A proclamation was read and waiata swelled as the flag of the movement was raised.

“Today we honour the past and carry its weight into the future,” a senior elder said, urging unity, or kotahitanga, across iwi and hapū. In a brief address, the queen thanked supporters for their aroha and pledged to serve with humility. “I stand here for our people, guided by our tikanga and by the example of my father,” she said.

Dignitaries from across the motu, including government and local leaders, took their places alongside representatives of Pacific and Indigenous communities. Many spoke to the continuity of the Kīngitanga, established in the 19th century to safeguard lands and uphold mana Māori, and its evolving role as a moral voice on social and economic issues.

Outside the barriers, schoolchildren in piupiu performed haka, and vendors handed out hot kai to those who had waited through drizzle and wind. As the crowd dispersed, aides signalled the queen would embark on a series of marae visits in the coming weeks, meeting with iwi leaders and kaumātua. “Our grief remains,” one mourner said, “but so does our purpose.”

Albania has imposed a one-year nationwide ban on TikTok following a fatal stabbing that authorities say was preceded by an online dispute involving videos shared on the platform. In an emergency decree adopted late Thursday, the government said the temporary suspension was necessary to “prevent imminent risks to public safety” while investigators examine how violent or inciting content circulates among young users. The country’s electronic communications regulator has ordered internet service providers to block access to the app and instructed app stores to disable downloads for users in Albania starting this week.

Police said a suspect is in custody and that the probe is ongoing, cautioning that any direct causal link between online content and the incident remains under investigation. Officials argued that platforms “cannot be neutral conduits” when harmful trends or targeted harassment escalate offline, and outlined conditions under which the ban could be lifted early, including stricter age verification, stronger Albanian-language moderation, and faster takedown procedures for content promoting violence.

The move drew swift criticism from digital rights groups and opposition lawmakers, who called it a disproportionate response that risks curbing free expression and harming the livelihoods of creators and small businesses that rely on the app. Education advocates, however, welcomed the pause as an opportunity to strengthen media literacy and update school guidelines on social media use.

TikTok said it removes content that incites violence and is “ready to engage with authorities” to address concerns, adding it has increased investments in safety features and local language review. The ban, one of the most sweeping in Europe in recent years, places Albania among a growing number of countries that have restricted the platform over security or safety issues.

Officials said an interagency taskforce will report quarterly on progress, with the first review due in three months. Users were warned that attempts to circumvent the block may be subject to penalties, though enforcement details have not been finalized.

Drake has filed a second legal action connected to Kendrick Lamar’s chart-topping diss track Not Like Us, escalating a months-long feud that has leapt from studios to courtrooms. The new complaint, lodged Thursday in Los Angeles County Superior Court, accuses Lamar and affiliated companies of defamation, false light, and violation of Drake’s right of publicity, and seeks an injunction against what it describes as ongoing commercial exploitation of Drake’s name and likeness in connection with the song and its promotional materials. Damages were not specified.

According to the filing, the track and its accompanying video contain statements Drake contends are false and were published with reckless disregard for the truth, causing reputational and economic harm as the record surged across radio, streaming platforms and social media. The complaint also challenges what Drake’s attorneys call “misleading contextual edits” in online clips that, they argue, amplify disputed claims for virality.

Representatives for Drake declined to comment. A spokesperson for Lamar did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The latest suit follows an earlier legal move this summer in which Drake sought relief over the use of his image in user-generated content tied to Not Like Us, arguing the clips implied endorsement. That matter remains pending. Legal experts note defamation cases brought by public figures face a high bar, requiring proof of actual malice—knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard—which can be difficult to establish when speech touches on matters of public interest in music and culture.

Produced by Mustard, Not Like Us has dominated the Billboard Hot 100 and shattered streaming milestones since its release, becoming the unofficial soundtrack of the rivalry and spawning a wave of memes, dance videos and think pieces. A hearing on Drake’s request for a preliminary injunction in the new case is expected next month. No court date has been set for trial.

Federal investigators now believe the suspect behind last week’s attack in New Orleans acted alone, concluding there is no credible evidence of additional plotters or an organized network, according to officials familiar with the inquiry. The assessment, reached after days of reviewing digital communications, financial records and surveillance footage, marks a shift from the immediate aftermath of the incident, when authorities cautioned that multiple leads were being explored.

In a brief statement Tuesday, the FBI’s New Orleans Field Office said agents had “found no indication of co-conspirators,” though the investigation remains active. Detectives are continuing to map the suspect’s movements in the days leading up to the attack and to reconstruct a timeline using cell-site data, license-plate readers and witnesses who have come forward. Forensic analysts have also completed preliminary examinations of a laptop and two mobile phones recovered during searches executed over the weekend, the statement said.

Officials have not publicly identified the suspect, citing ongoing investigative steps and notifications. Motive remains a central question. Investigators are scrutinizing online writings and recent employment and housing records while working with behavioral specialists for insight into potential grievances or triggers. Authorities said there is, at this stage, no evidence linking the incident to foreign groups or to a broader ideological campaign.

City leaders emphasized that the reassessment does not lessen the seriousness of the crime. Additional patrols and temporary security measures will continue in the affected area this week, and a designated assistance center has been opened for witnesses and those seeking support. Community organizations have scheduled blood drives and counseling sessions.

Officials urged patience as evidence is processed and warned against circulating unverified claims on social media. “The facts are still being gathered,” one law enforcement official said. “If the evidence changes, our conclusions will, too.”

US Secretary of State Antony Blinken said the toll of the Israel-Gaza war on children is “far too high,” urging steps to better protect civilians and to dramatically expand humanitarian access as fighting drags on. Speaking during a visit to the region, Blinken pressed Israeli officials to narrow the scope of military operations, open additional corridors for aid, and support sustained pauses long enough for relief groups to move food, medicine, and fuel to hard‑hit areas. He also reiterated Washington’s call for the immediate release of hostages and for all sides to avoid actions that could ignite a broader regional conflict.

Israeli leaders maintain their campaign is aimed at dismantling Hamas’s military and governing capabilities following the group’s deadly attack in Israel, and say they take precautions to limit civilian casualties. They blame Hamas for operating within densely populated neighborhoods and using civilians as human shields, an accusation the group denies.

Inside Gaza, aid agencies describe a worsening humanitarian emergency. Hospitals report severe shortages of critical supplies, while schools and makeshift shelters are overflowing with displaced families. UN officials warn that children face acute risks from malnutrition, disease, and trauma, and have appealed for predictable, secure access for convoys. Relief organizations say sporadic deliveries cannot meet the scale of need without more entry points and improved coordination on the ground.

Blinken’s comments underscore growing international unease over the war’s civilian impact and the political strain it is creating abroad. US officials say they are working with regional partners, including Egypt and Qatar, on frameworks that could pair hostage releases with pauses in fighting and expanded aid, while also sketching out steps toward governance and reconstruction plans for Gaza. Blinken reiterated that a durable end to the cycle of violence requires a credible pathway to a Palestinian state alongside Israel, with security guarantees for both peoples.

Lucy Bronze believes England’s capacity to change on the fly will be decisive when the Lionesses face Spain in the Nations League, describing Sarina Wiegman’s side as “one of the most adaptive teams in international football.” The Barcelona defender, who trains weekly against many of Spain’s core players, said England’s strength lies in their ability to tweak shape, tempo and personnel without losing identity. “We’ve shown we can press high or sit in, build patiently or go direct. Whatever the game asks for, we find an answer,” Bronze said. “Against Spain you need more than one plan.”

England’s adaptability will be tested by the world champions’ rhythm and control. Spain’s midfield carousel, anchored by quick combinations and clever rotations, has troubled most opponents since their World Cup triumph. Bronze suggested England’s approach would be elastic: compressing the middle to disrupt passing lanes, then switching quickly to exploit space left by Spain’s adventurous full-backs. “They want to draw you in and play through you,” she added. “We have to decide together when to jump, when to delay, and be brave when the counter is on.”

Wiegman’s willingness to adjust has underpinned England’s recent resilience amid injuries and changing personnel. The Lionesses have alternated between a back four and a back three, used inverted full-backs to add an extra midfielder, and rotated wide forwards to press from different angles. “Sarina is clear and detailed,” Bronze said. “If we need to change at 20 minutes or 70, everyone knows the triggers.”

Beyond tactical intrigue, the tie offers a measuring stick after Spain edged the Lionesses in last year’s global showpiece. Bronze framed it less as revenge than a chance to show evolution. “We respect them massively. But we’ve grown too,” she said. “This team learns fast. That’s our edge.”

Red Bull have confirmed that Yuki Tsunoda will replace Liam Lawson for this weekend’s Japanese Grand Prix at Suzuka, reinstating the Japanese driver for his home race amid ongoing evaluations of the team’s wider driver programme. In a brief statement, the team said the switch is part of its planning for the upcoming phase of the season, citing continuity, car development goals and Tsunoda’s extensive experience at Suzuka as factors in the decision.

Lawson, who has impressed during his recent appearances, will remain on standby and continue his duties within the Red Bull stable, including simulation work and potential future sessions as required. Tsunoda’s return is expected to be a focal point for local fans, with strong home support and commercial commitments building around the Suzuka weekend. The 5.8km figure-eight circuit is among the calendar’s most technically demanding, rewarding drivers who can manage high-speed transitions through the Esses and extract confidence in the high-load Degner and 130R sections—areas where track knowledge can translate into incremental but crucial lap-time gains.

Friday practice will provide the first look at Tsunoda’s setup direction and headline pace, with qualifying on Saturday expected to be tightly contested given the circuit’s narrow margins and evolving grip. Lawson is set to support from the garage as the team targets a clean execution in front of a capacity Suzuka crowd.

On campuses from Boston to Berkeley, international students say group chats have morphed into ad‑hoc crisis lines, swapping checklists for border interviews and reminders to carry meticulously organized folders of I‑20s, funding letters, transcripts and proof of housing. The anxiety follows a spate of incidents in which students arriving for the new term were questioned for hours at U.S. airports and then placed on flights back home, according to students, campus officials and immigration attorneys. “People are cancelling conferences and skipping funerals because they’re scared they won’t be allowed back,” said a graduate student from India who asked not to be named.

Universities have convened town halls, circulated step‑by‑step travel advisories, and extended the hours of international offices. Several institutions said they have retained outside counsel to staff 24/7 hotlines during peak travel weeks and are urging students not to travel without consulting an advisor. Lab directors worry about losing key researchers mid‑project; deans report last‑minute course coverage scrambles when teaching assistants are delayed abroad. Counseling centers at multiple campuses say they are seeing an uptick in students citing immigration stress and sleep disruption.

Customs and Border Protection said in a brief statement that all travelers must be “admissible” and that officers make case‑by‑case determinations at ports of entry. Immigration lawyers note that even minor discrepancies—confusion over on‑campus employment rules, outdated financial statements, or a missing signature—can snowball in secondary inspection. “The policy hasn’t changed on paper, but enforcement feels sharper and less predictable,” said one attorney who advises several universities.

For students, the uncertainty is the hardest part. A first‑year master’s candidate from Nigeria described keeping a packed bag by her door but postponing a long‑planned trip to see family. “I refresh my email waiting for guidance,” she said. “We came to study, not to feel like we’re one question away from losing everything.”

King Charles III’s first official portrait since his coronation has been unveiled in London, a striking, large-scale oil on canvas by British portraitist Jonathan Yeo. The work presents the King in the uniform of the Welsh Guards, his figure emerging from a saturated field of crimson that blends with the scarlet tunic. A small butterfly rests near his shoulder, an arresting detail that punctuates the monochrome palette and invites symbolic readings of change and continuity.

The portrait was commissioned in 2020 by the Worshipful Company of Drapers, with initial sittings taking place when the subject was still Prince of Wales and further work continuing after his accession. According to those involved with the project, Yeo set out to bridge tradition and modernity, adopting the formal language of state portraiture while emphasizing immediacy through bold color and visible brushwork. The butterfly, incorporated late in the process, is intended to acknowledge the passage from heir to sovereign and, more broadly, the King’s long-standing interest in conservation.

Unveiled at a private ceremony attended by the King, Queen Camilla and the artist, the portrait will go on short public display in the capital before taking up its permanent position at Drapers’ Hall. It is the first in what is expected to be a series of official images produced during the reign, as institutions update their collections and civic buildings seek new likenesses.

Early reaction from art commentators and the public has been robust, with praise for the painting’s contemporary sensibility and debate about the intensity of its palette. Supporters have described the composition as a confident reimagining of royal portraiture for a new era, while others have questioned its uncompromising tonal unity. For Yeo—whose sitters have ranged from political leaders to cultural figures—the commission marks one of the most high-profile works of his career, situating his style firmly within a centuries-old national tradition.

Swiss authorities and Jewish groups expressed shock on Sunday after a handwritten notice reading “No skis for Jews” appeared in the window of a Davos equipment rental shop, prompting a police inquiry and a flurry of condemnation across the alpine resort. A photograph of the sign, posted by a passerby and widely shared online, drew hundreds of comments within hours and revived concerns about overt antisemitism resurfacing in public spaces.

Cantonal police in Graubünden confirmed they had opened an investigation into a potential breach of Switzerland’s anti-racism law, which prohibits public discrimination and incitement against protected groups. Local officials said inspectors visited the premises shortly after the image spread, and the notice was removed. The shop remained closed for the rest of the day as officers collected statements and reviewed security footage. “There is zero tolerance for hatred in Davos,” a spokesperson for the town council said, adding that the case would be referred to prosecutors if criminal elements were found.

Management of the store issued a written apology, saying the paper was put up by an employee following a dispute with customers and “does not reflect our values.” The statement said the staff member had been suspended pending an internal review and that the company would introduce mandatory training on anti-discrimination standards. Lawyers for the business declined further comment while the investigation is ongoing.

Jewish community leaders called the incident a chilling reminder that bigotry can surface even in places reliant on international visitors. The Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities urged authorities to pursue the matter “with the utmost seriousness” and pressed the tourism sector to adopt clear protocols to prevent discriminatory refusals of service.

The Davos tourism board said it was working with hoteliers and retailers to reinforce codes of conduct, noting that the resort “welcomes guests of every background.” Rights advocates described the uproar as a test of Switzerland’s legal and social resolve to confront antisemitism promptly and publicly.

Barclays has agreed to acquire most of Tesco Bank’s retail banking operations in a deal valued at about £600m, the companies said. The transaction will see Barclays take on Tesco-branded credit cards, unsecured personal loans and the bank’s savings book, alongside a long-term partnership to distribute financial products through Tesco’s stores and digital channels. The purchase price will be paid in cash and is expected to be adjusted for the net assets transferred at completion. For Barclays, the move expands its UK consumer finance franchise and opens access to a large base of Tesco Clubcard customers, while allowing the supermarket group to streamline its portfolio and focus capital on its core retail business.

Under the agreement, existing customers are expected to see no immediate change to their accounts. Cards and savings products will continue to operate as normal until completion, after which they will migrate to Barclays systems in phases. Terms and conditions are due to be honoured, and deposits will remain protected under the Financial Services Compensation Scheme. Tesco will retain certain activities outside the scope of the sale, including its insurance and other ancillary services, and will continue to market Tesco-branded products under the new distribution arrangement. Employees directly supporting the transferring operations are expected to move to Barclays under existing employment protections.

The sale marks the latest retreat by UK supermarkets from owning full-service banks, following Tesco’s earlier exits from current accounts and mortgages. Rising regulatory and funding costs, higher technology investment requirements and intense competition from specialist lenders and fintechs have pushed grocers to seek partnerships rather than operate stand-alone banks. Analysts said the deal should provide Tesco with upfront proceeds and ongoing income from the branding alliance, while giving Barclays a larger book of card receivables and a broadened pipeline of retail customers.

Completion is subject to customary approvals, including change-of-control clearances, and is expected to occur later this year. Until then, Tesco Bank will continue to serve customers as usual. Both companies said they would communicate any required actions well in advance of migration, and that service levels and support channels would be maintained throughout the transition.

Flights were disrupted and parts of Gatwick Airport were cordoned off on Thursday after a security alert over a suspect package, with two people subsequently detained in connection with the incident, police said. The pair were stopped by officers at the airport shortly after the discovery, and were being questioned on Thursday evening. No injuries were reported.

Bomb disposal experts were called to assess the package and a controlled safety protocol was carried out at the scene. Sussex Police said the situation was brought under control within hours and there was no indication of any wider threat.

Passengers described being ushered away from shops and check-in desks as announcements instructed travellers to leave belongings and move to designated points. “Everyone stayed calm, but it was unsettling,” said one traveller who had been queuing for a short-haul flight. Another passenger reported missing their boarding slot as airlines paused check-in.

Gatwick officials said some departures were delayed and a small number of flights were diverted or held on stand during the alert, though the runway remained open. Operations in the affected areas resumed gradually once the terminal was declared safe, but airlines warned of knock-on delays into the evening as schedules were re-sequenced. Travellers were urged to check with their carriers and allow extra time for security screening.

Police did not provide details about the detained individuals or the nature of the package, citing the ongoing investigation. Additional patrols were visible across both terminals following the incident. Airport management thanked passengers for their patience and said staff would work to minimise further disruption, adding that safety “will always come first.” Authorities appealed for anyone with information or footage from the area around the time of the discovery to come forward.

Police Scotland has confirmed it is considering a formal request to deploy public order officers to Northern Ireland after consecutive nights of rioting left multiple people injured and caused significant damage to businesses and public infrastructure. Senior officers said contingency plans are being drawn up in case a mutual aid operation is triggered, a standard mechanism that allows forces across the UK to share resources during major incidents.

Assistant Chief Constable Laura MacDonald said specialist units trained in evidence gathering, crowd management and riot control were being identified for potential short-notice mobilisation. “We are in close contact with colleagues in Northern Ireland and with the National Police Coordination Centre,” she said. “If a request is made and authorised, we will respond swiftly while maintaining essential policing services across Scotland.” She stressed any deployment would be risk-assessed, with appropriate protective equipment and welfare support in place.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland has been under intense pressure after sporadic violence flared in several urban areas, where officers faced petrol bombs, fireworks and makeshift barricades. The unrest has led to a number of arrests and injuries among both officers and members of the public. Community leaders have appealed for calm as investigators review CCTV and body-worn footage to identify ringleaders.

Scottish ministers signalled they would back a mutual aid deployment if required. A Scottish Government spokesperson said safeguarding the public was the “overriding priority” and that costs associated with any operation would be recouped under established agreements. The Scottish Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, said it supported mutual assistance in principle but urged “robust guarantees” on officer safety, rest provisions and clear command structures on the ground.

Civil liberties groups called for a proportionate response and renewed efforts at community mediation. No final decision on deployment had been taken on Wednesday evening, but sources indicated an assessment of numbers, transport options and shift patterns was under way, with clarity expected within 24 to 48 hours if disorder persists.

An Israeli airstrike hit a UN-run school sheltering displaced families in Gaza, reportedly killing at least 35 people, according to local health officials and the UN agency for Palestinian refugees. Medics said dozens more were wounded, many of them women and children, as emergency crews worked through mangled classrooms and courtyards strewn with debris. The Israel Defense Forces said it was targeting militants it alleged were operating from within or adjacent to the compound and said the incident is under review.

UNRWA said thousands of people had been sleeping in the school after fleeing fighting elsewhere and reiterated that its facilities are civilian sites protected under international law. The agency called for an independent investigation and renewed safe passage for aid and evacuations, warning that repeated strikes on shelters have eroded any sense of refuge for displaced families. It denied that its premises are used for military purposes.

The IDF said it takes steps to minimize civilian harm and accused armed groups of embedding within densely populated areas and civilian infrastructure, a charge those groups deny. There was no immediate release of evidence to substantiate claims about militant activity at the school. Independent verification of battlefield accounts remains difficult amid ongoing hostilities and periodic communications blackouts.

The strike comes as fighting intensifies across several areas of the enclave, where hospitals report being overwhelmed and short of fuel, anesthesia, and surgical supplies. Humanitarian organizations say that repeated hits on protected sites, including schools and clinics, risk violating the laws of war and underscore the need for stricter adherence to precautions in attack. International officials renewed calls for accountability and for all parties to distinguish between civilians and combatants.

Tens of thousands of people have been killed in Gaza since the war began, according to local health authorities, with many more displaced multiple times. Israel launched its campaign after Hamas-led attacks that killed civilians and took hostages, vowing to dismantle the group.

The hymns are barely above a whisper. In a shuttered apartment on the edge of a major Iranian city, a dozen worshippers stand shoulder to shoulder around a low table, a single candle pooling light over a cracked Bible and a plate of sweets. It is Easter Sunday, but there are no bells or choirs here—only the creak of the floorboards and the soft murmur of a prayer said quickly, in case someone is listening.

“We come because we need the story of resurrection,” says “Mina,” a convert who asked that her real name not be used for security reasons. “But we also come with our shoes on, ready to leave if we must.” She glances at the door, where a coat rack has become a makeshift cross draped with a scarf.

Iran’s constitution recognizes historic Christian minorities—chiefly Armenian and Assyrian communities—with reserved parliamentary seats and centuries-old churches. But Persian-speaking converts face far stricter limits, and rights groups say authorities have closed Farsi-language services and detained scores of people over their religious activity, particularly around major holidays. Security forces have periodically raided informal gatherings, accusing attendees of acting against national security. Officials deny targeting citizens for their beliefs, saying the state responds to illegal proselytizing and foreign influence.

The small congregation here has pared Easter to its essentials. There is no public procession, no choir rehearsal, no printed programs. A child is hushed as an elder reads the resurrection story by memory. The bread is broken quietly; the cup is passed hand to hand. “We try not to sing,” says “Arash,” an organizer. “We listen.”

In parts of Tehran and Isfahan, recognized churches still fill with families speaking Armenian or Assyrian; some congregations restrict access to registered members and conduct services in their traditional languages. For converts who cannot enter those sanctuaries, the holiday moves into kitchens and back rooms, its joy folded into caution.

When the candle is finally snuffed, someone whispers, “Next year, maybe openly.” No one answers, but smiles flicker in the dark.

Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson has signalled she is “open‑minded” about outlawing the smacking of children in England, saying she will consider evidence from Scotland and Wales alongside the views of parents, teachers and child‑protection experts. “I want to be led by what works to keep children safe and support families,” she said, while stressing there were “no immediate plans” and that any move would follow “careful consultation and cross‑government discussion.”

England and Northern Ireland remain the only parts of the UK where parents can still claim a defence of “reasonable punishment” for common assault. Campaigners argue that leaves children with weaker protections than adults and sends a confusing message about violence in the home. The NSPCC and children’s charities welcomed Phillipson’s tone, saying a ban would align the law with modern understanding of child development and the harms of physical punishment. “Positive, non‑violent discipline is more effective and safer,” one charity said.

Opponents, including some Conservative backbenchers and parental groups, warned a ban could criminalise “ordinary mums and dads” for momentary lapses and place extra pressure on stretched police and social services. They called instead for more parenting support and early‑help programmes. Teaching unions said clear, consistent messaging on non‑violent discipline would be helpful in schools, but urged ministers to pair any change with investment in family services.

Any reform would likely require primary legislation to remove the reasonable‑punishment defence and updated guidance for police, prosecutors and social workers. Ministers are expected to study the rollout in Wales and Scotland, where officials emphasised early on that low‑level incidents should be addressed through education and support rather than prosecution. Early monitoring there has not shown a surge in court cases, according to government updates.

Phillipson said the Department for Education would work with the Ministry of Justice and Home Office on next steps. “We’ll look carefully at the evidence and listen to families. No decisions have been made,” she said.

A mother of two being treated for a rare cancer linked to breast implants is urging others to learn the warning signs and ask questions at routine check-ups. Emma Lewis, 39, from Bristol, was diagnosed last summer with breast implant–associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), an uncommon cancer of the immune system that forms in the scar tissue and fluid around an implant rather than in the breast itself. She had textured implants placed after cosmetic surgery in 2012 and says she first noticed one breast becoming “suddenly fuller and tight” more than a decade later.

“I’d never heard of this,” Lewis said. “If I had, I would have known that swelling years after surgery isn’t normal. I don’t want to frighten anyone, but people deserve clear information so they can act early.”

Regulators in several countries have identified an association between BIA-ALCL and certain textured implants; some models were recalled in 2019. The condition remains rare: international registries and health agencies estimate risks ranging from roughly 1 in 3,000 to 1 in 30,000 among people with textured devices, varying by implant type and time in place. Most reported cases present years after implantation with persistent swelling, a buildup of fluid, breast firmness, or a new lump.

Specialists stress that the vast majority of implant recipients will never develop BIA-ALCL and that smooth implants appear to carry a much lower risk. Routine removal of asymptomatic implants is not recommended by regulators, who advise patients to attend regular health checks and to seek medical assessment for any changes. An even rarer tumor, squamous cell carcinoma arising in the tissue capsule, has also been reported in isolated cases.

Lewis, now undergoing treatment following surgery to remove her implants and surrounding tissue, says she hopes sharing her experience will prompt clearer consent discussions. “Cosmetic or reconstructive, people should be told the risks—however small—so they can make an informed choice,” she said.

Lewis Hamilton said he “could not be more excited” as his Ferrari career formally begins, describing the switch as a fresh challenge and “a dream many years in the making.” The seven-time world champion arrived in Maranello to a rapturous welcome from the Tifosi, completing a seat fit, simulator sessions and a shakedown run at Fiorano as he acclimatised to life in red. Hamilton, who left Mercedes after 11 seasons and six titles with the Brackley team, framed the move as both a personal reset and a bid to help restore Ferrari to title-winning contention.

“This team’s history is unmatched, and the passion is on another level,” Hamilton said. “I’m here to learn fast, bring my experience, and push everyone—including myself. I could not be more excited to get started.”

Ferrari last won the drivers’ championship in 2007 and the constructors’ crown in 2008. Team principal Frédéric Vasseur has long argued that Hamilton’s racecraft and development instincts can be decisive in tight title fights, while pairing him with Charles Leclerc gives Ferrari one of the grid’s most formidable line-ups. Internally, the focus has been on building consistent race pace and operational sharpness after seasons defined by flashes of speed offset by narrow margins and strategic missteps.

Hamilton acknowledged the weight of expectation but rejected the notion that pressure would be a burden. “The standards here are sky-high. That’s why you come—because you want to meet them,” he said. “We’re not making promises, but we’re committed to doing the work.”

Early mileage will center on correlation between wind tunnel data and on-track behaviour, alongside fine-tuning Hamilton’s preference for braking stability and rear-end confidence. With pre-season running imminent and the opener fast approaching, Ferrari hopes an experienced new voice can convert potential into points from the outset, turning anticipation into momentum.

Anna Henderson delivered a composed, quietly ferocious ride to secure silver in the women’s individual time trial, handing Team GB its first cycling medal of the Games as Josh Tarling later missed the men’s podium by agonising seconds. On a twitchy, wind-prone course that rewarded rhythm as much as raw power, Henderson settled early into a low, unwavering position, threading the fastest lines through a series of tight urban corners before emptying the tank on the exposed run-in. She trailed the eventual champion by a narrow margin at the first time check, but clawed back time on the rolling middle sector and held her nerve under pressure to post a mark that proved good enough for second.

“I knew the middle part would decide it,” Henderson said. “We’d mapped out where to be patient and where to commit, and I hit those targets. You don’t get many chances like this. I’m proud of how I paced it and proud to bring a medal home.”

British Cycling performance staff hailed the execution as “near-flawless,” noting Henderson’s clean cornering and even negative splits despite strengthening crosswinds. The medal underscores her continued evolution from promising all-rounder to world-class specialist against the clock.

Tarling, who started among the late seeds in the men’s race, looked on course for a medal through the opening split, only to cede time as gusts picked up and the course tipped subtly upward. The 20-year-old fought to stabilise his cadence on the final sector but slipped off the virtual podium in the last kilometres, ultimately finishing just outside the medals.

“It stings,” Tarling admitted. “I was right there and didn’t quite finish it off. That said, I committed to the plan, and there’s a lot to take forward. I’ll be back.”

Attention for Team GB now pivots to the road races, buoyed by Henderson’s silver and encouraged by Tarling’s form despite the narrow miss.

As cardinals gather in Rome to elect the next leader of the Roman Catholic Church, Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David of Kalookan enters the conclave with a reputation forged on Manila’s gritty streets and in an era of political confrontation at home. The 67-year-old prelate, known widely as “Bishop Ambo,” became one of the most prominent ecclesial voices against the Philippines’ bloody anti-drug campaign under then-President Rodrigo Duterte, presiding over funerals, consoling widows and orphans, and urging accountability for thousands of killings documented by rights groups.

During those tense years, David faced online harassment, legal threats and public taunts from Duterte, but he did not step back. He expanded parish-based support for grieving families, encouraged rehabilitation efforts for users seeking treatment, and repeatedly framed the Church’s response as a defense of life and human dignity. In Rome, Pope Francis signaled support for bishops under pressure in the Philippines and gave David a platform in the Church’s global conversations, later elevating him to the College of Cardinals. Colleagues say that trajectory — from a diocese synonymous with the drug war’s toll to the upper ranks of the hierarchy — reflects Francis’ preference for pastors rooted in the “peripheries,” attentive to the poor and unafraid to challenge abuses.

Now one of more than a hundred cardinal-electors convening behind closed doors, David brings to the Sistine Chapel the experience of shepherding a community that has confronted fear, violence and impunity. Allies in the Philippine Church describe him as a careful listener steeped in Scripture and social realities; critics of his advocacy once accused him of politicizing the pulpit. His supporters counter that his stance drew from the Church’s longstanding teaching on the sanctity of life and the rule of law.

Whatever emerges from the balloting, David’s path to the conclave underscores how the global Church under Francis has elevated voices from places where faith is lived amid frailty and fracture — and how those voices may now help shape its future.

After the mauling in Mumbai, the task facing head coach Brendon McCullum is unambiguous: restore clarity of method without stripping England of the daring that has defined his tenure. India’s spinners prised open technical and mental gaps on a sharply responsive surface, and England’s ultra-attacking instincts—so often a weapon—too frequently turned into a release valve. The sweep and reverse-sweep, cornerstones of their approach to subcontinental spin, appeared premeditated rather than situational, inviting fields and lengths that magnified risk. When the ball bit and bounced, indecision followed.

Selection is now as much a philosophical question as a tactical one. England crave control through spin but remain short on proven, long-haul operators in Asian conditions. Balancing a frontline slow-bowling trio with enough batting depth and a wicketkeeper comfortable standing up to the stumps is central to recalibrating. The seam attack, blunted in the heat and humidity, needs a plan that prizes relentlessness—reducing boundary options, exploiting reverse swing late, and accepting that maidens can matter more than miracle balls.

For the batting core, the next steps look less about tempering intent than sequencing it. England’s best passages under McCullum have mixed early information-gathering with targeted bursts of pressure; that rhythm deserted them as collapses followed clustered errors. Expect training to emphasize late contact, hitting with the spin, and clearer decision trees against the ball turning away from the bat. Just as vital is a renewed appetite for attrition: rotating singles, trusting the forward press, riding sessions where 2.5 runs an over is a win.

McCullum’s strength has been cultural: simplicity of message, conviction in players. He will need both now. There is no quick fix in India, only adherence to plans under duress. England do not have to abandon their identity; they must prove it can stretch to the Wankhede as well as to home comforts. The next Test will reveal whether boldness can be backed by discipline.

Welsh ministers have warned that up to £1bn of planned spending could be jeopardised if opposition parties refuse to support the government’s draft budget in the Senedd, ahead of a crunch vote expected next week. The finance minister said failure to pass the package on time would trigger contingency arrangements that cap monthly spending and delay new allocations, forcing health boards, councils and transport operators to pause or scale back programmes. Officials say some capital projects and time‑limited funds tied to the end of the financial year could be lost or pushed into higher-cost delivery, with knock‑on effects for NHS waiting times, school maintenance, housing and flood defences.

Opposition parties accused the government of manufacturing a crisis, insisting the threats are “scare tactics” designed to avoid scrutiny of what they describe as misdirected priorities. The Welsh Conservatives have called for deeper cuts to back‑office costs and non-essential programmes to channel more money into frontline NHS and social care, while Plaid Cymru wants stronger commitments on local government funding and rural services. The Liberal Democrats have pressed for additional mental health support and targeted help for small businesses facing higher rates bills.

Ministers insist the fiscal envelope is “extremely tight” after inflation, higher pay pressures and a smaller-than-expected uplift in the block grant, arguing that significant changes would require offsetting reductions elsewhere. They say they remain open to “targeted adjustments” if parties engage “constructively,” but warn that prolonged deadlock would increase costs and uncertainty. Senior officials have briefed committee chairs that procurement timetables, borrowing plans and grant profiles are aligned to the current budget, and that slippage could void matched funding or breach delivery milestones.

If the budget is defeated, the government could bring back a revised plan or seek short-term authorisation to keep services running under temporary limits. Business groups urged all sides to reach a deal, citing the risk to construction pipelines and skills programmes. Trade unions similarly pressed for certainty, warning that delays would complicate pay talks and workforce planning.

Downing Street has insisted the government’s multi‑year spending review is “now settled,” seeking to draw a line under days of speculation about fresh bids for cash from Whitehall departments amid mounting cost pressures. A No 10 spokesperson said departmental budgets had been confirmed and would not be reopened, with ministers instructed to “deliver on the priorities the public expects within the agreed envelopes.”

The government said those priorities include cutting NHS waiting times, maintaining defence commitments, improving transport reliability, expanding childcare provision and accelerating energy security and net zero investments. Officials indicated that any emerging pressures from higher‑than‑anticipated inflation or pay settlements would be met through reprioritisation and efficiency savings, rather than additional top‑ups. “We are focused on outcomes, not just inputs,” the spokesperson said, adding that the Chancellor would set out implementation details in Parliament in the coming days.

The reassurance follows lobbying by several departments highlighting rising bills for public sector pay, asylum accommodation, school maintenance and prison capacity. Treasury sources said a small central reserve would be retained for “genuinely unforeseen events,” but stressed that routine overspends would not be underwritten. Capital programmes face a tighter squeeze, with some lower‑value or lower‑readiness projects expected to be delayed to protect frontline services.

Opposition parties accused ministers of “papering over cracks,” warning that flat cash settlements in real terms risk further strain on local councils and policing. Unions urged the government to guarantee that agreed pay awards would be fully funded to avoid cuts elsewhere. Business groups welcomed the clarity but called for “predictable delivery timetables” on infrastructure and skills, arguing that repeated resets erode investor confidence.

Devolved administrations are awaiting confirmation of consequential funding, with officials in Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast pressing for flexibility to carry over underspends. Senior backbenchers privately signalled they would judge the review by its impact on waiting lists, classroom standards and crime, underscoring No 10’s message that delivery, rather than additional announcements, will now be the measure of success.

For days the kilted carnival rolled through Germany—pipe bands at breakfast, impromptu ceilidhs by mid-afternoon, and choruses of “No Scotland, No Party” swelling at dusk. By the small hours in Stuttgart, though, the soundtrack had thinned to zip ties on bin bags and the scrape of plastic cups across cobbles. A stoppage‑time winner against Scotland turned the fan zone’s roar into a groan, and with it the Tartan Army’s summer adventure slipped from celebration to farewell.

On the pitch, Scotland had played with the nervy bravery that has become their tournament hallmark—stretches of controlled possession, a handful of half‑chances, and a penalty appeal that flickered, then died, under the cold light of review. The margins were always going to be cruel. When the decisive counter arrived deep into added time, it broke not only the line but the spell that had enchanted host cities since opening night.

Outside, the reaction was stoic rather than stormy. Flags were folded, not flung. In Schlossplatz, supporters posed for one last photo before helping stewards gather litter into neat piles—another night of good‑humoured order that endeared them to locals and police alike. Pubs that had set record takings all week called last orders to a smattering of applause for bar staff; the streets, awash in navy and saltire blue at sunset, drained quietly toward tram stops and night trains.

Travel apps glowed with rebooked flights to Glasgow and Edinburgh, while hotel clerks swapped extension requests for early checkouts. There was pride, if not solace, in the manner of the send‑off: applause for the players who trudged over to say thanks, scarves aloft for a final chorus, then the recognisable shuffle toward tomorrow.

Attention turns now to the next campaign and the perennial Scottish arithmetic of hope and hard lessons. The party may be over, but anyone who has heard that song rise from a distant square knows it never stays quiet for long.

Twickenham expects a show as England return home knowing substance alone may not be enough. Victory is non‑negotiable to keep their Six Nations ambitions alive, but the message from the camp all week has been just as much about tone: quicker ruck speed, bolder decisions with ball in hand, and the kind of attacking clarity that can turn pressure into points and, crucially, a bonus point. Selection hints point to extra zip across the backline and greater mobility in the pack, with an emphasis on distributing forwards and varied runners out wide. The hosts want tempo from the first whistle, and with it a more ruthless edge inside the 22 where, in recent campaigns, opportunities too often bled away.

Italy arrive emboldened by steady gains over the past two seasons and a growing refusal to play to type. Their breakdown contest has teeth, their kicking game is more purposeful, and they carry real counterattacking threat through evasive backs who punish loose exits. They have not beaten England in the championship, but recent away‑day upsets elsewhere serve as a timely caution for any side that drifts. Disrupt England’s set‑piece rhythm, squeeze the nine and ten, and the noise of a restless crowd can quickly turn into opportunity.

Key battles will pivot on control: England’s scrum and line‑out accuracy against Italian spoiling, discipline at the contact to avoid inviting territory, and the aerial exchanges that so often tilt momentum. Tactical kicking will matter, but the hosts have spoken of variety—short passes to punch around the corner, double‑pull shapes to stress the edges, and strike moves on turnover ball rather than settling for reset phases.

For England, the stakes are twofold: bank the result and convince their supporters that evolution is underway. For Italy, the brief is simpler—hang in, hang on, and make belief spread. Either way, the margin for error is thin, and the championship arithmetic may hinge on style as much as score.

Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson has said trans women should use toilets based on their biological sex, arguing that clearer, consistent rules are needed across schools and public services to reduce confusion and conflict. The stance, she said, is intended to protect the integrity of single-sex spaces while expanding availability of alternative, single-occupancy facilities for anyone who prefers them.

Officials confirmed the position will inform forthcoming guidance for schools, hospitals and other public buildings, with an emphasis on providing a mix of female-only and male-only toilets alongside more self-contained, gender-neutral cubicles. Ministers say the approach aims to balance dignity and privacy for all users, including trans people, while giving institutions a clearer legal footing when setting policies.

Phillipson’s remarks align with Labour’s pledge to clarify equality law so that service providers can more confidently maintain single-sex spaces where justified. The government is consulting with regulators and service leaders on practical implications, including signage, safeguarding, supervision in education settings, and the costs of retrofitting older estates.

The comments drew sharply divided reactions. Women’s rights groups largely welcomed what they called long-overdue clarity, saying it would enhance safeguarding and privacy. LGBTQ+ organisations warned the approach risks further marginalising trans people and could expose them to greater harassment if gender-neutral provision is limited or poorly implemented. Some headteachers and NHS managers cautioned that upgrading facilities at pace will be challenging without dedicated funding and detailed, sector-specific guidance.

Phillipson insisted support for trans pupils, patients and staff remains central, highlighting plans for staff training, case-by-case pastoral support in schools, and clear routes to gender-neutral options. Opposition critics accused the government of fuelling a culture-war row; Conservatives said Labour was belatedly aligning with their approach, while some on the left called it a retreat from earlier inclusive rhetoric. Legal experts noted that any change in practice will hinge on how “biological sex” is defined in statute and how exemptions in equality law are applied in specific services.

Southampton’s home league match was postponed on Saturday after a major fire broke out at an industrial site close to St Mary’s Stadium, sending thick smoke across surrounding roads and residential areas. The decision was confirmed less than two hours before the scheduled kick-off, following consultations between match officials, the club and emergency services. Supporters already en route were advised not to travel to the ground, while those in the vicinity were directed away from closed perimeter routes as crews worked to contain the blaze.

Flames and a dense plume were visible from the stadium concourses, prompting stewards to suspend entry and keep turnstiles shut as a precaution. Emergency services established a cordon and urged residents to keep windows closed, citing concerns about air quality. Several local bus routes were diverted and traffic built up on main approaches to the city centre as road closures were put in place. There were no immediate reports of injuries, and the cause of the fire has not yet been established.

In a statement, the club said the safety of supporters, staff and players was paramount and confirmed that tickets would remain valid for the rearranged fixture. Details on a new date and any necessary refund procedures will be communicated in due course after discussions with the league and the visiting team. The squad and stadium personnel were reported to be safe, with access to non-public areas restricted while the situation developed nearby.

Fans who had gathered around the stadium were directed to leave the area calmly, and public-address announcements urged people to follow instructions from stewards and police. Local authorities asked motorists to avoid the affected routes to allow emergency vehicles clear passage. Fire investigators are expected to begin an assessment once the site is deemed secure, but officials warned that disruption could continue into the evening as damping-down operations proceed and structural checks are carried out.

If pop has felt a little too polished lately, Chappell Roan is here to muss the glitter. The 26-year-old singer, born Kayleigh Rose Amstutz in Missouri, has built a fervent following by treating the stage like a drag runway and the dance floor like a church revival. She arrives in towering wigs, clown-red lips and shoulder pads you could see from the cheap seats, then belts diaristic hooks about queer longing, bad decisions and being gloriously too much. It’s freaky, it’s fun, and—crucially—it’s precise: Roan’s songs crackle with crisp synths, sticky melodies and a wink that keeps her catharsis from curdling.

Her breakout came in waves. Early cult favorite “Pink Pony Club” sketched her origin story: a small-town dreamer discovering the life-saving excess of the club. TikTok canonized the spelling-bee choreography to “HOT TO GO!,” and this spring’s “Good Luck, Babe!” vaulted from a queer-bar staple to bona fide hit, a kiss-off so euphoric it sounds like fireworks ricocheting around a roller rink. The through-line is theatrical honesty—camp as an amplifier for feeling, not a mask to hide behind.

Roan’s world extends offstage. Each tour stop comes with a dress code—mermaids, prom, “your gay awakening”—and she routinely spotlights local drag performers as openers, a meaningful gesture as queens face mounting political backlash. Fans, many of them young and newly out, show up bedazzled and loud, finding community in the line outside the venue before the doors even open. It’s as close to a traveling queer prom as pop currently offers.

Musically, Roan’s palette nods to neon-soaked ’80s synth-pop and the kitchen-sink maximalism of modern indie-pop, but her voice—husky, elastic, theatrically exasperated—keeps the spectacle anchored. After high-profile support slots and buzzy festival appearances, she’s not just having a moment; she’s building a movement, one lipstick-smeared anthem at a time. In a year crowded with careful branding, Roan’s audacity feels like the real headline.

A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder following the deaths of three women in Bushey, Hertfordshire, in what police believe was a targeted attack involving a crossbow. Hertfordshire Constabulary said officers detained a 26-year-old man on Wednesday afternoon after an intensive overnight search that involved armed units, specialist dog teams and support from the National Police Air Service. He was found in the Enfield area with injuries and taken to hospital, where he remains under police guard. Detectives said they are not seeking anyone else in connection with the incident.

Emergency services were called to a property on Ashlyn Close just before 7pm on Tuesday, where three women were pronounced dead at the scene. Formal identification has not yet taken place, but next of kin have been informed and specially trained officers are supporting relatives. Post-mortem examinations will be carried out in due course. Police said a crossbow is believed to have been used and that other weapons may also have been involved, though no shots were fired by attending officers.

Detective Superintendent Rob Hall described the killings as “horrific” and urged anyone with information or relevant footage from the surrounding area between 5pm and 8pm on Tuesday to come forward. Officers conducted house-to-house inquiries overnight and increased patrols remain in place to reassure residents rattled by the violence. The quiet cul-de-sac was cordoned off through Wednesday as forensic teams examined the scene and collected evidence.

Local leaders expressed shock and offered condolences to the victims’ family, while community groups set up vigils and support hubs. The Home Office said it is liaising with police and noted that work is under way to review controls on powerful crossbows, which are currently legal to own without a licence in the UK. Anyone with information is urged to contact Hertfordshire Constabulary or Crimestoppers anonymously.

Peter Sullivan, who has always protested his innocence, had his 1988 conviction for the 1986 murder of a young woman quashed by the Court of Appeal on Thursday after judges ruled key evidence had been withheld from his defence and fresh forensic analysis undermined the case against him. In a unanimous judgment, Lord Justice Hale said the conviction was “unsafe,” citing undisclosed police notes pointing to an alternative suspect and modern DNA testing that excluded Sullivan from items central to the prosecution’s timeline.

Sullivan, now in his early 60s, served more than three decades in prison before being released on licence in 2021. Speaking outside court, he said: “I lost my family, my future, and the years you can’t get back. Today doesn’t give me those years, but it gives me my name.” His legal team thanked the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) for referring the case after a two-year re-examination of the original investigation.

According to documents disclosed during the appeal, detectives failed to share witness statements describing a man seen near the crime scene who did not match Sullivan, and relied heavily on hair-comparison techniques later discredited. A partial DNA profile recovered from preserved exhibits, tested with contemporary methods, was found not to be Sullivan’s.

The police force involved issued an apology “for the distress caused” and announced an independent review of the investigation. “Standards and practices have evolved considerably since the 1980s,” a spokesperson said. “We will cooperate fully with any further scrutiny.”

The Crown Prosecution Service said it would not seek a retrial, acknowledging there was no longer a realistic prospect of conviction. Sullivan’s solicitor confirmed he will pursue compensation under Section 133 of the Criminal Justice Act, while calling for a broader inquiry into disclosure failures. Campaigners against miscarriages of justice welcomed the ruling but urged ministers to reform evidence retention and oversight, warning that “systemic blind spots” risk more wrongful convictions.

Fiona Harvey, the Scottish woman who publicly identified herself as the real-life inspiration for the stalker character in Netflix’s hit drama Baby Reindeer, says she will sue both the streamer and the show’s creator and star, Richard Gadd. In statements made following a wave of attention sparked by the series, Harvey alleges the program defamed her by leading viewers to believe she is a criminal stalker and by failing to take adequate steps to prevent her being identified. She also claims she has suffered severe harassment online, reputational damage and distress since the show’s release. Harvey denies stalking Gadd or engaging in any criminal behavior and says the portrayal misrepresents events.

Representatives for Harvey say legal filings are being prepared and could include claims for defamation, misuse of private information and negligence, with damages expected to be substantial. They add that action may be pursued in more than one jurisdiction. Netflix has previously said Baby Reindeer is a dramatized work and that names and details were changed, while Gadd has publicly urged viewers not to speculate about real identities. Asked about the threatened lawsuit, a Netflix spokesperson declined to comment on potential litigation. Gadd’s representatives did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The limited series, which Gadd wrote and in which he plays a version of himself, became one of Netflix’s most-watched titles this spring, drawing critical acclaim and igniting intense online sleuthing. Legal analysts note that defamation claims over fictionalized works often turn on whether a reasonable viewer could identify a real person from the portrayal and whether key allegations are false. If Harvey proceeds, the case could test how far “based on a true story” dramas can go while relying on disclaimers.

Harvey’s lawyers say pre-action correspondence has been sent and that they expect to file suit soon. No hearing date has been set, and neither side has provided a detailed timeline for next steps.

A U.S. food scientist has stirred a transatlantic tempest in a teacup by recommending a pinch of salt as the final step to a “perfect” brew, arguing that sodium ions help blunt bitterness and coax out sweetness without making the drink taste briny. The advice, shared this week by sensory chemist Dr. Lauren Mitchell during a webinar on beverage flavor, suggests adding only a few grains—“far less than a shake,” she emphasized—either to the pot or the cup immediately after steeping.

“We’re not seasoning tea like soup,” Mitchell said. “At vanishingly low levels, sodium suppresses bitter receptors and softens astringency from polyphenols like catechins and theaflavins. The result is rounder, smoother tea, especially in hard-water regions.”

Mitchell’s lab tests compared identical black-tea infusions with and without salt across multiple water profiles. In blind tastings of 48 panelists, lightly salted brews were preferred 68% of the time, particularly when prepared with very hard water, she said. The recommended dose: roughly two or three crystals per mug, or a tiny pinch—no more than 0.3 grams per liter—added after a 3–4 minute steep. “If you can taste salt, you added too much,” she said.

The guidance rapidly drew sharp responses from British tea traditionalists. “Over my teapot,” wrote one Londoner on X, while others invoked long-standing etiquette debates about milk-first versus tea-first. “Salt is not part of British tea culture,” said Maya Clark, a UK-based tea historian. “But as a corrective for bitterness in poor water, it’s not heresy—just unusual.”

Mitchell paired the salt tip with familiar fundamentals: start with freshly boiled water, pre-warm the pot, don’t squeeze the bag, and avoid oversteeping. For green and oolong teas, she advised cooler water and even greater restraint with salt. “It’s a tool, not a rule,” she said. “If your tea already tastes great, skip it. But if it’s harsh, a barely-there pinch can make it sing.”

An American spacecraft that had been heading for the Moon has been destroyed after re-entering Earth’s atmosphere over the South Pacific.

The Peregrine lander was in space for just over 10 days. It lifted off from Cape Canaveral in Florida on 8 January, but a propellant leak discovered shortly after launch made a lunar landing impossible.

Astrobotic, the Pittsburgh company that built and operated the spacecraft, said it lost contact with Peregrine at about 20:59 GMT on Thursday, 18 January, at the time it was expected to re-enter. The company had directed the lander towards a remote stretch of ocean to minimise the risk of any surviving debris reaching populated areas.

Although engineers could not stop the leak, they managed to turn the spacecraft so that its solar panels faced the Sun, allowing it to recharge its batteries. That bought the team time to switch on several of the instruments and collect data before the mission ended.

Peregrine carried five NASA payloads, including instruments designed to study the radiation environment and look for signs of water on the Moon. It was the first mission to launch under a NASA programme that pays private companies to deliver scientific equipment to the lunar surface, rather than building and operating the landers itself.

The failure dashed hopes that Peregrine would make the first American soft landing on the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. The launch itself, the debut flight of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket, had put the spacecraft on its intended trajectory. The problem developed after the lander separated from the rocket.

Another American company, Intuitive Machines, was preparing to send its own lander to the Moon as early as February. Astrobotic, meanwhile, was already working on a larger lander, Griffin, intended to carry a NASA rover to the lunar south polar region.

If Ruben Amorim needed a live audit of the job awaiting him, the draw with Chelsea supplied it in stark, sequential chapters. United oscillated between surges of energy and long stretches of tactical drift, a team without stable distances between the lines. When they pressed, the front three jumped, but the midfield arrived a beat late; when they sat off, the back four dropped too deep, inviting Chelsea to play between them and turn. The result was a familiar pattern: hurried clearances, second balls conceded, transitions defended in retreat rather than on the front foot.

Amorim’s Sporting sides are defined by synchronized pressing and a clear rest-defense, often from a back three with aggressive wing-backs. United looked miles from that cohesion. Full-backs were caught in two minds, neither pinning the touchline nor tucking in decisively, while the wide forwards offered inconsistent cover to their flanks. In possession, Bruno Fernandes roamed to spark something, but the rotations around him felt improvised; Hojlund was isolated for long spells, and United’s best moments came from individual breaks rather than rehearsed patterns. Set pieces, too, underlined the workload: zonal assignments were loose, the blocking and runs at attacking corners unrefined.

This is not a task of tweaks but of alignment. Personnel will matter—United lack a truly mobile holding midfielder to anchor Amorim’s transitions, and the pool of wide centre-backs comfortable defending big spaces is shallow—but the bigger shift is behavioral. Distances must shrink, triggers must be automatic, and fitness loads need to support a more aggressive approach.
