That demands time, absolute buy-in from senior players, and clarity in recruitment to match the model. The atmosphere around Old Trafford, taut and quick to turn, will not grant many grace periods. The draw made plain that flashes of talent are plentiful; frameworks that turn them into repeatable advantages are not.

ICICI Bank is facing scrutiny after an Indian woman alleged that a branch manager siphoned $1.9 million from her savings account, according to a complaint lodged with local police and financial authorities. The customer, a business owner in her 40s, says a series of unauthorized transfers and redemptions were executed over an extended period, allegedly exploiting her long-standing relationship with the branch. The withdrawals, which she claims she did not authorize, totaled roughly Rs 16 crore at current exchange rates.

The irregularities came to light during a routine review of her finances, when the woman noticed multiple high-value debits and unfamiliar beneficiary accounts in recent statements. She says initial requests for clarification were met with vague assurances and delays, prompting her to seek independent advice and formally escalate the matter. Her complaint names a branch manager and several unknown beneficiaries, and alleges falsification of records and misuse of internal systems. None of these claims has been proven.

In a brief statement, ICICI Bank said it takes such allegations very seriously, has initiated an internal review, and is cooperating with law-enforcement agencies. The bank declined to comment on individual customers or staff while inquiries are under way, citing confidentiality. The status of the employee identified in the complaint could not be independently confirmed, and no charges had been announced at the time of publication.

Consumer-rights advocates said the case, if substantiated, would raise fresh questions about internal controls and maker-checker protocols in India’s banking sector. Under Reserve Bank of India guidelines, lenders are required to promptly report suspected fraud and apprise customers of material account activity. Legal experts note that banks can be held liable for losses stemming from employee misconduct, though recovery and restitution can take months or even years if civil and criminal proceedings run in parallel.

The complainant said she is seeking full restitution and assurances that similar incidents cannot recur.

New Zealand booked their place in the Women’s T20 World Cup semi-finals with a composed 28-run win over Pakistan, built on disciplined batting through the middle overs and an exacting display of spin and seam control with the ball. After being asked to bat, New Zealand posted 152 for 6, a total that always looked competitive on a surface offering grip for slow bowlers and variable bounce under lights. Suzie Bates anchored the innings with a measured 47, sharing a steadying stand with Amelia Kerr, whose 36 off 30 balls provided the shift in tempo after a cautious powerplay. Maddy Green added a brisk, unbeaten 28 to lift the total beyond 150, nudging and sweeping cleverly to exploit the vacant pockets as Pakistan’s death bowling otherwise held its lines.

Pakistan’s chase began brightly at 36 for 1 after six, but the innings stalled once New Zealand’s spinners took hold. Kerr’s leg-spin and Fran Jonas’s left-arm orthodox combined for figures of 4 for 40 across eight overs, cranking up the pressure with attacking fields and a tight stump-to-stump plan. Lea Tahuhu’s return at the death yielded two key wickets, including a slicing edge to third, as Pakistan were restricted to 124 for 8. Bismah Maroof top-scored with 35, while Muneeba Ali’s 27 promised more than it delivered before she was undone by a quicker one skidding on. Two sharp run-outs, the first from a direct hit at cover and the second off a quick relay from the deep, underlined New Zealand’s superior fielding.

The result confirms New Zealand’s progress from the group with one match to spare, while Pakistan are left needing favours elsewhere to keep faint mathematical hopes alive. For New Zealand, the balance between early restraint and late acceleration with the bat will please the coaching staff, as will the clarity of roles in the bowling unit ahead of a step up in opposition in the knockout phase.

Darwin Nunez marked his return from injury with a 99th-minute winner at the City Ground, heading Liverpool to a 1-0 victory over Nottingham Forest and sending Jurgen Klopp’s side four points clear at the top of the Premier League.

Liverpool had struggled to create clear chances and looked set to drop two points until Forest failed to clear a late corner. The ball came back to Alexis Mac Allister, who lifted a cross into the crowded penalty area. Nunez, who had come on shortly after the hour mark, glanced his header past Matz Sels and celebrated in front of the travelling supporters.

Forest had chances to win it themselves. Anthony Elanga broke clear in the first half but was denied by Caoimhin Kelleher, then sent a first-time effort wide after the break. Liverpool saw plenty of the ball without finding a way through, and Klopp turned to Nunez and Wataru Endo as the visitors chased a breakthrough.

The goal came after a disputed restart. Forest had possession when referee Paul Tierney stopped play because Liverpool defender Ibrahima Konate had gone down with a head injury. Tierney restarted with a dropped ball to Kelleher rather than returning possession to Forest. Nearly two minutes elapsed before Nunez scored, but the decision drew angry protests from the home side at the final whistle.

For Liverpool, it was a first league win at the City Ground since 1984 and a narrow escape in a tight title race. Nunez had missed the previous three matches, including the League Cup final victory over Chelsea, but his return gave Klopp a decisive option from the bench. The result put pressure on second-placed Manchester City, who could cut the gap back to a point when they faced Manchester United the following day.

The parents of a toddler who was killed by a runaway car say they have been “utterly let down” after no one was prosecuted over her death.

Pearl Black, who was 22 months old, was walking with her father and brother in Heolgerrig, Merthyr Tydfil, in August 2017 when a Range Rover rolled down a sloping driveway. The vehicle struck a wall, which collapsed onto the family.

Pearl’s parents said they could not understand how a parked car could roll onto a road and kill their daughter without anyone being held criminally responsible.

The fact that the vehicle had been parked on private property was central to the decision not to bring charges. Road traffic offences generally apply to conduct on a road or in a public place. In Pearl’s case, the vehicle reached the road only after it had begun to move, with nobody at the wheel.

Her family said the distinction made little sense to them. They argued that the consequences for someone walking past were the same whether a vehicle had been left on a driveway or on the street.

They want the law reviewed so that, in future, prosecutors can consider how a vehicle was left on private land if it rolls into a public place and kills someone. They said a change in the law would not alter what happened to Pearl, but could spare another family the experience of being told that no charges could be brought.

For Pearl’s parents, the decision not to prosecute left a question separate from how their daughter died: whether the law adequately protects people on the road from vehicles parked just beyond it. They said they would continue pressing for a review so that the same distinction did not determine the outcome of another case.

Millions of bus passengers in England are set to pay more for local journeys after ministers confirmed the nationwide cap on single fares will rise by £1. The cap, introduced as a cost-of-living measure during the energy and inflation crisis, will increase from £2 to £3 on most routes outside London from early spring, with the Department for Transport saying the higher ceiling will remain in place for the rest of the financial year while support for operators is tapered.

The government argues the change balances help for passengers with mounting pressures on the industry, pointing to higher fuel, insurance and wage costs that have left many operators struggling to keep services running. Bus companies have lobbied for a higher limit or a return to market pricing, warning that frozen fares were becoming harder to sustain without additional subsidy, particularly on longer or lightly used routes.

Passenger groups and some local leaders warn the move could hit low-paid and rural riders hardest, where alternatives are limited and car ownership is lower. They fear even a £1 rise could reverse recent gains in ridership since the cap was introduced in January 2023, when usage recovered more quickly than expected in several towns and cities. Councils working on Bus Service Improvement Plans said they would monitor demand closely and consider targeted concessions if patronage drops.

The change does not affect London, where fares are set by Transport for London under a separate system. Devolved governments in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own arrangements and are not covered by the England-only cap.

Officials insist the cap remains a temporary intervention and say longer-term reforms, including local franchising powers and multi-operator ticketing, are intended to simplify fares and make services more reliable. The DfT said it would review the impact of the higher cap later in the year, alongside decisions on future funding for networks that continue to face post-pandemic demand uncertainty. Operators cautioned that without a clear path to stable financing, communities could still see further timetable changes or route withdrawals.

Aston Villa have completed the signing of Marco Asensio from Paris Saint‑Germain, with the Spain international agreeing a multi‑year contract after finalising terms and completing a medical at Bodymoor Heath. The fee is officially undisclosed but is understood to be structured with performance‑related add‑ons, reflecting Villa’s determination to add proven European pedigree to Unai Emery’s attacking options ahead of the club’s return to the Champions League. Asensio, who can operate off the right, as a No 10 or on the left, brings elite experience from trophy‑laden spells in Madrid and Paris and is expected to add goals, set‑piece quality and versatility across the forward line.

Villa have also reached an agreement in principle with Chelsea for the season‑long loan of centre‑back Axel Disasi, subject to a medical and final paperwork. The deal is believed to include an option to buy next summer, giving Villa flexibility within profitability and sustainability rules while bolstering Emery’s defensive depth for a congested campaign. Personal terms are not expected to be an issue, and the club are aiming to complete formalities in time for registration ahead of next week’s European squad deadline.

Asensio’s arrival addresses a long‑standing brief to add another creative outlet and goal threat from wide areas, easing the load on Moussa Diaby and Leon Bailey while offering cover across multiple positions. Disasi, meanwhile, will compete immediately for minutes at centre‑half alongside Pau Torres, Ezri Konsa and Diego Carlos, with his aerial presence and recovery pace seen as complementary to Villa’s high defensive line.

Villa sources describe the window as targeted rather than expansive, with senior figures emphasising “quality over quantity” to meet the dual demands of domestic and European competition. The club are not ruling out further movement before the deadline but view the double breakthrough as key to maintaining momentum built under Emery, who has pushed for additions capable of influencing high‑leverage moments in Europe and the Premier League.

People in Bushmills have spoken of their shock after a man was found with nails through both hands in a car park in the County Antrim village.

The man, who is in his 20s, was found shortly after midnight on Sunday. Police said he had been nailed to a fence and had also suffered an injury to his nose. He was taken to hospital for treatment.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said his injuries were not believed to be life-threatening, but could be life-changing.

Two vans were found on fire in the car park, one of which belonged to the injured man. Police are treating the fires as arson.

The attack happened in the Dundarave Park area of Bushmills. News of the assault spread through the village on Sunday, with people in the community describing what had happened as “awful” and expressing concern for the man and his family.

Police described the assault as a “sinister” attack. Detectives appealed for anyone who had been in the area around the time of the incident to come forward, including people who may have seen something unusual but not realised it was connected to the assault.

Officers also asked anyone with CCTV or dashcam footage from the area to check their recordings. They are seeking information about both the assault and the vehicles that were set alight.

Bushmills, on the north Antrim coast, draws visitors to its distillery and is a short drive from the Giant’s Causeway. For those living in the village, the attack was all the more unsettling because it took place in a car park they knew and used.

Police urged anyone with information to contact them directly or to pass it on anonymously through Crimestoppers.

On the shaded paths of Dhaka University, where protests surged only weeks ago, students now sit in small circles sketching out the future they want. With Sheikh Hasina gone and an interim administration pledging a roadmap to elections, the sense on campus is equal parts relief and resolve. Hand-painted placards—some still flecked with rain and tear gas—lean against benches: justice for those killed, end to patronage, fair jobs, free speech.

The movement began with anger over a system students said was stacked against them, but it has widened into a program for reform. They talk about independent oversight of the police, safeguards for academic autonomy, and rolling back restrictive internet and speech laws. Many demand a nonpartisan election commission, audited campaign finance, and transparent recruitment to civil service posts. “We don’t want a reset that just restores old habits,” says a third-year engineering student, noting that party-linked groups long dominated dormitories and student unions. “This time, institutions must be stronger than any leader.”

Across campus, makeshift memorials list the names of those who died in the clashes. Volunteers have compiled testimonies and video footage for rights groups and a fledgling truth-finding panel. The interim authorities have promised investigations and compensation, but students insist on prosecutions where evidence warrants it and public reporting on each case.

The economy looms over their ambitions. Graduates eye a job market wracked by inflation and cronyism; they want a growth plan that favors small firms, internships tied to skills rather than connections, and safety nets for families hit by shutdowns. University classes are slowly resuming, though lecture halls open under banners calling for campus elections supervised by neutral observers.

Caution tempers the optimism. Protesters have seen cycles of upheaval before. Yet as evening falls over the TSC, a group unfurls a fresh sheet of paper and writes: “Back to books, forward to change.”

Erik ten Hag will remain in charge of Manchester United after the club’s end-of-season review concluded that he should continue as manager.

United finished eighth in the Premier League, their lowest position in the competition’s history, but ended the campaign by beating Manchester City 2-1 in the FA Cup final at Wembley. That victory secured a place in next season’s Europa League and gave Ten Hag a second trophy in as many seasons at Old Trafford.

United held talks with Ten Hag after completing the review and are expected to discuss an extension to his contract, which has one year left to run. The club also hold an option to extend it by a further year.

The review was led by United’s football leadership following Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s acquisition of a minority stake in the club. Ratcliffe’s Ineos group took control of football operations in February and assessed the team’s performances across the season before deciding to retain the Dutchman.

United lost 14 league games and finished with a negative goal difference. They also went out of the Champions League at the group stage. Ten Hag repeatedly pointed to injuries, particularly in defence, as a reason for the team’s inconsistency. Lisandro Martínez and Raphaël Varane, who started together in central defence at Wembley, had both missed substantial parts of the season.

Alejandro Garnacho and Kobbie Mainoo scored United’s goals in the final, with City replying late through Jérémy Doku. The win came amid intense speculation over Ten Hag’s future and denied City a second successive league and cup double.

Ten Hag joined United from Ajax in 2022. In his first season, he guided the club to third place in the Premier League and won the League Cup, ending a six-year trophy drought. He will now prepare for a third season in charge.

The FBI has launched a renewed effort to identify and contact relatives of every person killed in the 1988 Lockerbie bombing, as the Libyan man accused of building the device moves closer to trial in the United States. Officials said the initiative, led by the bureau’s Victim Services Division in coordination with the US Department of Justice, Police Scotland and Scottish prosecutors, aims to ensure families across multiple countries are notified of key court dates, can submit victim impact statements and, if they choose, attend proceedings.

The bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 on 21 December 1988 killed 270 people, including 11 on the ground in the Scottish town of Lockerbie. The case remains one of the deadliest terror attacks in UK history and a defining moment in transatlantic counter-terrorism cooperation. Authorities acknowledged that, more than three decades on, contact information for some families is incomplete or out of date, and they are appealing for relatives who have not been reached to register through a dedicated portal.

Abu Agila Mohammad Mas’ud Kheir Al-Marimi, who US prosecutors allege assembled the bomb, has been in American custody since 2022 and faces federal charges in Washington, DC. He has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors have indicated they will rely in part on statements Mas’ud purportedly made to Libyan officials in 2012, while defense lawyers are challenging the admissibility of those statements and have questioned aspects of the evidence chain. A trial date has not been publicly confirmed, but pre-trial hearings are under way.

Scottish and US authorities said the outreach reflects a commitment to give every affected family a chance to be heard, whether they are in North America, Europe, Africa or beyond. With the attack’s anniversary approaching, advocacy groups representing victims welcomed the effort but urged transparency about timelines and access to support, noting that many relatives have waited decades for a full accounting in court.

Paula Vennells, the former chief executive of the Post Office, was challenged at the Horizon IT inquiry over the accuracy of assurances she gave as concerns mounted about the software used to prosecute sub-postmasters.

Ms Vennells denied deliberately misleading anyone. She told the inquiry that she had relied on information from colleagues and regretted that she had not asked more questions about the system and the prosecutions that depended on it.

One issue was whether staff at Fujitsu, the company that supplied Horizon, could remotely alter records in branch accounts. That mattered because sub-postmasters had been held responsible for shortfalls shown on the system, even when they insisted they had not taken any money.

The inquiry examined an email Ms Vennells sent before appearing before a parliamentary committee in 2015. Asking colleagues for a briefing on remote access, she wrote: “I need to say no, it is not possible and that we are sure of this because of xx.”

Ms Vennells told the inquiry that the wording reflected what she understood at the time, rather than an instruction to colleagues to give her a particular answer. She accepted that the email was poorly worded.

The inquiry has been examining what senior figures at the Post Office knew about faults in Horizon, when they learned of them and what they did with that information. Hundreds of sub-postmasters were prosecuted after the software showed apparent shortfalls. Others used their own money to make up the deficits, lost their businesses or were driven into bankruptcy.

Ms Vennells, who ran the Post Office from 2012 to 2019, apologised to sub-postmasters and their families during her evidence. She also acknowledged that the Post Office had been too quick to dismiss accounts from people who reported problems with Horizon.

David Lammy will travel to New Delhi this week in one of his first overseas visits as foreign secretary, as the new Labour government seeks to revive trade talks with India and broaden a relationship that has often been defined by them.

Lammy is due to meet his Indian counterpart, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, for discussions on trade, technology and security. The timing of the visit, less than three weeks after Labour’s election victory, is intended to signal that Britain sees India as a priority in its own right, rather than simply as a market for British exports.

Negotiations on a free trade agreement began in 2022 under the Conservatives, but successive rounds failed to resolve differences over tariffs and access to each other’s markets. Britain wants India to lower duties on products including Scotch whisky and cars, while New Delhi is seeking easier access for Indian professionals working in the UK. Elections in both countries made it harder to reach a deal this year.

A breakthrough is not expected during Lammy’s visit. The two governments are also working on a technology partnership covering areas such as telecommunications and semiconductors, where they can make progress without waiting for a trade agreement. Clean energy and climate finance are expected to feature in the talks.

For Labour, the trip is also a chance to build ties with Narendra Modi’s government after a period of friction over Kashmir. Lammy visited India while in opposition and has argued that Britain’s relationship with the country should reflect its growing influence in global affairs.

There will still be points of disagreement. India has maintained close ties with Russia since the invasion of Ukraine, buying Russian oil and declining to join Western sanctions. Lammy’s challenge is to show that Britain can deepen co-operation with New Delhi without expecting it to fall into line on foreign policy.

EE has advised parents not to give smartphones to children under 11, saying a handset that can make calls and send texts is a better option for primary school pupils who need to stay in touch with their families.

The UK mobile operator’s guidance recommends that children aged 11 to 13 can use smartphones, but that parents should set up controls, restrict access to social media and agree limits on screen time. For 13- to 16-year-olds, EE says smartphones are appropriate but recommends keeping parental controls in place to manage access to unsuitable websites and apps.

The advice comes as families prepare for the new school year, when some parents buy a first phone for children who will be travelling to and from school on their own. A basic handset can allow a child to call home if a bus is late or plans change without giving them access to social media or an app store.

Research published by Ofcom in 2024 found that about a quarter of children aged five to seven owned a smartphone. The communications regulator also reported that more children in that age group were using social media than a year earlier, even though most major platforms set a minimum age of 13.

The guidance is not a ban, and parents can still buy a smartphone for a younger child. It also addresses a different question from whether pupils should be allowed to use phones at school. Schools in England have been encouraged by the government to prohibit their use during the school day, including at break and lunchtime, but individual schools decide how to apply that guidance.

For families who do choose a smartphone, EE’s advice is to set the rules before handing it over, rather than waiting until disagreements arise over downloads, social media or how late the phone can be used.

Novak Djokovic and Roger Federer led the tributes to Rafael Nadal after the 22-time Grand Slam singles champion announced that he would retire from professional tennis following November’s Davis Cup finals in Málaga.

Nadal, 38, said in a video released on Thursday that injuries had made it increasingly difficult for him to compete. “The reality is that it has been some difficult years, these last two especially,” he said. He described the chance to finish his career representing Spain as a fitting end, recalling the country’s Davis Cup triumph in 2004, when he was 18.

Federer, who faced Nadal 40 times, said he had hoped the day would never come. “Thank you for the unforgettable memories and all your incredible achievements in the game we love,” he wrote. The pair contested nine Grand Slam finals, including the 2008 Wimbledon final, which Nadal won in five sets as daylight faded. They played on the same side in Federer’s final competitive match, a doubles defeat at the 2022 Laver Cup.

Djokovic, who won 31 of his 60 matches against Nadal, said the Spaniard’s influence reached far beyond his results. He credited Nadal with inspiring millions of children to take up tennis and said his determination and fighting spirit would be taught for decades. “Your legacy will live forever,” he wrote.

Nadal won 14 French Open singles titles, a record at any Grand Slam tournament, and completed the career Grand Slam by winning the US Open in 2010. He also won Olympic singles gold in Beijing in 2008 and doubles gold with Marc López in Rio eight years later.

A hip injury kept Nadal out for most of 2023, and his return to competition the following year was fitful. His last meeting with Djokovic came at the Paris Olympics, where he lost in straight sets at Roland Garros, the venue that had defined his career.

A 27-year-old Māori queen was crowned in New Zealand on Thursday, hours before her father was carried by canoe along the Waikato River to his burial place on the sacred mountain of Taupiri.

Ngā Wai hono i te pō was chosen by a council of Māori chiefs to succeed King Tūheitia Pōtatau Te Wherowhero VII, who died aged 69 after undergoing heart surgery. She is the eighth monarch of the Kīngitanga, or Māori King movement, and only the second woman to hold the position. The first was her grandmother, Te Atairangikaahu, who reigned for 40 years.

Thousands gathered at Tūrangawaewae marae, the movement’s headquarters in Ngāruawāhia, for the ceremony. A Bible used at the installation of the first Māori king in 1858 was placed on the new queen’s head. Her father’s coffin lay nearby as she took her seat before tribal leaders and mourners.

After the ceremony, paddlers carried the late king’s coffin upriver in a waka, a traditional Māori canoe. At Taupiri, the coffin was borne up the steep hillside to the burial ground where earlier Māori monarchs are buried. The funeral followed six days of mourning in which visitors from across the country came to pay their respects.

The Kīngitanga was founded in the 19th century to unite Māori tribes and resist the loss of their land to British settlers. Its monarch has no formal role in New Zealand’s government but remains an influential voice in Māori affairs.

Tūheitia, who reigned for 18 years, had made unity a theme of his final months. In January, he convened a national gathering at Tūrangawaewae amid concerns over government policies affecting Māori. His daughter, the youngest of his three children, takes up the role at a time of renewed debate over the country’s obligations under the Treaty of Waitangi.

Drake has filed a second legal petition over Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us”, alleging that Universal Music Group (UMG) knew the track contained false accusations about him but released and promoted it anyway.

The petition, filed in Texas in November 2024, seeks evidence from UMG and iHeartMedia ahead of a possible lawsuit. Drake’s lawyers allege that UMG funneled payments to iHeartMedia as part of a scheme to secure radio airplay for the track. The filing does not establish that any payments were made, and it is not itself a defamation lawsuit.

“Not Like Us”, released in May at the height of the rappers’ feud, accuses Drake of being a paedophile. Drake has denied the accusation. His lawyers argue that UMG could have declined to release the song or required changes to its lyrics, but instead promoted it despite knowing, they allege, that the claims were false.

The Texas filing followed a separate petition in New York in which Drake’s company, Frozen Moments LLC, accused UMG of working with Spotify to artificially inflate the song’s popularity. That filing alleged that bots and other tactics were used to drive up streams and steer listeners towards the track.

In response to the New York petition, a UMG spokesperson called the suggestion that it would undermine its own artists “offensive and untrue” and said the company uses ethical practices in its marketing and promotional campaigns.

Both rappers release music through labels within UMG. Their feud produced a rapid succession of diss tracks in the spring, with each artist responding to the other in increasingly personal terms. “Not Like Us” became the biggest commercial hit to emerge from the exchange, reaching No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 and earning five Grammy nominations, including for record and song of the year.

Albania’s government has announced a one-year ban on TikTok after the fatal stabbing of a 14-year-old boy in Tirana prompted a national debate about social media and violence among children.

Prime Minister Edi Rama announced the decision on 21 December 2024 after meeting with parents and teachers. He said the ban would take effect in early 2025 and would form part of a wider effort to make schools safer.

The boy, Martin Cani, was killed in November near his school in the Albanian capital. Another teenager was accused of carrying out the attack. Local media reported that the two had argued on social media before the stabbing. Videos later appeared on TikTok in which young people expressed support for the attack.

TikTok disputed suggestions that its platform had played a role in the dispute. The company said it had found no evidence that either the victim or the teenager accused of stabbing him had a TikTok account. It also said reports indicated that videos connected to the incident had been posted on another platform. The company asked the Albanian government to clarify the basis for the ban.

Rama argued that the issue went beyond whether the teenagers had used TikTok. He said the way the app recommends content could encourage children to imitate violent behaviour. The government consulted parents and teachers in the weeks after the stabbing before announcing the restriction.

Critics questioned whether blocking a single app would address the causes of violence among teenagers. Opposition politicians also raised concerns about restricting a platform that Albanians use to communicate and share information.

At the time of the announcement, the government had not explained in detail how it would enforce the ban. Rama said the year-long pause would give officials time to assess how TikTok responds to concerns about child safety.

A senior manager at the Countess of Chester Hospital believed Lucy Letby was innocent even after doctors had raised concerns about her presence when babies died or unexpectedly collapsed, a public inquiry has heard.

The Thirlwall Inquiry is examining how the hospital responded to a series of deaths and collapses on its neonatal unit in 2015 and 2016, and why concerns raised by consultants did not lead to a police investigation sooner.

Doctors on the unit had noticed that Letby was on duty during a number of the incidents. That pattern did not, on its own, establish what had happened to the babies, but the inquiry has heard that consultants became increasingly concerned as further collapses occurred.

Letby was moved away from clinical duties in July 2016. She later raised a grievance over her treatment, and consultants were asked to apologise to her. The inquiry has examined how managers handled that grievance while doctors’ concerns about patient safety remained unresolved.

Cheshire Police began investigating in 2017. Letby was convicted in 2023 of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder six others. She was convicted the following year of attempting to murder another baby after a retrial on a charge on which the first jury had been unable to reach a verdict.

The inquiry, chaired by Lady Justice Thirlwall, is not re-examining those convictions. Its focus is on what hospital leaders knew at the time, how they responded to warnings from staff and what families were told about the deaths and collapses.

One of the questions it is considering is what managers should do when clinicians raise a serious concern but cannot yet explain what caused the harm. The inquiry is also looking at whether changes to procedures for reporting and investigating such concerns could help prevent similar failures elsewhere in the NHS.

The FBI said Thursday that it now believes the man who drove a pickup truck into a crowd of New Year’s revelers in New Orleans acted alone, reversing an initial assessment that he may have had accomplices.

Investigators identified the attacker as Shamsud-Din Jabbar, a 42-year-old Army veteran from Texas. Authorities said he killed 14 people and injured dozens more on Bourbon Street early Wednesday before he was fatally shot by police. Two officers were wounded in the exchange of gunfire.

“This was an act of terrorism,” Christopher Raia, a deputy assistant director of the FBI, said at a news conference. “It was premeditated and an evil act.”

Raia said investigators had found no indication that anyone helped Jabbar carry out the attack. On Wednesday, officials had urged the public to be on the lookout for possible accomplices. The FBI revised that assessment after reviewing surveillance footage and following up on leads, though officials said they were still examining Jabbar’s contacts and activities in the days before the attack.

The FBI said Jabbar posted several videos on Facebook in the hours before the attack in which he expressed support for the Islamic State group. An Islamic State flag was recovered from the truck. Investigators said the evidence pointed to an attacker inspired by the group, but they had not found evidence that it directed him.

Authorities also said they had found no definitive link between the New Orleans attack and the explosion of a Tesla Cybertruck outside the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas later on New Year’s Day.

In New Orleans, officials began reopening Bourbon Street on Thursday as the city prepared to host the Sugar Bowl, which had been postponed by a day. The FBI continued to ask anyone with information, photographs or video that could help the investigation to come forward.

Ange Postecoglou says he is “in a fight” but will not abandon the principles that have defined his Tottenham rebuild, insisting he intends to “double down” on front‑foot football despite recent scrutiny. The Spurs head coach acknowledged a run of uneven results has amplified external noise, yet framed the pressure as part of a longer journey to embed a clear identity and culture at the club.

Postecoglou stressed that bravery in possession, an aggressive press and a willingness to take risks are non-negotiables under his watch, arguing that short-term setbacks should not dictate a strategic retreat. He accepted responsibility for performances, saying the burden sits with him rather than the players, and pointed to underlying markers of progress—chance creation, territory, and intensity—as evidence the plan remains sound even when the scoreline does not.

The Australian conceded there are areas requiring sharper execution, including set-piece reliability and late-game control, and said staff are addressing details on the training ground. But he pushed back at calls to compromise the high defensive line or alter the team’s expansive approach, saying such changes would blur Tottenham’s identity and stall development. He also reiterated his trust in younger squad members, arguing that clarity and consistency give emerging players the best platform to grow.

Supporters’ backing, Postecoglou added, has been vital in sustaining momentum through injuries and suspensions, while he acknowledged that patience must be repaid with performances. The “fight,” as he framed it, is less about critics and more about raising internal standards in a league where fine margins decide outcomes. He urged perspective without deflecting accountability, noting that difficult spells are inevitable when implementing significant change.

“What we’re building,” he said, “requires conviction.” The path forward, in his view, lies not in dilution but in deepening the principles that have brought Spurs this far—trusting the process, embracing risk, and playing on the front foot regardless of circumstance.

Yuki Tsunoda will replace Liam Lawson at Red Bull from next weekend’s Japanese Grand Prix, giving the 24-year-old a debut for the team at his home race. Lawson will return to sister team Racing Bulls, where he will partner Isack Hadjar.

The decision comes just two rounds into the Formula 1 season. Lawson failed to score in Australia or China after being chosen over Tsunoda in December to replace Sergio Pérez as Max Verstappen’s team-mate. The New Zealander crashed out in wet conditions in Melbourne and qualified last for both the sprint and the grand prix in Shanghai.

Red Bull team principal Christian Horner said the team had found the RB21 difficult to drive and that Tsunoda’s experience would help as it worked to improve the car. He added that Red Bull had a “duty of care to protect and develop Liam” and believed the move back to Racing Bulls would give him a better environment in which to regain his confidence.

Tsunoda is in his fifth Formula 1 season, having raced for Red Bull’s junior team since making his debut in 2021. He qualified fifth for the Australian Grand Prix and scored his first points of the year with sixth place in the Shanghai sprint. His promotion means his first race alongside four-time world champion Verstappen will come at Suzuka.

Lawson made 11 grand prix starts for the junior team across 2023 and 2024 before his promotion. His return reunites him with a team he knows well, although he and Hadjar have not previously raced as team-mates.

The Japanese Grand Prix, which runs from 4 to 6 April, opens a run of three races on consecutive weekends, with Bahrain and Saudi Arabia to follow. That schedule gives Tsunoda little time to settle in before Red Bull has to assess how he is adapting to the car.

US Secretary of State Antony Blinken has said the toll of the war in Gaza on children is “far too high”, as he urged Israel to do more to protect civilians and allow humanitarian aid into the territory.

Speaking in Tel Aviv after talks with Israeli leaders, Mr Blinken reiterated Washington’s support for Israel’s right to defend itself following the 7 October attacks by Hamas. But he said Israel needed to take greater care to avoid civilian casualties and ensure that food, water and medicine reached people in need.

“The daily toll on civilians in Gaza, particularly on children, is far too high,” he said.

Mr Blinken said Israel had agreed to allow a United Nations assessment mission into northern Gaza to determine what would be needed for displaced Palestinians to return. Much of the north had been devastated by fighting, and many families who fled south were living in overcrowded shelters. He stressed that civilians should be able to go home when conditions allowed and must not be pressured to leave Gaza.

The visit came as aid agencies warned that many families were struggling to find enough food and clean water, while hospitals faced shortages of fuel and medical supplies. More than 23,000 people had been killed in Gaza since the start of the war, according to the territory’s Hamas-run health ministry. Israel launched its offensive after Hamas-led attacks killed about 1,200 people in Israel and some 250 others were taken hostage.

Mr Blinken also used his regional tour to try to prevent the war from spreading and to discuss Gaza’s future with Arab leaders. He said neighbouring countries were willing to help with reconstruction, but that any lasting agreement would require a credible path to a Palestinian state. In the meantime, he said, more aid had to reach civilians and the remaining hostages had to be released.

Lucy Bronze says England are “one of the most adaptive teams” as they prepare to face world champions Spain in a match that will decide who reaches the Nations League semi-finals.

The Lionesses go into Tuesday’s game at the RCDE Stadium near Barcelona two points behind Spain and must win to finish top of their group. A draw will be enough for the hosts.

England won the reverse fixture 1-0 at Wembley in February, when Jess Park scored in the first half and Sarina Wiegman’s side held off Spain after the break. Bronze said England’s ability to change their approach during a match would be important against opponents who are comfortable keeping the ball for long spells.

The Lionesses warmed up for the trip with a 6-0 win over Portugal at Wembley on Friday. Aggie Beever-Jones scored a first-half hat-trick as England raced into a 5-0 lead before the interval. That victory kept them in contention for top spot after a 3-2 defeat by Belgium in April had handed Spain the advantage.

England will have to manage the game differently on Tuesday. At Wembley in February, they had a lead to protect; this time, if the scores are level late on, they will have to decide how much to risk in pursuit of a winner. Committing more players forward could leave space for Spain to exploit on the break.

The match is England’s last competitive fixture before they begin the defence of their European title in Switzerland in July. They face France, the Netherlands and Wales in the group stage, three opponents likely to pose very different problems. For Wiegman, the trip to Spain offers a chance to see how her side handles a game in which the opposition can afford to wait and England cannot.

International students at universities across the United States are reconsidering travel plans and turning to campus lawyers after a series of immigration arrests and visa cancellations left some unsure whether they could finish the semester.

University officials have urged students to check with international student advisers before leaving the country. In some cases, schools discovered that students’ records in a federal immigration database had been terminated before the students themselves received any notice. A visa cancellation does not necessarily mean a student must immediately leave the country, but losing student status can jeopardize their ability to remain enrolled or work legally.

The arrest of Rümeysa Öztürk, a Turkish doctoral student at Tufts University, intensified those fears. Federal agents detained her in March near her home in Somerville, Massachusetts. Öztürk had co-written an opinion piece in the student newspaper criticizing the university’s response to calls to divest from companies with ties to Israel. Her lawyers challenged her detention, arguing that the government had targeted her for protected speech.

The Trump administration has defended its use of immigration powers against some foreign students involved in pro-Palestinian activism, saying it is acting to combat antisemitism and protect national security. Civil liberties groups say the actions could chill campus debate. The cases have not all followed the same course: some students have been detained while they challenge efforts to remove them, while others have left the country after their visas were revoked.

The uncertainty extends beyond students who took part in protests. Campus advisers have fielded questions about whether a trip home could leave a student unable to return, and whether a change in immigration status could cost them a campus job. With graduation approaching, some students are weighing whether to ask relatives to cancel visits rather than risk being separated from them after the ceremony.

When Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs left families in Bishop Pablo Virgilio David’s diocese grieving and afraid, David spoke out against the killings. Duterte lashed out at him in public. Pope Francis backed him.

Now David, whom Francis made a cardinal in December, is among the church leaders gathering at the Vatican to choose his successor. The conclave will be his first. For the bishop of Kalookan, it follows years of seeing how decisions made far from his parishes can shape the lives of the people who worship in them.

David’s diocese includes some of the poorest neighborhoods in metropolitan Manila, where police raids and other killings linked to the anti-drug campaign left families struggling not only with the loss of relatives, but also with the stigma of having been accused of involvement with drugs. David challenged the idea that those accusations made the deaths any less deserving of scrutiny. Church workers helped families who had lost relatives, while David used his public position to question a campaign that retained broad support among Filipinos.

Duterte, who left office in 2022, was arrested in March and transferred to the custody of the International Criminal Court in The Hague. He faces an allegation of crimes against humanity related to the drug crackdown. The former president has defended the campaign as necessary to combat crime.

Francis’ decision to elevate David brought international attention to a bishop whose work had largely unfolded in crowded parishes far from Rome. It also gave David a vote in a decision that will shape how the church responds to conflicts like the one that defined much of his episcopate: what to say, and whom to stand beside, when a popular government’s policies put vulnerable people at risk.

Police in the Swiss canton of Graubünden opened an investigation after a ski rental outlet near Davos posted a notice in Hebrew saying it would no longer rent equipment to Jewish customers.

The sign appeared at a mountain restaurant in the Pischa ski area. It cited several incidents, including the alleged theft of a sled, and said the ban covered skis, sledges, snowshoes and other equipment. A photograph of the notice circulated online, drawing condemnation from Jewish organisations and local tourism officials.

The Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities said the notice was discriminatory. It argued that a business could hold individual customers responsible for missing or damaged equipment, but could not use those incidents to deny service to an entire group. The federation said it was considering legal action.

The operator initially defended the decision in comments to Swiss media, saying staff had repeatedly had to retrieve equipment left on the slopes. The notice was subsequently removed, and the operator apologised. The dispute concerned the rental counter rather than access to the ski area, which remained open to Jewish visitors.

Davos is best known internationally for hosting the World Economic Forum, but the resort has also long been a holiday destination for Orthodox Jewish families. Local tourism officials have worked with Jewish community representatives to address friction between some businesses and visitors, including disagreements over local customs and the use of rented accommodation.

For Jewish community representatives, the central issue was not whether equipment had gone missing. It was that the notice singled out customers by religion, including people who had never rented from the outlet before. The police inquiry was expected to examine whether the sign breached Swiss anti-discrimination law, which prohibits refusing a publicly offered service on grounds including religion.

For some Christians in Iran, Easter is marked not by bells or a service in a church, but by a quiet gathering in a living room. A few passages from the Bible are read in Persian, prayers are said and, if it feels safe to sing, hymns are sung softly. Some worshippers join services online rather than risk being seen at a gathering.

Iran’s constitution recognises Christianity as a minority religion, and long-established Armenian and Assyrian communities have churches where they can celebrate Easter openly. The situation is different for Iranians who have converted from Islam. Converts are often unable to worship in recognised churches, and restrictions on services in Persian limit their options further. Many instead meet in private homes, in informal congregations known as house churches.

Human rights groups have documented raids on these gatherings, as well as arrests and prison sentences for some of those who attend or lead them. Iranian authorities have brought national security charges in some cases. Rights groups say such charges have been used to punish people for ordinary religious activities, including praying together and sharing religious texts.

The secrecy can extend beyond the service itself. A convert may celebrate Easter without telling parents or siblings why the day matters, or may have no one nearby with whom to share it. Online worship offers a connection to Persian-speaking Christians abroad, though it cannot replace sitting down to a meal with others after a service.

The contrast is especially visible at Easter. In an established church, families can arrive together, greet friends at the door and stay to talk after the service. For those gathering in a private home, even inviting someone new means deciding whom they can trust. The prayers may be much the same. It is the ordinary act of coming together that carries the risk.

An Israeli air strike on a United Nations school sheltering displaced Palestinians in central Gaza killed at least 35 people, according to officials at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, where the dead and wounded were taken. The school, in the Nuseirat refugee camp, was hit before dawn on Thursday.

The Israeli military said it had targeted members of Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad who were operating from classrooms in the compound. It said some of those targeted had taken part in the 7 October attacks on Israel and that it had taken steps to reduce the risk to civilians. Those claims could not be independently verified. Gaza officials said women and children were among the dead, and casualty counts varied in the hours after the strike.

The UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA, said about 6,000 people had been sheltering at the school. Its commissioner-general, Philippe Lazzarini, said the agency had shared the compound’s coordinates with the Israeli military and that the school had been struck without warning. The agency said it could not verify Israel’s claim that armed groups were using the building.

Footage from the scene showed people picking through rubble outside the school and examining damage to upper-storey classrooms. At Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in nearby Deir al-Balah, the casualties arrived as staff were already treating people wounded in other strikes across central Gaza.

The strike came a day after the Israeli military announced a new operation in parts of central Gaza, including around Nuseirat and Bureij. Families who had fled fighting elsewhere in the territory had crowded into schools and other public buildings, many of which had stopped functioning as classrooms months earlier. UN officials have warned that repeated displacement has left families with fewer places to seek shelter and has made it harder for aid workers to reach them.

The first official painted portrait of King Charles III since his coronation has been unveiled at Buckingham Palace, with the monarch depicted in the red uniform of the Welsh Guards against a vivid red background.

The painting, by British artist Jonathan Yeo, shows the King resting his hands on the hilt of a sword, with a butterfly hovering just above his shoulder. The uniform nearly disappears into the loose brushwork around it, leaving the King’s face as the most sharply defined part of the canvas.

The Drapers’ Company commissioned the portrait in 2020 to mark 50 years of Charles’s membership of the livery company. Yeo began work while Charles was still Prince of Wales. The King sat for him four times, beginning at Highgrove in June 2021 and ending at Clarence House in November 2023, six months after the coronation.

Yeo said the butterfly was the King’s suggestion. The two had discussed including a detail that might give schoolchildren something to notice beyond the figure in uniform. For Yeo, the butterfly also offered a way to acknowledge the King’s longstanding interest in the natural world and the change in his role while the portrait was being painted.

Queen Camilla attended the unveiling. Yeo recalled that when she saw the finished painting, she told him: “Yes, you’ve got him.”

Yeo, whose previous subjects include the late Duke of Edinburgh, said he wanted the painting to reflect the traditions of royal portraiture while making the King recognisable as an individual. Charles is Colonel-in-Chief of the Welsh Guards, a role he took on as Prince of Wales in 1975.

The portrait will go on public display at the Philip Mould Gallery in London from 16 May to 14 June before moving to Drapers’ Hall in the City of London.

Barclays has agreed to buy Tesco Bank’s credit card, personal loan and savings businesses for about £600m, in a deal that will see around 2,800 Tesco staff transfer to the bank.

Tesco will keep its insurance, cash machine, travel money and gift card operations. It has also agreed a 10-year partnership with Barclays, which will offer financial products under the Tesco brand. That means the supermarket’s name will remain on banking products even though Barclays will run the business behind them.

Tesco said customers did not need to take any action and could continue to use their accounts as usual. The sale is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to be completed in the second half of 2024.

Ken Murphy, Tesco’s chief executive, said the deal would allow the supermarket to focus on the financial services that were most closely linked to its retail business. Barclays chief executive C.S. Venkatakrishnan said the acquisition would help the bank expand its UK consumer business and give it a route to reach more customers through Tesco.

Tesco expects to receive a further £100m in cash from the banking business before the sale is completed, on top of the price Barclays has agreed to pay. The supermarket said it intended to return most of the proceeds to shareholders through a share buyback.

Tesco entered banking in 1997 through a joint venture with Royal Bank of Scotland and took full ownership of the business in 2008. It has already withdrawn from some areas of lending, selling its mortgage portfolio to Lloyds Banking Group in 2019. The Barclays deal takes that retreat further: Tesco will no longer run its own credit card, loan or savings business, but it will still be able to offer those products to shoppers through the partnership.

Anna Henderson won silver in the women’s individual time trial at the Paris Olympics as rain turned the 32.4km course into a test of bike handling as well as speed.

The 25-year-old finished in 41 minutes 9.83 seconds, just 0.87 seconds ahead of American world champion Chloé Dygert, who took bronze after crashing on a corner. Australia’s Grace Brown won gold by a commanding margin of one minute 31.59 seconds.

Henderson, who broke her collarbone twice earlier in the season, stayed upright on the slick streets of the French capital and crossed the finish line on Pont Alexandre III with several of the favourites still to come. Dygert recovered from her fall to threaten Henderson’s time, but fell just short, giving the British rider a medal on her Olympic debut.

There was frustration for Josh Tarling in the men’s race, however, as the 20-year-old finished fourth after an early puncture forced him to change bikes. The European champion got back up to speed and remained in contention for a medal, but missed bronze by just over two seconds.

Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel took gold in 36 minutes 12.16 seconds, beating Italy’s Filippo Ganna by just over 15 seconds. Wout van Aert took bronze to give Belgium two riders on the podium.

Both races were held on the same course, starting at Les Invalides and heading east before returning to central Paris. The rain made the corners particularly treacherous in the women’s event, with several riders falling. Brown was in a class of her own, but less than a second separated Henderson and Dygert after more than 41 minutes of racing.

For Tarling, the margins were nearly as tight. Despite closing the gap to Van Aert in the latter part of his ride, he could not make up enough time to join Henderson on the podium.

Police Scotland could send officers to Northern Ireland to help local police deal with further disorder following a series of riots. Any deployment would be made under mutual aid arrangements, which allow police forces across the UK to request extra officers when local resources are stretched.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) would remain in charge of the operation. Officers sent from Scotland would work under its direction, with the number deployed and the length of their stay depending on what support was needed. The possibility of sending officers does not mean a deployment has been agreed.

Public order policing can draw officers away from their usual duties for several days. As well as responding to disturbances, local teams have to investigate offences, take statements and maintain a visible presence in neighbourhoods affected by the violence. Bringing in officers from elsewhere can help a force cover those duties while keeping enough staff available to respond to emergencies.

Police Scotland would have to assess what it could spare without disrupting its own operations. A mutual aid request would normally set out the number of officers needed, the roles they would be expected to fill and how long they might be required. Those details could change if the disorder subsided or spread to other areas.

For residents and businesses in the areas affected, the immediate concern is whether it is safe to return to normal routines. An increased police presence could continue after the streets quieten, both to reassure people and to allow investigators to speak to witnesses and review footage. Those inquiries would remain the responsibility of the PSNI, regardless of whether officers from Scotland were brought in to help. The decision on whether to ask for additional support would rest with the Northern Ireland force.

A woman diagnosed with a rare cancer linked to breast implants is urging people who have them to get checked if they notice swelling or a change in the shape of a breast, even if their surgery was years ago.

The cancer, known as breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma, or BIA-ALCL, is not breast cancer. It is a form of lymphoma that usually develops in the fluid or scar tissue surrounding an implant. It has been reported more often in people with textured implants, which have a rough outer surface, than in those with smooth implants.

The most common warning sign is persistent swelling, often caused by fluid that collects around an implant long after the site has healed. Other symptoms can include a lump, pain or a breast that becomes noticeably firmer. These changes can have other causes, but doctors say they should not be dismissed simply because the implants have been in place for years without problems.

An ultrasound can help determine whether fluid has built up. If it has, a clinician can take a sample and send it to a laboratory to test for lymphoma. When the disease is found early and is confined to the tissue around the implant, surgery to remove the implant and the surrounding scar tissue is often enough. People whose cancer has spread may need additional treatment.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration does not recommend routine removal of breast implants in people who have no symptoms, even if their implants are among those recalled because of the risk. People who are unsure what type they have can check their implant card or ask the clinic that performed the surgery. Anyone who notices new swelling, a lump or persistent pain should contact a health care provider rather than wait for a routine checkup.

The education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, has said she is “open-minded” about banning smacking in England, where parents can still rely on a legal defence of “reasonable punishment” in some circumstances.

Her comments come amid calls from children’s charities and doctors for England to follow Scotland and Wales in changing the law. Phillipson did not commit to a ban or set out a timetable for legislation.

Under the current law in England, a parent accused of common assault or battery against a child can argue that the use of force amounted to reasonable punishment. Whether that defence applies depends on the circumstances. It cannot be used in cases involving more serious offences, such as assault occasioning actual bodily harm or child cruelty.

Scotland removed the defence in 2020, and Wales followed in 2022. The changes did not create a separate offence of smacking. Instead, they removed a defence that was available when an adult used physical force to punish a child, giving children the same legal protection from assault as adults.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health has called for England and Northern Ireland to do the same. It argues that the current law leaves parents and professionals without a clear line between lawful punishment and assault, and points to evidence linking physical punishment with poorer mental health and increased aggression in children.

Critics of a ban have questioned whether a change in the law could draw families into the criminal justice system over isolated incidents. Supporters say decisions about whether to prosecute would still depend on the evidence and the public interest, and that a change in the law should be accompanied by practical advice for parents on managing difficult behaviour without physical punishment.

For now, the position in England remains unchanged. Removing the defence would require legislation.

Two people detained after a suspect package was found in luggage at Gatwick Airport were later allowed to continue their journeys, Sussex Police said.

The airport’s South Terminal was evacuated on Friday morning after officers were called at about 08:20 GMT to reports of a suspected prohibited item. A bomb disposal team was sent to the terminal as a precaution, and police said the package was made safe.

Passengers were told to leave the building while officers investigated, and people due to fly from the South Terminal were asked not to travel to the airport. Trains did not stop at Gatwick Airport station during the evacuation, leaving some passengers to make alternative arrangements.

The terminal reopened in the afternoon, but the airport warned that delays would continue as airlines worked through the backlog. Passengers were advised to check with their airline before setting off, as some flights had been cancelled and others were running behind schedule.

The North Terminal remained open during the incident. However, the closure of the railway station affected passengers travelling to both terminals. Train services resumed once the cordon was lifted.

For passengers already at Gatwick, the reopening meant returning to the terminal and, for those whose flights had not departed, going through security again. Those whose flights had been cancelled were advised to contact their airlines about rebooking.

Sussex Police said the two people had been detained while officers made inquiries and were subsequently allowed to travel. The force did not say what the package contained.

Gatwick thanked passengers for their patience and said staff were working with airlines to get people on their way. It urged travellers to keep checking for updates, as the reopening of the terminal did not mean that flights would immediately return to their published schedules.

More than £1bn in extra spending on public services could be put at risk if opposition parties refuse to back the Welsh government's budget, ministers have warned.

Labour does not have a majority in the Senedd and needs at least one opposition member to vote in favour of its plans or abstain. The draft budget sets out extra funding for the NHS and councils, but ministers cannot assume those increases will go ahead until the final plans have been approved.

The £1bn figure refers to additional spending the government wants to make in the coming financial year. A defeat would not mean that hospitals and councils immediately lost money they already receive. It would, however, leave ministers having to find a way to secure approval for their spending plans while public bodies were trying to set budgets of their own.

That timing matters particularly for councils. They need to know how much they will receive from the Welsh government before deciding how much to raise through council tax and where they might need to cut services.

Opposition parties can use the vote to press for changes before the final budget is published. The government has presented the extra funding as a reason to support the package, but the vote is on the whole budget, not just the increases for health and local government. An opposition member could therefore help the budget pass by abstaining without having to endorse all of Labour's spending choices.

The draft is being examined by Senedd committees, which can question ministers about how they decided where to put the extra money. That scrutiny is separate from the final vote. For ministers, the immediate task is to find enough support to get the budget through; for councils and health boards, the question is how much of the promised funding they can count on.

Lewis Hamilton says he “could not be more excited” about the year ahead as he begins his Ferrari career after 12 seasons with Mercedes.

The seven-time world champion, who turns 40 on 7 January, will partner Charles Leclerc at the Italian team. His move was announced in February 2024, before he had started his final season with Mercedes.

In a post on LinkedIn marking the start of the new year, Hamilton reflected on the decision to leave the team with which he won six of his seven drivers’ titles.

“Moving to Scuderia Ferrari, there’s a lot to reflect on,” he wrote. “To anyone considering their next move in 2025: embrace the change. Whether you’re switching industries, learning a new skill, or even just taking on new challenges, remember that reinvention is powerful.”

Hamilton has spent his entire Formula 1 career driving cars powered by Mercedes engines, first with McLaren, where he won his first championship in 2008, and then with the Mercedes works team from 2013. He won two races in his final season with the team, ending a winless run that stretched back to December 2021 with victory at the British Grand Prix.

At Ferrari, he replaces Carlos Sainz, who has joined Williams. Ferrari finished 14 points behind McLaren in the 2024 constructors’ championship, with Leclerc winning three races and Sainz two. The team has not won the constructors’ title since 2008, while Kimi Raikkonen remains its most recent drivers’ champion, having won in 2007.

An eighth title would take Hamilton clear of Michael Schumacher, with whom he shares the record. Schumacher won five of his seven championships with Ferrari.

Hamilton’s first race for the team will be the Australian Grand Prix in Melbourne on 16 March, following three days of pre-season testing in Bahrain in late February.

Trans women should use toilets according to their biological sex, the equalities secretary Bridget Phillipson has said, following a Supreme Court ruling on the definition of a woman under the Equality Act.

Phillipson said employers and other organisations should follow interim guidance from the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) while the watchdog draws up a revised code of practice. She pointed to the option of providing single, lockable toilets that anyone can use alongside separate facilities for men and women.

The Supreme Court ruled in April that the terms “woman” and “sex” in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex. The case was brought by the campaign group For Women Scotland and concerned Scottish government guidance on who could be counted as a woman on public boards. It did not directly concern access to toilets.

In its interim guidance, the EHRC said trans women should not be permitted to use women’s facilities in workplaces or services that provide separate facilities for men and women, and that trans men should not be permitted to use men’s facilities. It added that in some circumstances trans people could also be excluded from facilities corresponding to their biological sex, but said they should not be left without any facilities to use.

The judges stressed that trans people remain protected against discrimination under the Equality Act, including through the protected characteristic of gender reassignment.

Trans rights campaigners have warned that the guidance could leave people unsure which toilets they can use, particularly in buildings without individual cubicles that open onto a public corridor. They have also raised concerns that people could be challenged about their sex based on their appearance.

The EHRC’s interim update is not a statutory code of practice. Its revised code will set out how the watchdog expects service providers to apply the ruling.

England return to Twickenham on Saturday knowing that victory over Italy may not be enough on its own to keep their Six Nations title challenge on track. After losing to Wales in Cardiff, Eddie Jones’s side are likely to need a bonus point as well as a favour from one of the championship leaders’ remaining opponents.

The defeat in Cardiff checked England’s momentum after impressive wins over Ireland and France. They led at half-time but struggled to regain control as Wales kept the ball through long spells in the second half. Against Italy, the challenge will be to turn possession into tries without forcing the play in pursuit of a fourth.

Jones has picked a backline built to test the Italian defence at close quarters. Ben Te’o comes in at inside centre alongside Manu Tuilagi, with Owen Farrell at fly-half, while Joe Cokanasiga makes his first Six Nations start on the wing. The changes give England several powerful carriers, but how quickly they can move the ball after the first collision may matter more than the initial breakthrough.

Italy have never beaten England, and their losing run in the championship stretches back to 2015. Yet their last visit to Twickenham offered a reminder of how awkward they can make life for the hosts. Two years ago, their decision not to contest the ruck left England unsure where the offside line was and helped the visitors take a half-time lead before England pulled away.

Wales play Scotland at Murrayfield earlier in the day, so England will know by kick-off whether the leaders have slipped up. Whatever happens in Edinburgh, there is little incentive for Jones’s side to settle for a narrow win. With Scotland still to visit Twickenham on the final weekend, four tries against Italy would give England the best chance of making that match count.

The scale of England’s defeat in Mumbai was startling enough. More troubling for Brendon McCullum was how familiar it felt by the end of his first series in charge of the white-ball side.

India made 247-9, inspired by Abhishek Sharma’s 135 from 54 balls, and bowled England out for 97 in 10.3 overs. The 150-run defeat sealed a 4-1 series loss and left England with little time to regroup before three one-day internationals against India and the Champions Trophy.

Phil Salt struck 55 from 23 balls, showing that there were still runs to be had on the surface where Abhishek had hit 13 sixes. But no other England batter reached double figures. By the time Salt fell in the eighth over, the chase was already beyond them.

McCullum was never likely to ask England to become more cautious. The question is whether they can pick their moments better. India’s spinners had already exposed England’s tendency to reach for a boundary when a few singles might have eased the pressure. In Mumbai, with the required rate above 12 from the start and wickets falling around Salt, that option quickly disappeared.

There is work to do with the ball, too. England’s pace is an asset, but when Abhishek was able to use it to hit through and over the off side, they struggled to find a length that denied him room. India had raced to 95 by the end of the powerplay.

The switch to 50-over cricket offers McCullum and captain Jos Buttler a chance to reset, though it will also test the same skills over a longer innings. England need to find ways of keeping a chase alive when boundaries dry up and slowing an innings down when the opposition takes charge. Neither requires them to abandon their attacking instincts. Both require more than those instincts alone.

An American chemist has suggested that the secret to a better cup of tea may be an ingredient more commonly found on the dinner table: a pinch of salt.

Michelle Francl, a professor of chemistry at Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania, says a few grains can take the edge off a bitter brew without making it taste salty. The recommendation, set out in her book *Steeped: The Chemistry of Tea*, is based on the ability of sodium ions to suppress some bitter tastes.

The amount matters. The aim is not to season a mug as one would a pot of soup, but to add so little that the salt itself goes unnoticed. The difference is likely to be more apparent in a strongly brewed cup than in one that was not particularly bitter to begin with.

The suggestion drew a tongue-in-cheek response from the US embassy in London, which assured tea drinkers that adding salt was not official American policy. It then risked a second dispute by suggesting that tea should be made by microwaving the water. The UK Cabinet Office replied that it could only be made with a kettle.

Not all of Francl’s advice is likely to cause such a stir. She recommends warming the cup before pouring in the water and choosing a short, stout mug to help keep the drink hot. For those who take milk, she advises adding it after the tea has been poured.

A pinch of salt is not the only way to make a cup less bitter. A shorter steep can also help, though it changes the strength of the brew as well. Tea drinkers curious about the difference can make two cups from the same pot, leave one untouched and add a few grains to the other. If the second cup tastes salty, they have already added too much.

Downing Street has confirmed that all government departments have agreed their budgets ahead of Wednesday’s spending review, ending weeks of negotiations with the Treasury.

The review, to be presented to MPs by Chancellor Rachel Reeves, will set day-to-day budgets for the next three years and investment plans for the next four. It will determine how much departments have to spend on delivering the government’s promises, from cutting NHS waiting lists to recruiting more police officers.

The Home Office was among the last departments to reach an agreement. Its talks with the Treasury focused in part on police funding, with forces facing rising costs as ministers seek to put more officers and other staff into neighbourhood teams. The terms of the settlement have not yet been made public.

Health is expected to receive one of the biggest increases. With the government also committed to raising defence spending to 2.5% of national income from April 2027, other departments face tighter limits on what they can spend.

Some investment decisions have already been announced, including £15.6bn for transport projects in English city regions outside London. The money is intended to fund improvements to tram, rail and bus networks. Such capital funding pays for infrastructure and is separate from the budgets departments use to pay staff and run services.

The announcement that talks have concluded does not mean every department will have more money to spend once inflation is taken into account. The detail on Wednesday will show which services are expected to absorb higher costs within their existing budgets and which will receive extra funding.

Unlike a Budget, the spending review is primarily about how the government divides up its resources rather than how it raises them. For ministers who have spent weeks making the case for their departments, the next task will be explaining what their settlements mean for the public.

Southampton’s Championship match against Preston North End was postponed after a major fire broke out at an industrial site next to St Mary’s Stadium.

The match had been due to kick off at 19:45 GMT on Wednesday, but Southampton said it had been called off after consultation with the emergency services. Roads around the ground were closed while firefighters tackled the blaze, and supporters were asked to stay away from the area.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service was called to the industrial units on Marine Parade shortly after 13:00. Thick black smoke rose above the stadium and could be seen from across the city. People living nearby were advised to keep their windows and doors closed.

Crews from several fire stations were sent to the scene. The stadium itself was not reported to have been affected by the fire, but the road closures restricted access to the ground as emergency vehicles continued to arrive.

Southampton said it regretted the inconvenience to supporters, particularly Preston fans who had already set off for the south coast. The club said tickets bought for Wednesday’s match would remain valid for the rearranged fixture. A new date had yet to be announced.

The postponement came as Southampton were chasing automatic promotion to the Premier League and Preston were competing for a play-off place. The teams had drawn 2–2 at Deepdale in October, when a stoppage-time own goal earned Southampton a point.
