Police urged drivers to avoid the roads around the stadium while the emergency services worked at the site. Firefighters remained there into the evening, and residents were asked to continue following the advice about smoke. The cause of the fire was not immediately known.

Peter Sullivan has had his conviction for the murder of Diane Sindall quashed after spending 38 years in prison, following new DNA tests that excluded him as the source of a sample recovered from the crime scene.

Sullivan, 68, was convicted in 1987 of murdering Sindall, a 21-year-old florist who was attacked in Birkenhead, Merseyside, in August 1986. The Court of Appeal overturned his conviction on Tuesday after hearing that DNA found on samples taken at the time belonged to an unknown man.

Merseyside Police said it was continuing to investigate the murder. The DNA evidence that led to Sullivan’s conviction being overturned has not yet led to the identification of another suspect.

At a Chappell Roan show, the dress code is less about looking good than about committing to the bit. That invitation runs through *The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess*, her 2023 debut album. On “HOT TO GO!,” she turns a come-on into a cheer routine simple enough for thousands of people to learn on the spot. On “Casual,” she’s considerably less in control, trying to reconcile the intimacy of a relationship with someone else’s insistence that it doesn’t mean much. The songs sound at home on the same record: Roan is as willing to look foolish over a crush as she is to make a joke about it.

Raised in Willard, Missouri, Roan moved to Los Angeles to pursue music and was dropped by her first label before releasing her debut album. “Pink Pony Club,” originally released in 2020, took years to become the kind of song a festival crowd would sing back to her. Its story, about a young woman leaving home to dance at a gay club, makes room for both the thrill of finding somewhere you belong and the ache of knowing your family might not understand why.

The costumes are an easy way to explain Roan’s appeal, especially if you’ve only seen a few seconds of her on your phone. But watch a crowd during “Pink Pony Club”: by the final chorus, people who came dressed as cowboys are singing about missing their mothers.

The FBI is asking relatives of those killed in the Lockerbie bombing and others directly affected by the attack to contact the agency ahead of the trial of a Libyan man accused of making the bomb that brought down Pan Am Flight 103.

"Pearl was everything to us," she said, her voice breaking. "She was funny and kind and she had her whole life ahead of her. And the man who took that away from her walks out of here today and goes home to his family. We don't get to do that. We never will."

Pearl's father, Mark Black, 41, said the family had been poorly supported throughout the investigation and that they had received no formal victim liaison contact for several months following their daughter's death.

"We were left completely in the dark," he said. "We had to chase information ourselves. We had to fight to even understand what charges were being brought. No family should have to go through that on top of their grief."

The Astrobotic Peregrine lunar lander has met a fiery end over the Pacific Ocean, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after a troubled mission that never came close to achieving its goal of landing on the Moon.

The spacecraft, which launched on 8 January aboard United Launch Alliance's new Vulcan Centaur rocket, suffered a critical propellant leak shortly after separating from the rocket. Engineers at Astrobotic worked frantically in the hours and days that followed to stabilise the vehicle and preserve what power remained, but it quickly became clear that a lunar landing was no longer possible.

Mission controllers made the decision to guide the stricken spacecraft back toward Earth rather than allow it to drift uncontrolled through space. Astrobotic confirmed that Peregrine re-entered the atmosphere on Thursday, with the vehicle disintegrating as it plunged through the upper atmosphere at high speed. The destruction occurred over the South Pacific Ocean, a remote stretch of water that has become a designated graveyard for decommissioned spacecraft.

The mission had been heralded as a landmark moment for NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme, which seeks to use private companies to deliver scientific instruments and other cargo to the lunar surface. Peregrine carried 20 payloads on behalf of multiple customers, including five NASA science instruments intended to study the lunar environment ahead of future crewed Artemis missions.

Despite the failure to reach the Moon, some officials at NASA and Astrobotic sought to put a positive face on the outcome. The company said that data gathered during the mission had provided valuable insights that would inform the development of its next lander, Griffin, which is intended to carry NASA's VIPER rover to the lunar south pole. NASA administrator Bill Nelson said the agency remained committed to its commercial lunar partnerships and expressed confidence that future missions would succeed.

Residents in the small north Antrim town of Bushmills have expressed disbelief and distress following a violent attack in which a man was assaulted with a nail in a local car park in the early hours of Saturday morning.

The victim, a man in his thirties, was taken to Causeway Hospital in Coleraine following the incident, which is understood to have taken place near the town centre shortly after midnight. His injuries were described as serious but not life-threatening.

Locals who spoke to reporters outside nearby businesses on Monday morning said the attack had left many people in the close-knit community deeply unsettled. "You just don't expect something like this here," said one woman, who declined to give her name. "Bushmills is a quiet place. Everyone knows everyone. It's awful, just awful."

A shopkeeper on Main Street said he had heard about the attack through neighbours and was shocked by its nature. "It's not the kind of thing you associate with this town at all. People are shaken up about it."

The Police Service of Northern Ireland confirmed it was investigating the assault and appealed for anyone who had been in the area at the relevant time to come forward with information. A spokesperson said officers were following a number of lines of enquiry and that no arrests had been made at this stage.

Councillors representing the area also condemned the attack. Alderman Patricia McAllister described it as "deeply disturbing" and called on the community to assist police in their investigation. "Violence of this nature has no place in our town or anywhere else," she said. "I would urge anyone with any information at all to contact the PSNI without delay."

Bushmills, best known internationally as the home of the Old Bushmills Distillery, has a population of around 1,300 people.

The Foreign Secretary travelled to New Delhi on Monday for talks with his Indian counterpart, S. Jaishankar, in what officials described as an effort to inject fresh momentum into a bilateral relationship that has been marked by periods of tension and diplomatic friction under previous governments.

Mr Lammy, who arrived accompanied by a small delegation of trade and security officials, said he was keen to demonstrate that the new Labour administration regarded India as a partner of the first order, not merely in economic terms but across a broad range of shared strategic interests. The visit, coming just months after the general election, was widely seen in Westminster as a signal that Downing Street wishes to place the relationship on a more stable and productive footing.

Central to the discussions was the long-delayed free trade agreement, negotiations for which have dragged on for several years amid disagreements over tariffs, professional visas and market access in sectors including whisky and automobiles. Sources close to the talks indicated that both sides expressed a renewed willingness to find compromise, though no breakthrough was announced and officials cautioned against expecting a swift conclusion to what remains a complicated set of negotiations.

The Foreign Secretary also raised issues of regional security, including the situation in the Indo-Pacific, where both countries have expressed concern about Chinese assertiveness. Climate cooperation and the transition to clean energy were also on the agenda, with Britain hoping to draw on Indian expertise and scale in renewable technology.

Mr Lammy acknowledged at a press conference alongside Dr Jaishankar that the two nations had not always seen eye to eye, but argued that the foundations for a deeper partnership were firmly in place. "This is a relationship with enormous potential," he said, "and this government intends to realise it."

The Dutchman's position had been the subject of intense speculation following a turbulent start to the Premier League season, with United suffering a string of disappointing results that left the club languishing in the lower half of the table. Senior figures at Old Trafford had been understood to be considering their options, with several high-profile names linked with the vacancy that many believed was imminent.

However, following a lengthy board meeting on Thursday, club co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the INEOS leadership team announced that Ten Hag would continue in his role, at least in the short term. The decision came as a surprise to many within the game, given the mounting pressure that had been building around the manager in recent weeks.

In a statement released by the club, Manchester United said they remained confident in Ten Hag's ability to turn results around and that the squad, despite its struggles, contained enough quality to climb the table. The statement added that the manager had been given the full backing of the ownership group and the board of directors.

Ten Hag, speaking to reporters at the club's Carrington training complex on Friday morning, expressed his gratitude for the continued support and vowed to repay the faith shown in him. "I am fully committed to this club and to these players," he said. "We know the results have not been good enough and I take responsibility for that. But I believe in what we are building here and I know we can turn this around."

The 54-year-old guided United to two major trophies during his first two seasons at the helm, including an FA Cup victory over rivals Manchester City at Wembley last May. Many within the club believe that record, combined with the broader rebuilding project under way, warranted giving the manager more time.

Paula Vennells, the former chief executive of the Post Office, made a false statement to the independent inquiry examining the Horizon IT scandal, a barrister representing subpostmasters told the inquiry on Thursday.

The accusation came during a tense session of the ongoing public inquiry, which has been examining how hundreds of subpostmasters were wrongly prosecuted on the basis of faulty data produced by the Horizon computer system. Lawyers acting for victims alleged that Vennells had given misleading evidence in her written submissions to the inquiry, contradicting documents and testimony already heard by the panel.

Jason Beer KC, counsel to the inquiry, pressed Vennells on a series of internal emails and reports that appeared to show senior Post Office executives had been made aware of significant problems with the Horizon system far earlier than she had previously suggested. Vennells, who led the organisation from 2012 to 2019, maintained that she had not been informed of the full extent of the system's flaws during her tenure, a claim that drew scepticism from several of the lawyers present.

Deirdre Smith, representing a group of affected subpostmasters, told the inquiry that Vennells had given an account "that simply cannot be reconciled with the documentary evidence before this inquiry" and urged the chair, Sir Wyn Williams, to treat her testimony with considerable caution.

Vennells, who gave evidence via video link, appeared visibly distressed at several points during the session, pausing repeatedly before answering questions. She apologised once again to those who had been wrongly prosecuted, telling the inquiry that she was "devastated" by the suffering caused.

The inquiry, which has heard evidence from dozens of witnesses over the past two years, is expected to publish its final report later this year. Prosecutors and regulators are separately examining whether criminal charges should be brought against individuals connected to the scandal.

Darwin Nunez marked his return from a three-week injury absence in the most dramatic fashion possible, heading home a stoppage-time winner to send Liverpool's travelling supporters into raptures and hand Nottingham Forest a devastating defeat at the City Ground.

The Uruguayan striker, who had been sidelined with a hamstring problem, came off the bench in the 74th minute to replace the tireless Diogo Jota, and looked sharp from the moment he stepped onto the pitch. For long periods, however, it appeared as though Liverpool would have to settle for a point in a game that had largely frustrated Arne Slot's side.

Forest had been resolute and well-organised throughout, sitting deep and looking to threaten on the counter-attack. Matz Sels had been largely untroubled in the home goal, with Liverpool struggling to find the spaces in behind a disciplined defensive unit marshalled effectively by Nikola Milenkovic and Murillo.

The breakthrough, when it finally came, was both stunning and chaotic. Andrew Robertson drove forward on the left flank and swung in a looping cross that evaded everyone until it dropped perfectly for Nunez, arriving at the back post, to plant a firm header beyond the despairing dive of Sels in the 99th minute. The striker wheeled away towards the away end in celebration, pursued by his delirious teammates.

The goal extended Liverpool's lead at the top of the Premier League to five points, though Slot was quick to acknowledge the performance had not been among his side's finest.

"We made it very difficult for ourselves today," the Dutch head coach said afterwards. "But the character of the squad to find a winner so late tells you a lot about this group. Darwin showed exactly why we have missed him."

Forest manager Nuno Espírito Santo cut a deflated figure in his post-match press conference, admitting the late concession had been "very hard to take."

Britain's largest mobile network has urged parents to resist pressure to buy smartphones for young children, warning that primary school-age pupils are not emotionally or developmentally ready to handle the risks that come with internet-connected devices.

EE, which has more than 20 million customers across the UK, published guidance on Wednesday calling on parents to delay giving children a smartphone until they reach secondary school age, typically around 11 or 12. The company said it felt a responsibility to speak openly about the issue despite the commercial tension inherent in a mobile operator discouraging handset use among a significant portion of the population.

Marc Allera, chief executive of BT's consumer division, which includes EE, said the network had spoken to child development experts, online safety campaigners and thousands of parents before drawing up its recommendations. "We know this is not an easy message for us to deliver, but we think it is the right one," he said. "Parents are telling us they feel enormous pressure from their children and from other parents, and they want someone to give them permission to say no."

The guidance stops short of calling for an outright ban, instead encouraging parents to consider alternative devices such as basic phones capable only of calls and texts, or GPS-enabled watches that allow contact with family members without providing access to social media or the broader internet.

EE said it would also introduce new family-focused tools within its own app designed to give parents greater control over how connected devices are used within the home, including the ability to set screen time limits and restrict access to certain categories of content. The announcement was welcomed by campaigners including Smartphone Free Childhood, whose co-founder said it marked a meaningful shift in how the telecoms industry was engaging with the debate.

Albania has become the first country in the world to impose a nationwide ban on TikTok after a teenage boy was stabbed to death following a dispute that escalated on the platform, the government has announced.

Prime Minister Edi Rama said the social media app would be shut down for a period of one year, describing TikTok as a space filled with "violence, insults and provocation" that was having a deeply damaging effect on young people. The decision follows weeks of pressure from parents and teachers who had been calling on the government to take action against the platform in the aftermath of the fatal incident, which involved two teenagers.

The killing prompted widespread outrage across Albania, with thousands of parents and educators joining protests and signing petitions demanding that authorities act to protect children from what they described as an increasingly toxic online environment. Schools across the country had also raised concerns about bullying and threats being coordinated and amplified through TikTok, with teachers reporting a deterioration in behaviour they linked to content circulating on the app.

Rama said the ban would take effect in the coming weeks and that the government had been in contact with internet service providers to ensure the platform was blocked across the country. During the year-long suspension, he said, officials would engage with school communities, parents and child psychologists to assess what long-term measures might be needed.

TikTok said it was "disappointed" by the decision and that it remained willing to work with Albanian authorities to address their concerns. The company said it had invested heavily in safety tools and moderation systems designed to protect younger users, and that an outright ban was not the most effective solution to the challenges posed by social media.

The tennis world united in an outpouring of emotion and admiration on Thursday as the sport's greatest names paid tribute to Rafael Nadal following the Spanish champion's announcement that he would retire from professional tennis at the age of 38.

Novak Djokovic, who waged some of the most fierce and memorable battles with Nadal across nearly two decades of competition, was among the first to respond, describing his long-time rival as "one of the greatest champions the sport has ever seen and ever will see." The Serbian world number one, who like Nadal pushed the boundaries of what was thought physically and mentally possible in the modern game, added that facing the Spaniard across the net had made him a better player. "Every time I played Rafa, I knew I had to be at my absolute best," Djokovic said in a statement posted to social media. "He brought something out of me that nobody else could."

Roger Federer, who retired from the tour in 2022 and shared one of sport's most celebrated rivalries with Nadal, posted a heartfelt video message in which he struggled to contain his emotions. "This is a sad day for me personally and for all of us who love this sport," the Swiss legend said. "Rafa, what you have done for tennis, what you have done for all of us, cannot be put into words. You were my greatest rival and you became one of my closest friends. I will miss you on that court more than you know."

Andy Murray, himself recently retired, described Nadal as the "toughest opponent I ever faced," while women's world number one Iga Swiatek called him "an inspiration to every professional player on tour." Messages of support continued to flood in from across the sporting world throughout the morning.

The legal dispute between the two rap superstars escalated significantly on Tuesday as Drake's team confirmed it had filed a second lawsuit against Kendrick Lamar and Universal Music Group, broadening the scope of its original complaint and intensifying what has become one of the most closely watched feuds in hip-hop history.

The new filing, submitted in a federal court in New York, expands on claims first raised in an earlier action lodged in January, in which Drake's legal representatives alleged that Universal Music Group had used bots and other artificial means to manipulate streaming numbers for Not Like Us, Lamar's scathing diss track that dominated charts throughout much of last year. The second suit adds further allegations relating to defamation, claiming that specific lyrics on the track made false and damaging assertions about Drake's personal conduct that caused measurable harm to his reputation and business interests.

Attorneys representing Drake, whose legal name is Aubrey Drake Graham, argued in the filing that the song's repeated and commercially amplified distribution constituted a deliberate campaign to damage their client rather than a legitimate exercise of artistic expression. The suit seeks substantial financial damages and calls for the track to be removed from streaming platforms pending the outcome of the litigation.

Universal Music Group declined to comment directly on the new filing but previously pushed back against the original lawsuit, calling its claims without merit and describing the action as an attempt to relitigate a cultural moment that had not gone in Drake's favour.

Lamar's representatives have not yet issued a formal response to the second filing. The Grammy-winning rapper performed Not Like Us at the Super Bowl halftime show in February to widespread acclaim, a moment that many observers believe added further commercial and symbolic weight to the ongoing dispute between the two artists.

Ngā Wai hono i te pō Paki was crowned the eighth Māori queen on Saturday in an emotionally charged ceremony held at Tūrangawaewae Marae in Ngāruawāhia, as thousands of mourners gathered to farewell her father, the late Kīngi Tūheitia, who passed away last week at the age of 58.

The coronation, which took place during the tangihanga — the traditional Māori funeral proceedings — marked a historic moment, as Ngā Wai, just 27 years old, became the youngest person and only the second woman to hold the title of Māori monarch since the Kīngitanga movement was established in 1858.

Dressed in traditional garments and draped with a korowai, an ornate feathered cloak, the new queen stood before an enormous crowd that had swelled to tens of thousands over several days of mourning. Representatives from iwi across the country, as well as dignitaries and community leaders, had converged on the marae to pay their respects to Kīngi Tūheitia and to witness the transfer of leadership to his daughter.

The selection of Ngā Wai was made by a gathering of paramount chiefs, known as the kaumātua council, who deliberated following the king's death before announcing their decision. The announcement drew an emotional response from the crowd, with many wiping tears as they applauded the young woman stepping forward to accept the responsibility.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon offered his condolences and congratulations, describing the moment as deeply significant for all of New Zealand. "Ngā Wai carries with her the weight of her father's legacy and the hopes of her people," he said. "We wish her strength and wisdom as she leads."

Kīngi Tūheitia, who reigned for 17 years, was widely respected for his efforts to strengthen Māori identity and foster unity among the country's diverse iwi.

Federal investigators now believe that Shamsud-Din Jabbar acted entirely alone when he drove a rented truck into a crowd of New Year's revelers on Bourbon Street, killing multiple people and injuring dozens more, according to officials familiar with the investigation.

The FBI initially expressed concern that Jabbar may have had accomplices who helped plan or coordinate the attack, and agents spent the days following the assault combing through his communications, financial records and travel history in an effort to identify any co-conspirators. Two improvised explosive devices discovered in the French Quarter on the night of the attack had also raised fears that others might have been involved in a broader plot.

However, after conducting extensive interviews and reviewing a substantial volume of digital evidence, investigators have concluded that no other individuals played a role in planning or carrying out the massacre. Officials said the explosive devices, while functional, appeared to have been constructed and planted by Jabbar himself in the hours before the attack.

"Based on everything we have gathered to this point, we believe this was the act of a single individual," one federal law enforcement official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because the investigation remains ongoing.

Investigators say Jabbar, a United States Army veteran from Texas, had expressed support for the Islamic State in videos he recorded before the attack. The FBI is continuing to examine whether he was formally directed by the group or had been radicalized independently through online material and acted on his own initiative without direct operational guidance from any overseas network.

Authorities have not ruled out the possibility that new evidence could emerge, and the investigation remains active. The FBI has urged anyone with information about Jabbar's movements or associations in the weeks before the attack to come forward.

Lucy Bronze has insisted England are capable of causing Spain problems on Tuesday night, describing the Lionesses as one of the most adaptive teams in international football ahead of the Nations League clash in Seville.

The Barcelona defender, who has experienced Spanish football at close quarters during her time at the Catalan club, believes Sarina Wiegman's side have developed a unique ability to adjust their approach depending on the opposition, a quality she argues will be crucial against the reigning world champions.

"I think we're one of the most adaptive teams out there," Bronze said in her pre-match press conference. "We've shown over the last few years that we can change our shape, change our style, and still perform at the highest level. That's something Sarina has really drilled into us."

England head into the fixture having already secured their place in the Nations League finals, but Bronze was keen to stress that there would be no complacency within the camp, insisting the squad were treating the game with the same intensity they would a major tournament fixture.

Spain, who lifted the World Cup in Australia last summer, have been in impressive form throughout the competition and will be backed by a vocal home crowd at the Estadio de La Cartuja. For Bronze, who knows several of the Spanish players from her time at Barcelona, the encounter carries a particular personal significance.

"Playing against friends is always a strange feeling, but once you're on the pitch none of that matters," she said. "They're a world-class team and we have huge respect for them, but we genuinely believe we can win this game."

Wiegman is expected to make several changes to her starting lineup following the victory over the Republic of Ireland, though Bronze herself is likely to retain her place at right back.

When Rodrigo Duterte was presiding over his bloody war on drugs, ordering the killings of thousands of suspected narcotics users and dealers across the Philippines, many institutions fell silent. Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David was not among them.

The bishop of Caloocan, one of the most densely populated dioceses in Metro Manila and a district where Duterte's enforcers were particularly active, became one of the most prominent voices demanding accountability. He opened his churches as sanctuaries for families fleeing the violence, celebrated Masses for the victims, and repeatedly condemned what human rights groups were calling extrajudicial executions. It was dangerous work in a country where critics of the administration faced intimidation, arrest and worse.

It was also the kind of witness that caught the attention of Jorge Mario Bergoglio. Pope Francis, who has consistently pushed the Catholic Church toward the margins and toward the poor, elevated David to the College of Cardinals in 2024, a signal widely interpreted as papal endorsement of a churchman who had placed himself squarely in harm's way.

"The Holy Father knows what is happening in the world," David said in an interview at the time of his elevation. "He does not want the Church to be a museum piece. He wants us out in the streets, with the people."

Now, with Francis dead and the Church preparing to choose his successor, David is among the more than a hundred cardinals filing into the Sistine Chapel to cast their votes in one of the most consequential conclaves in decades. He arrives carrying with him the credibility of someone tested not in chanceries and diplomatic receptions but in the alleyways of Caloocan, where the bodies of the poor were once found each morning in the grey light before dawn.

A senior hospital executive believed Lucy Letby was innocent and resisted pressure to remove her from the neonatal unit before the full scale of her crimes became apparent, the public inquiry into her killings has heard.

The inquiry, chaired by Lady Justice Thirlwall, was told that the former chief executive of the Countess of Chester Hospital held firm to the view that the nurse had been wrongly accused by consultant paediatricians who had raised concerns about a pattern of infant deaths and collapses on the ward.

Giving evidence to the panel, a former colleague described how the executive had spoken of Letby with what was characterised as a sense of protectiveness, expressing frustration at what were described internally as the "unfounded allegations" being made against her by medical staff.

The paediatricians, who had repeatedly escalated their concerns between 2015 and 2016, were instead summoned to meetings and told to apologise to Letby for the distress their suspicions had caused her. The inquiry has previously heard that at least one of those consultants felt intimidated and professionally undermined during that period.

Counsel to the inquiry put it to witnesses that the hospital's leadership had prioritised the reputation of the institution and the welfare of a single member of staff over the safety of the babies in its care. The suggestion prompted visible discomfort among several of those present in the hearing room.

Letby, now 34, was convicted in August 2023 of the murders of seven babies and the attempted murders of six others at the hospital between 2015 and 2016. She is serving 15 whole-life prison terms. The inquiry is examining how warnings about her conduct were handled by hospital management and what lessons can be learned to prevent similar failures occurring elsewhere in the National Health Service.

At universities across the country, international students are quietly recalibrating their lives — cancelling spring break travel, deleting social media posts and consulting immigration lawyers — as a wave of visa revocations and deportations sends a chill through one of American higher education's most vital communities.

The anxiety has spread rapidly in recent weeks following a series of high-profile cases in which students were detained by federal immigration authorities, in some instances with little warning and no clear explanation beyond broad references to national security or public safety. Several of the students affected had no criminal records, and some were in the process of completing graduate degrees at prestigious institutions.

"I used to feel safe here," said one doctoral student from India studying engineering at a large Midwestern university, who asked not to be named for fear of jeopardising her visa status. "Now I think twice before I say anything in class or post anything online. I don't know what the rules are anymore."

University administrators are struggling to respond. Some institutions have hired additional immigration attorneys and set up dedicated hotlines for affected students. Others have issued guidance advising foreign nationals to carry documentation at all times and to contact legal counsel immediately if approached by immigration officers. A handful of university presidents have released public statements expressing concern, though several have stopped short of directly criticising federal authorities, wary of jeopardising funding relationships with the government.

The situation is particularly acute for students from countries that have experienced heightened diplomatic tensions with Washington. Chinese, Iranian and Russian students have reported feeling especially vulnerable, though the anxiety is by no means limited to those groups. Campus counselling centres at multiple universities report a noticeable increase in students seeking support for stress and uncertainty about their futures.

Red Bull Racing have confirmed that Yuki Tsunoda will take the place of Liam Lawson at this weekend's Japanese Grand Prix, bringing an end to the New Zealander's brief and turbulent stint alongside Max Verstappen in the senior team.

The decision, announced by the Milton Keynes-based outfit on Thursday morning, comes after Lawson struggled to make a significant impression during the opening races of the season, failing to consistently score points and finding himself outpaced by the reigning world champion on a regular basis.

Tsunoda, who has spent the majority of his Formula 1 career with the junior team previously known as AlphaTauri and now operating as Racing Bulls, had long been considered a strong candidate for a promotion that many within the paddock felt was overdue. The 24-year-old Japanese driver has shown considerable development in recent seasons and arrives at his home race amid an enormous wave of local support.

Speaking at a press conference ahead of the Suzuka weekend, Red Bull's advisor Helmut Marko said the team felt the time was right to make the change. "We have been monitoring both drivers closely and we believe Yuki gives us the best opportunity to challenge at the front of the grid," Marko said. "He knows the car well and his performances over the past two years have demonstrated that he is ready for this opportunity."

Lawson, who had replaced Sergio Perez over the winter after the Mexican veteran was dropped following a disappointing end to the previous campaign, expressed his disappointment in a brief statement posted to social media, thanking the team for the opportunity while insisting his Formula 1 journey was far from over.

For Tsunoda, the move represents the fulfilment of an ambition he has spoken about openly throughout his career, and he will be hoping to deliver in front of an expectant home crowd.

Speaking at an emergency session of the United Nations Security Council, US Secretary of State Antony Blinken delivered some of his most pointed remarks yet about the humanitarian toll of the war in Gaza, acknowledging that the number of children killed and wounded in the conflict had reached levels that could no longer be justified or ignored.

"The cost of this conflict on children is far too high," Blinken told the assembled delegates, his voice measured but carrying an unmistakable gravity. "Every child killed, every child maimed, every child left without parents, without a home, without a future, represents a failure that we all must reckon with."

The comments came as the Gaza Health Ministry reported that the death toll in the territory had surpassed 14,000, with children accounting for a significant proportion of those killed since the conflict escalated following the Hamas attacks on southern Israel on October 7th. Aid organisations including UNICEF and Save the Children have repeatedly described the situation as catastrophic, warning that medical facilities are overwhelmed and supplies of food, water and medicine remain critically low.

Blinken reiterated the United States' commitment to Israel's right to defend itself against Hamas, but stressed that international humanitarian law must be upheld and that greater efforts were needed to protect civilian lives. He called on all parties to facilitate the unimpeded flow of humanitarian aid into Gaza and urged Israel to take additional precautions to minimise civilian casualties.

Palestinian Authority representatives and several other member states responded with frustration, arguing that American statements of concern had not been matched by sufficient pressure on Israel to halt its military operations. Several ambassadors called for an immediate ceasefire, a position the United States has so far declined to support at the Security Council level.

The acquisition, which is expected to be completed by the second half of 2024, will see Barclays take on approximately 2.3 million customer accounts along with around £4.2 billion in outstanding credit card balances. The deal represents one of the most significant moves in British retail banking in recent years and signals Barclays' ambition to strengthen its position in the consumer credit market.

Tesco Bank, which was established in 1997 as a joint venture between the supermarket giant and Royal Bank of Scotland before Tesco took full ownership in 2008, has long offered a range of financial products to millions of loyal shoppers. However, the bank has struggled in recent years to compete with the rapid growth of digital challenger banks and has faced increasing pressure on its profit margins.

For Tesco, the sale allows the retailer to sharpen its focus on its core grocery and retail operations at a time when the supermarket sector faces significant challenges from rising costs and shifting consumer habits. Chief executive Ken Murphy said the deal represented "excellent value" for shareholders and would allow the company to invest further in its retail business.

Barclays, which already operates one of the largest credit card businesses in the United Kingdom through its Barclaycard division, said the takeover would bring considerable benefits of scale and add millions of potential customers to its existing portfolio. The bank's chief executive, C.S. Venkatakrishnan, described the acquisition as a "highly attractive opportunity" that was consistent with the bank's broader strategy of growing its consumer lending operations.

The deal is subject to regulatory approval from the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority. Consumer groups have urged regulators to scrutinise the takeover closely to ensure that existing Tesco Bank customers are protected throughout the transition process.

A sign displayed in the window of a ski rental shop in Davos has sparked widespread outrage and condemnation after it appeared to bar Jewish customers from hiring equipment, reopening painful memories of the persecution and discrimination that defined one of the darkest periods in European history.

The handwritten notice, photographed by a visitor and rapidly shared across social media platforms, read "No ski rentals for Jews" in German. The image spread internationally within hours, drawing immediate responses from Jewish organisations, Swiss politicians and human rights groups who demanded swift action from local authorities.

The Central Council of Jews in Switzerland described the sign as "deeply shocking and completely unacceptable," calling on police to investigate the incident as a potential hate crime. The organisation's president said the display was a stark reminder that antisemitism had not been eradicated from European society and that vigilance remained essential.

Swiss federal authorities confirmed they were aware of the incident and that cantonal police in Graubünden had opened a preliminary inquiry. Under Swiss law, public incitement to hatred or discrimination based on religion or ethnicity carries potential criminal penalties including fines or imprisonment.

The town of Davos, famously associated with the annual World Economic Forum gathering attended by global leaders and business figures, now finds itself at the centre of an altogether different kind of international attention. Local officials expressed embarrassment and distress over the incident, with the mayor issuing a statement emphasising that the sign did not reflect the values of the community.

The shop's owner had not publicly commented by the time of publication, and it remained unclear whether the establishment had been temporarily closed by authorities. Several witnesses reported that the sign had been removed shortly after being photographed, though the damage to the town's reputation had already spread far beyond the Alpine resort.

The portrait, which has been in development for over a year, was unveiled at Buckingham Palace on Tuesday in a ceremony attended by members of the royal family and senior figures from the arts world. The painting, executed in oil on canvas and measuring over two metres in height, depicts the King in the uniform of the Welsh Guards, of which he has served as Colonel since 1975.

Jonathan Yeo, one of Britain's most celebrated portrait artists, known for his works depicting figures including Tony Blair, Nicole Kidman and Desmond Tutu, described the commission as one of the most significant of his career. Speaking at the unveiling, Yeo said he had hoped to capture not simply the ceremonial weight of the monarchy but also the warmth and humanity he encountered during their sittings together at Clarence House and Windsor Castle.

The portrait is dominated by a vivid crimson background, with the King emerging from a wash of red that some early observers have described as simultaneously dramatic and unsettling. A butterfly, rendered in precise detail, is depicted resting on the King's shoulder, an image Yeo has suggested carries symbolic resonance relating to themes of transformation and renewal.

Reactions to the work have been mixed since images were circulated ahead of the official unveiling. While many commentators praised Yeo's technical skill and the boldness of the composition, others questioned whether the intensity of the colour palette served the subject well. Art critic Alastair Sooke, writing in The Daily Telegraph, described it as a genuinely courageous piece of work that would divide opinion for years to come.

The King himself is understood to have been closely involved in discussions about the portrait and expressed his admiration for the finished work at Tuesday's ceremony. It will hang permanently at the Drapers' Hall in London.

Deep in the back rooms of ordinary apartments in Tehran, behind drawn curtains and locked doors, small groups of men and women gather to mark the resurrection of Jesus Christ. They speak in hushed tones, share homemade bread and grape juice in place of wine, and pray together with one eye always on the door. For Iran's growing community of Christian converts, this is what Easter looks like.

Christianity has ancient roots in Iran, and the country's recognised Armenian and Assyrian communities are permitted to worship, though under strict conditions. But a different and far more vulnerable population has emerged in recent years: Iranians who have converted from Islam to Christianity, a act that authorities consider apostasy and which can carry severe legal consequences. These converts have no recognised churches. They have no legal protection. They meet where they can.

"We call it a house church," says one woman in her thirties, whose name we have agreed not to publish for her safety. "It looks like a dinner party from the outside. That is the point." She has been a Christian for seven years, baptised in secret by a pastor who has since fled the country after his arrest and brief imprisonment.

According to rights groups including Open Doors, Iran consistently ranks among the top ten most dangerous countries in the world for Christians. Hundreds of converts have been arrested in recent years, with many charged under national security laws that make no mention of religion, allowing authorities to prosecute worshippers while maintaining a veneer of legal propriety.

Yet despite the risks, those involved in Iran's underground church movement say their congregations continue to grow. Easter, they say, holds a particular resonance for communities who understand persecution not as a distant biblical concept but as a lived daily reality.

An Israeli airstrike on a United Nations-run school sheltering displaced Palestinians in Gaza has killed at least 35 people, according to health officials and witnesses, in one of the deadliest single strikes on a civilian facility since the conflict began.

The attack struck the school in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza in the early hours of Tuesday morning, when hundreds of people were sleeping inside the compound, which had been converted into a shelter for families displaced by months of intense fighting. The Hamas-run health ministry said the death toll was expected to rise as rescue workers continued to pull bodies from the rubble.

Footage circulating on social media showed scenes of devastation inside the school courtyard, with rescuers carrying bloodied survivors through clouds of dust and smoke. Medical sources at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, where many of the casualties were taken, described overwhelming numbers of wounded arriving throughout the night.

The Israeli military said it had carried out a "precise strike" targeting Hamas militants who it said were using the school compound as a command and control centre to plan and execute attacks on Israeli forces. It said steps had been taken to minimize civilian harm but did not provide further details of the intelligence it claimed justified the strike.

The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees, known as UNRWA, confirmed the school was one of its facilities and said it was "horrified" by the attack. The agency's commissioner-general Philippe Lazzarini called for an immediate and independent investigation, stating that no justification could excuse the killing of civilians sheltering in UN premises.

The strike drew swift international condemnation, with several European governments summoning Israeli ambassadors and humanitarian organisations renewing calls for a ceasefire. Israel has repeatedly stated that Hamas deliberately embeds itself within civilian infrastructure, a claim the group denies.

Henderson crossed the line in a time of 35 minutes and 12 seconds, claiming silver behind dominant Swiss champion Marlen Reusser, who delivered a masterclass on the rain-soaked roads outside Paris to retain her Olympic title. The 25-year-old from Yorkshire had produced the ride of her career to that point, surpassing her previous best at a major championship and cementing her status as one of Britain's most exciting cycling talents.

Speaking in the finish area, an emotional Henderson said she had given everything on the course. "I just went as hard as I possibly could from the start. To come away with a silver medal at an Olympic Games is something I've dreamed about since I was a little girl. I'm absolutely overwhelmed."

The result drew immediate praise from British Cycling performance director Stephen Park, who described Henderson as a rider whose best years were still ahead of her.

However, it was a bittersweet afternoon for Team GB after Josh Tarling, widely tipped as a potential medallist in the men's event, missed the podium in an agonising fourth place finish. The 20-year-old Welshman, who had arrived in France having broken the world record for the distance earlier this year, could not quite reproduce that form on the day that mattered most.

Tarling, who turned professional with Ineos Grenadiers last season, was competitive through the early checkpoints but gradually fell away from the medal positions in the closing kilometres as Belgian star Remco Evenepoel stormed to gold with a devastating display of power and precision.

Despite the disappointment, Tarling remained composed in front of the television cameras. "Fourth place hurts, there's no other way to put it. But I'm 20 years old and I'll be back. This experience will make me stronger."

A mother of two who was diagnosed with a rare form of cancer linked to breast implants is urging other women to be aware of the potential risks after saying she was never warned about them when she underwent surgery.

Sarah Mitchell, 42, from Bristol, was diagnosed with breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma, known as BIA-ALCL, earlier this year after noticing persistent swelling around her left implant. The condition, which affects the immune system rather than the breast tissue itself, is associated primarily with textured implants and can develop years after the original procedure.

"I had my implants fitted in 2009 and nobody ever mentioned this was something I needed to watch out for," said Ms Mitchell, who had the implants following a double mastectomy. "I want women to know that this is real, and that early detection makes a huge difference."

BIA-ALCL is considered rare, with several hundred cases confirmed globally, but campaigners argue that the true number may be higher due to underreporting. When caught early and treated with surgery to remove the implants and surrounding tissue, survival rates are generally good. However, in advanced cases the cancer can spread and become life-threatening.

The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency has previously issued guidance advising surgeons to inform patients of the risk before any procedure involving textured implants, and several manufacturers have recalled certain products in recent years.

Ms Mitchell said she spent months being told her symptoms were the result of a minor infection before eventually receiving the correct diagnosis. She is now recovering following surgery and has launched an online campaign calling for mandatory patient information leaflets to be provided at all breast implant consultations.

"I am lucky they found it when they did," she said. "Other women might not be so fortunate."

The Education Secretary has said she is "open-minded" about introducing a ban on smacking children in England, suggesting the government may be willing to revisit a long-standing exemption in the law that allows parents to use physical punishment against their children.

Speaking at a fringe event at the party conference, she acknowledged that the current legal position in England, which permits "reasonable chastisement" as a defence for parents, was out of step with a growing number of countries and with the devolved nations of the United Kingdom. Scotland introduced a full smacking ban in 2020, followed by Wales in 2022, leaving England and Northern Ireland as the only parts of the UK where the practice remains legal.

Children's charities and campaigners welcomed her remarks, calling them the strongest signal yet from a senior government minister that change could be on the horizon. The NSPCC said it had long argued that the law sent a "confusing message" by affording children less protection from assault than adults, and urged the government to bring forward legislation as quickly as possible.

However, the Education Secretary stopped short of making any firm commitment, saying that she would want to look carefully at the evidence and consult widely before making any recommendations to cabinet colleagues. She also acknowledged that the issue remained sensitive for many families who did not believe the state should dictate how they disciplined their children at home.

Opposition MPs pressed her to go further, with one describing the current exemption as "an embarrassing anomaly" that had survived far too long. Conservative backbenchers, by contrast, cautioned against what they characterised as unnecessary state interference in family life.

The Department for Education confirmed that no formal review had yet been commissioned but said ministers were "actively considering the matter".

Police Scotland is considering deploying officers to Northern Ireland following a request for mutual aid as authorities in Belfast struggle to contain a wave of violent disorder that has swept across several towns and cities in recent days.

Senior figures within the force confirmed on Wednesday that discussions are ongoing with the Police Service of Northern Ireland regarding the potential transfer of officers, who could be used to bolster frontline resources stretched thin by successive nights of unrest. A formal decision is expected within the next 48 hours.

The violence, which erupted last week following a series of protests linked to far-right groups, has seen petrol bombs thrown at police lines, vehicles set alight and a number of community buildings attacked. More than 50 officers have been injured during the disorder, with some sustaining serious wounds. Dozens of arrests have been made across Belfast, Londonderry and several smaller towns.

Mutual aid arrangements between UK police forces allow officers to be seconded to other services during periods of significant pressure, with costs typically met centrally. English and Welsh forces have already indicated their willingness to contribute personnel, and Scotland's potential involvement would represent one of the largest cross-border policing operations in recent memory.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said the force was "carefully considering the request" and that any deployment would be subject to ensuring adequate coverage was maintained across Scotland. "We have a duty to support our colleagues where we are able to do so," the spokesperson added, "while also fulfilling our obligations to the communities we serve here at home."

Scottish Police Authority chair Martyn Evans said the board had been briefed on the developing situation and would meet on Thursday to discuss the implications of any significant redeployment of resources. Opposition politicians at Holyrood have called on the Scottish Government to confirm it will cover any additional costs arising from the operation.

Two people have been detained by police after a suspect package was discovered at Gatwick Airport, causing significant disruption to passengers and staff at one of Britain's busiest travel hubs.

Officers were called to the South Terminal shortly before midday after the package was identified by security personnel during routine screening procedures. A section of the terminal was cordoned off as a precautionary measure, with passengers asked to move away from the affected area while specialist officers assessed the situation.

Sussex Police confirmed that two individuals, a man and a woman both believed to be in their thirties, were detained at the scene and are currently being questioned in connection with the incident. Neither has been formally arrested at this stage, a spokesperson said.

Flights continued to operate during the incident, though delays were reported on a number of departures as additional security checks were carried out across the terminal. Some passengers described scenes of confusion as staff moved people away from certain gates without initially providing an explanation.

"We were just told to move back and wait," said one traveller who had been preparing to board a flight to Malaga. "Nobody really told us what was happening for quite a long time. It was unsettling, especially with families and children around."

A Gatwick Airport spokesperson said the safety of passengers and staff remained the absolute priority and that the airport was working closely with police throughout the operation. "We apologise for any inconvenience caused and thank passengers for their patience and understanding during this time," the statement read.

The Explosive Ordnance Disposal team was deployed to examine the package, though police were at pains to stress that the incident was being treated as precautionary and that there was no immediate indication of a wider threat to the airport or the surrounding area.

The Welsh Government has warned that more than £1bn of planned spending could be undelivered if opposition parties refuse to support its draft budget, as ministers pile pressure on Senedd members ahead of a crucial vote next week.

Finance Secretary Mark Drakeford said the minority Labour administration had made "significant concessions" in negotiations with other parties, but cautioned that failure to pass the budget would leave vital public services facing severe uncertainty heading into the new financial year.

Speaking in Cardiff Bay on Tuesday, he said: "We have worked in good faith with all parties across this chamber. What is at stake here is not a political point-scoring exercise. This is about £1bn worth of commitments to schools, hospitals, local authorities and communities across Wales. If this budget falls, those commitments fall with it."

The warning came as Plaid Cymru indicated it remained unsatisfied with the government's proposals on healthcare funding and the pace of infrastructure investment, raising the prospect that the budget could be defeated on the floor of the Senedd for the first time in a decade.

The Welsh Conservatives called the government's approach "reckless" and accused Labour of leaving negotiations too late to reach meaningful compromise, while the Liberal Democrats said they were still studying the revised figures presented to them last week.

Welsh Government officials confirmed that without a passed budget by the end of the month, a number of capital projects and third-sector grants would be placed in jeopardy, with local councils unable to finalise their own financial planning in time.

Community groups and trade unions have written to Senedd members urging them to reach a deal, warning that frontline services are already stretched to breaking point and cannot withstand further delay or disruption to funding streams.

Hamilton arrived at Ferrari's Maranello headquarters on Monday morning to begin what he has described as the fulfilment of a childhood dream, greeting staff and engineers with the kind of enthusiasm that suggested the seven-time world champion had lost none of his hunger for competition despite entering his 19th season in Formula 1.

The 40-year-old Briton, who left Mercedes after an extraordinary 12-year partnership that yielded six of his seven drivers' titles, spoke to media outside the famous factory gates before heading inside for his first full day of work with his new team.

"I could not be more excited," Hamilton said, his red Ferrari jacket marking a striking visual departure from the silver and black he wore for so long. "This is a moment I have thought about for a very long time. Walking through those gates this morning, seeing the history on the walls, meeting everyone here — it just feels right. It feels like where I am supposed to be."

Ferrari president John Elkann and team principal Frédéric Vasseur were on hand to welcome Hamilton, with Vasseur describing the arrival as "a historic day for the Scuderia." The Italian team has not won a constructors' or drivers' championship since 2008, and enormous pressure accompanies the hope that Hamilton's arrival alongside Charles Leclerc could finally end that drought.

Hamilton will spend the coming weeks in the simulator and in extensive technical briefings before the new season begins in Australia in March. He acknowledged there is much to learn about Ferrari's systems and working culture, but expressed confidence that the transition would be smoother than many expect.

"I have done this before," he said with a smile, referencing his move from McLaren to Mercedes in 2013. "Change can be a good thing. Sometimes you need a new challenge to bring out the very best in yourself."

The Education Secretary said that transgender women should use facilities that correspond with their biological sex, wading into one of the most contentious social debates of recent years and signalling a firmer stance from the government on the issue.

Bridget Phillipson made the comments during a media appearance on Sunday, stating that she believed single-sex spaces should be maintained on the basis of biological sex rather than legal gender recognition. Her remarks drew immediate reactions from across the political spectrum, with some welcoming the clarity while others condemned what they described as an attack on trans rights.

"I think it is important that we have spaces that are protected, and that those spaces are based on biological sex," Phillipson told the interviewer. "That is my personal view and I think it reflects the importance of ensuring that women feel safe and comfortable in those environments."

The comments came in the wake of the Supreme Court's landmark ruling earlier this year, which found that the legal definition of a woman under the Equality Act referred to biological sex, a judgment that sent shockwaves through public institutions and prompted urgent reviews of policies across the NHS, local councils and educational settings.

Campaign groups representing transgender people condemned Phillipson's remarks, arguing that they would cause real harm to trans women who already faced high levels of discrimination and hostility in daily life. Stonewall said the comments were "deeply concerning" and called on the government to protect the rights and dignity of transgender people.

However, women's rights groups including Sex Matters welcomed the Education Secretary's position, saying it reflected the legal reality established by the court and provided much-needed guidance for schools and other institutions that had been left uncertain about how to implement the ruling in practice.

Peter Sullivan walked free from the Court of Appeal on Tuesday after judges quashed his conviction for the murder of Diane Sindall, who was brutally attacked in Bebington, Merseyside, more than three decades ago.

Sullivan, now 68, had served nearly 38 years in prison — making his one of the longest miscarriages of justice in British legal history. He had maintained his innocence throughout his imprisonment, and his case was referred to the Court of Appeal by the Criminal Cases Review Commission following a re-examination of evidence gathered at the original crime scene.

The case was reopened after advances in DNA technology allowed forensic scientists to obtain a profile from biological material that had not been analysed at the time of the original investigation. The profile obtained did not match Sullivan, raising serious doubts about the safety of his conviction. Prosecutors accepted that the new scientific evidence undermined the case against him, and the Crown did not oppose his appeal.

Lord Justice Holroyde, sitting with two other judges, told the court that the conviction could no longer be regarded as safe. He acknowledged the profound impact the case had on the family of Diane Sindall, a 21-year-old florist's assistant who was killed after her van ran out of petrol late at night. The judges expressed their sympathies to her relatives while making clear that the interests of justice required Sullivan's release.

Speaking outside the court, Sullivan's legal team described the ruling as a vindication of a man who had never stopped fighting to clear his name. His solicitor said the decades he had spent behind bars represented an almost unimaginable ordeal and called on authorities to now do everything in their power to identify who was truly responsible for Diane Sindall's death.

Police confirmed that the investigation into her murder remains open.

England head coach Steve Borthwick has urged his side to deliver a performance that will excite the Twickenham faithful as his team look to keep their Six Nations title challenge firmly on track against a stubborn Italian side that has been transformed in recent seasons.

After a commanding victory over Wales in their opening fixture, England know that anything less than a convincing win at Twickenham on Saturday would put unnecessary pressure on their remaining campaign, with Ireland and France still to come in what promises to be an intensely competitive championship.

Borthwick spoke passionately at his pre-match press conference about the need for his players to express themselves and demonstrate the attacking intent that he has been carefully building into this squad since taking charge. "We want to give the supporters something to be proud of," he said. "We know the expectation that comes with playing at Twickenham and we want to meet that."

Italy, however, will arrive in south-west London with genuine belief following their stunning development under head coach Gonzalo Quesada, who has continued the progressive work of his predecessor. The Azzurri can no longer be dismissed as the Championship's whipping boys, and their recent scalps have served notice that any team that underestimates them does so at their peril.

England's back line will carry significant hopes of unlocking a resolute Italian defence, with Marcus Smith expected to orchestrate proceedings from fly-half alongside a pack that has shown considerable muscle in the set piece. Prop Ellis Genge is expected to bring his usual abrasive energy off the bench, providing a spark in the moments when the game potentially needs it most.

Kick-off is at three o'clock and a capacity crowd of over 82,000 is anticipated, with the atmosphere at Twickenham expected to reach a fervent pitch from the very first whistle.

The numbers told their own brutal story. Bowled out for 156 in their second innings, England surrendered the third Test inside four days to leave India with a 2-1 series lead and McCullum's side facing the kind of searching questions that do not have comfortable answers. The Bazball revolution, it turns out, requires substantial revision when it travels to the subcontinent.

For long stretches of this series, England have played with the freedom and imagination that McCullum and Ben Stokes have made their trademark. But the spinners on this surface exposed the fundamental limitations of a batting lineup that can still appear hopelessly ill-equipped for conditions so far removed from the green seaming tracks of home. Zak Crawley fell for three in each innings. Ollie Pope looked a man playing an entirely different game to the one being contested around him.

India, by contrast, were clinical and controlled. Ravichandran Ashwin was relentless throughout, turning deliveries at angles that seemed to defy geometry on a surface that grew more treacherous with each session. Kuldeep Yadav provided the variation that kept England's batters perpetually uncertain, never able to settle into the kind of counter-attacking rhythm that has served them so well in home conditions.

What McCullum must now confront is whether the philosophy he has built so carefully over the past two years is adaptable enough to survive this examination. His answer, in private at least, will almost certainly be yes. He is not a man given to public doubt or strategic retreat. But the evidence from Mumbai demands honest reflection, and even his most committed supporters would concede that England have yet to demonstrate convincingly that they can compete with India on Indian pitches over a full five-day examination. Hyderabad, where the fourth Test begins on Friday, will offer an immediate chance to respond.

Downing Street moved to draw a line under weeks of cabinet turbulence on Monday, insisting that the government's spending review had been finalised and that ministers were now united behind the chancellor's fiscal framework.

A spokesman for the Prime Minister said that the process of allocating departmental budgets had been concluded following a series of intense negotiations between the Treasury and Whitehall departments, some of which had pushed back against settlement figures they regarded as inadequate. The spokesman declined to characterise the discussions as fractious, instead describing them as "robust and thorough", consistent with any serious exercise in public finance.

The announcement came after several days of briefings and counter-briefings from unnamed officials, which had suggested that at least two cabinet ministers were threatening to go public with their frustration at cuts to their departmental budgets. Health and defence had both been cited in reports as areas of particular contention, though the spokesman refused to confirm or deny the specifics of individual settlements ahead of a formal statement to parliament later in the week.

Senior Conservative backbenchers had been pressing Number 10 for clarity, warning that prolonged uncertainty over public spending was undermining confidence in the government's economic management at a time when it could ill afford further bad headlines. Several had privately told the whips' office that they expected a credible commitment to protect front-line services alongside any efficiency savings being demanded of departments.

The chancellor is expected to deliver a full statement to the House of Commons on Thursday, setting out the envelope for each major department over the next three years. Treasury sources indicated that the overall fiscal position remained consistent with the government's stated aim of reducing borrowing as a share of national income, though independent forecasters are likely to scrutinise those projections closely when the figures are published.

The recommendation, which is likely to cause consternation among tea lovers across Britain, comes from Michelle Francl, a professor of chemistry at Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania, who has spent years analysing the molecular science behind the perfect brew.

In her new book, Steeped: The Chemistry of Tea, Francl argues that adding a small pinch of salt to a cup of tea can help counteract the bitter taste that many drinkers find unpleasant. The sodium ions in salt, she explains, have the ability to block the receptors on the tongue that are responsible for detecting bitterness, resulting in a smoother and more rounded flavour.

"The amount of salt we're talking about is tiny," Francl told reporters this week. "We are not talking about making tea taste salty. It is a very small pinch, far less than you would add to any food, but the chemistry suggests it genuinely makes a difference to how we perceive the flavour."

Francl, who describes herself as a devoted tea drinker, also recommends warming the cup before brewing, using water that is just off the boil, and storing tea away from both light and air to preserve the delicate aromatic compounds that give the drink its distinctive character.

The scientist's comments quickly attracted widespread attention on both sides of the Atlantic, with many British tea enthusiasts expressing firm resistance to the idea of tampering with a beverage that many consider a national institution. The US Embassy in London, apparently seeking to distance itself from any potential diplomatic incident, issued a tongue-in-cheek statement on social media declaring that it would not be endorsing the salting of tea.

Francl acknowledged the controversy with good humour, noting that science has never been particularly concerned with tradition, however cherished.

A major fire broke out in the vicinity of St Mary's Stadium on Saturday morning, forcing the postponement of Southampton's Premier League clash with Newcastle United just hours before kick-off.

Thick plumes of black smoke could be seen rising above the city skyline as firefighters from Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service rushed to the scene shortly after 9am. The blaze, which took hold in a commercial premises on Britannia Road, spread rapidly to neighbouring buildings, prompting authorities to establish a wide exclusion zone around the area.

Southampton Football Club released a statement confirming the match, which had been scheduled for a 3pm kick-off, would not go ahead as planned. "Following advice from Hampshire Constabulary and the local authority, we have taken the decision to postpone today's fixture," the statement read. "The safety of our supporters, staff and the wider community must always be our absolute priority."

Thousands of fans who had already begun travelling to the ground were urged to stay away from the area and return home. Stewards and club officials were deployed to key access points around the stadium to redirect supporters and provide information.

Hampshire Constabulary confirmed that road closures were in place across several streets surrounding the ground, with the cordon extending to parts of the city centre. Residents in nearby properties were also evacuated as a precautionary measure while crews worked to bring the fire under control.

No serious injuries had been reported as of early afternoon, though two people were treated at the scene for the effects of smoke inhalation.

The Premier League said it was working with both clubs to identify a suitable date for the rescheduled fixture. Southampton's next home match remains under review pending a full assessment of any structural impact on the surrounding area.

Fiona Harvey, the Scottish woman widely identified as the real-life inspiration behind the stalker character Martha in Netflix's hit drama Baby Reindeer, has announced her intention to pursue legal action against the streaming giant and the show's creator Richard Gadd, claiming the series defamed her and caused irreparable damage to her reputation.

Harvey, who gave a widely discussed interview to Piers Morgan in which she denied many of the central claims made in the drama, said she had instructed lawyers to begin proceedings against Netflix and Gadd. The show, which became one of Netflix's most-watched programmes of the year, depicts a character based on Gadd's own experiences of being stalked, with the Martha character portrayed as having a history of criminal convictions for harassment and stalking behaviour.

Speaking through her legal representatives, Harvey maintained that she had never been convicted of any criminal offence and that the portrayal of her as a dangerous and obsessive stalker was entirely false. She argued that Netflix's decision to market the drama as a "true story" had led millions of viewers to believe the fictionalised account was an accurate representation of real events, leaving her exposed to widespread public hatred and abuse online.

Netflix has previously defended the series, stating that Baby Reindeer is a "dramatised story inspired by real events" and that the characters depicted are fictionalised. The company added that it takes the welfare of all individuals connected to its productions seriously.

Legal experts have suggested that any defamation claim would face significant hurdles, noting that Harvey was never named directly in the series and that proving the show presented false facts rather than dramatic interpretation would be a considerable challenge in both British and American courts. Richard Gadd has not yet made any public statement in response to the announced legal action.

A retired schoolteacher from Mumbai has filed a police complaint alleging that a branch manager at one of India's largest private lenders siphoned nearly 160 million rupees — equivalent to approximately 1.9 million US dollars — from her savings account over a period of several years without her knowledge.

Meena Sharma, 67, told investigators that she first became aware of the alleged fraud when she visited her local ICICI Bank branch in the Andheri district of Mumbai last month to make a routine withdrawal and was informed that her account balance was significantly lower than expected. When she requested a detailed statement, she said she discovered hundreds of transactions she had never authorised.

"I trusted this man completely," Mrs Sharma said outside the city's Versova police station, where she filed her complaint last Tuesday. "He would call me personally, tell me my money was safe, and I believed him. I am completely devastated."

The accused, identified by police only as a 44-year-old branch manager who had worked at the bank for over a decade, was arrested on Wednesday and is currently being held in judicial custody. Investigators allege he used his privileged access to the bank's internal systems to divert funds into a network of third-party accounts, some of which have been traced to shell companies registered in Gujarat and Telangana.

A spokesperson for ICICI Bank issued a brief statement acknowledging the incident and expressing regret, saying the bank had cooperated fully with authorities from the moment the complaint was received. "We take any breach of customer trust with the utmost seriousness," the statement read. "An internal investigation is underway and we are committed to ensuring our customer is made whole."

The Economic Offences Wing of the Mumbai Police has taken over the investigation and officials say further arrests may follow as the probe widens.

She arrived at the MTV Video Music Awards dressed as a towering medieval queen, her crimson gown trailing behind her like a war banner, her makeup applied with the subtlety of a Renaissance painting brought to spectacular, gaudy life. For anyone who had not yet encountered Chappell Roan, the entrance was a statement of intent. For her devoted fanbase, who call themselves the Pink Pony Club, it was simply Tuesday.

The 26-year-old Missouri native born Kayleigh Rose Amstutz has spent the past year becoming one of the most thrilling and unlikely success stories in contemporary pop music. Her debut album, "The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess," released in 2023, took its time finding its audience, but when it did, it ignited something close to a cultural phenomenon. Songs like "Good Luck, Babe!" and "Red Wine Supernova" became inescapable fixtures of summer playlists, their euphoric synth hooks and emotionally raw lyrics connecting with listeners in a way that felt genuinely rare.

What separates Roan from the crowded field of singer-songwriters angling for a mainstream breakthrough is a commitment to spectacle that never feels cynical. Her live performances are elaborate, campy affairs that draw heavily from drag culture and 1980s pop theatrics, yet they carry an emotional sincerity that disarms even the most skeptical observers. She writes openly about queer identity, heartbreak and the disorienting experience of growing up in a small town while feeling fundamentally, irreparably different from everyone around you.

Industry insiders who watched her grind through years of relative obscurity, including a period when she was quietly dropped by her first record label, say her current success feels hard-won in a way that the music itself reflects. There is nothing accidental about Chappell Roan. Every sequin is deliberate.

A 26-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder following the deaths of three women who were killed in a crossbow attack at a house in Bushey, Hertfordshire, police have confirmed.

Officers were called to a property in Caldwell Road in the early hours of the morning after reports of a disturbance.
