Upon arrival, they discovered the bodies of three women, believed to be members of the same family, who had suffered fatal injuries consistent with crossbow wounds. Despite the efforts of paramedics, all three were pronounced dead at the scene.

The suspect, who has not been formally named by police, was located and detained a short distance from the property several hours after the alarm was raised. Hertfordshire Constabulary said the arrest followed an extensive search of the surrounding area, during which a number of roads were closed and residents were urged to remain indoors as a precautionary measure.

Detective Chief Superintendent Adam Willard, who is leading the investigation, said officers were not looking for anyone else in connection with the incident and that the public should not be alarmed. He added that specially trained family liaison officers had been deployed to support relatives of the victims at what he described as an "utterly devastating" time.

Neighbours in the quiet residential street expressed shock at the events, with several describing the area as a close-knit and peaceful community. One resident, who asked not to be named, said she had heard a commotion in the early hours but had not realised the gravity of what had occurred until police vehicles arrived in large numbers.

A scene guard remains in place at the property while forensic investigators carry out detailed examinations. The suspect is currently in police custody, where he is expected to be questioned by detectives in the coming hours.

For weeks, they had filled the streets in their thousands, facing down tear gas and rubber bullets, watching friends fall beside them in the sweltering summer heat. Now, with Sheikh Hasina gone — her helicopter lifting from the prime ministerial compound as the crowds surged toward the capital — the young people who drove her from power are beginning to imagine what Bangladesh might look like without the woman who governed it for fifteen years.

At Dhaka University, long considered the spiritual heart of the protest movement, students gathered in clusters on Tuesday, some still wearing the bandages that bore witness to the violence of recent weeks. The mood was cautious, electric, unsteady — the particular atmosphere of a country suspended between what it was and what it might become.

"We didn't do this for any party," said Nadia Rahman, 22, a third-year economics student who had been on the streets since the demonstrations began in July over civil service quotas and swelled into something far larger and harder to contain. "We did this for Bangladesh. Now we have to make sure nobody steals it from us."

That anxiety — that the sacrifice of hundreds of lives might be absorbed by old power structures, by the military, by opposition figures waiting in the wings — runs through almost every conversation here. The army has promised to maintain order and facilitate a transitional government, a pledge met with hope and deep suspicion in equal measure.

Muhammad Yunus, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning economist and microcredit pioneer, has emerged as a figure many protesters are willing to trust, at least for now. His name is spoken with a kind of tentative reverence among students who say they want technocrats and reformers rather than politicians who have simply been waiting for their turn.

Scotland's long-suffering football supporters have endured many dark nights over the decades, but few could have predicted quite how dramatically the curtain would come down on their latest campaign. A defeat in Seville on Tuesday evening, coupled with a draw in the other group fixture, confirmed what many had quietly feared since the opening match: Scotland will not be making the journey to next summer's tournament.

For the thousands of fans who had made the trip to Spain, draped in saltires and armed with the customary good humour that has become the Tartan Army's calling card on the international stage, there was no disguising the disappointment this time. The songs dried up long before the final whistle, and the walk back through the city's narrow streets had a hollow, deflated quality that no amount of local hospitality could soften.

The campaign had promised much after a bright start, and manager Steve Clarke had spoken with quiet confidence about his side's ability to compete with the group's stronger nations. But a combination of poor finishing, defensive uncertainty and two costly draws against opponents Scotland would have expected to beat ultimately proved fatal to their hopes. They finish the group with eight points, a tally that in almost any other section of the competition would have been sufficient to progress.

For the supporters, the familiar rituals of consolation will now begin. The post-mortem debates in pubs and podcasts, the pointed questions about squad selection and tactical decisions, the tentative glances toward the next qualifying cycle. Some of those in Seville last night have followed their country to every corner of the continent for thirty years or more. They know better than most how to absorb this kind of blow.

Whether the players feel that pain as keenly is the question Clarke will need to answer in the difficult weeks ahead.

Federal investigators have launched an extensive effort to locate and contact the families of all 270 people killed in the 1988 Lockerbie bombing, as the United States prepares for the trial of the only surviving suspect in the attack, the FBI has confirmed.

Agents have been working across multiple countries to trace relatives of victims who died when Pan Am Flight 103 was destroyed over the Scottish town of Lockerbie on December 21, 1988, in what remains one of the deadliest terrorist attacks in aviation history. The outreach effort is intended to ensure that families are kept informed of proceedings and have the opportunity to participate in the justice process.

Abu Agila Mohammad Masud, a former Libyan intelligence officer, was transferred to US custody in 2022 and faces charges of bombing a commercial aircraft and destroying a vehicle used in interstate commerce, among other counts. Prosecutors allege he constructed the improvised explosive device that brought down the Boeing 747, killing all 259 passengers and crew on board as well as 11 residents of Lockerbie on the ground.

FBI victim specialists have been coordinating with counterparts in Scotland, the United Kingdom and across Europe to reach families who have had little consistent contact with American authorities over the decades since the attack. Officials say they are determined that no family should feel excluded from the proceedings.

"Every single victim deserves to have their family represented and informed throughout this process," said one senior official familiar with the investigation. "We owe that to the people who have waited more than 35 years for justice."

Victim advocates have broadly welcomed the initiative, though some family members have expressed frustration at what they describe as the slow pace of the case, noting that many relatives who devoted their lives to pursuing justice have since died without seeing a conviction.

Ange Postecoglou has insisted he has no intention of abandoning the attacking philosophy that has defined his managerial career, despite Tottenham Hotspur's inconsistent form leaving the club languishing in the bottom half of the Premier League table.

The Australian head coach, who guided Spurs to an encouraging eighth-place finish in his debut season in north London, has faced mounting pressure in recent weeks following a string of damaging results that have left supporters and pundits questioning whether his high-risk, high-line approach is sustainable at the top level of English football.

But Postecoglou struck a defiant tone ahead of his side's upcoming fixture, making clear that any suggestion he might soften his methods or retreat into a more conservative tactical setup would be firmly rejected.

"I'm in a fight, and I know I'm in a fight," he told reporters at his pre-match press conference. "But the answer for me is never to walk away from what I believe in. If anything, I'm going to double down. That's always been my way. The moment you start compromising your principles because things get difficult, you've already lost something that you can't get back."

Postecoglou acknowledged that the squad's injury problems have significantly hampered his ability to implement his system with any consistency, with key players across all areas of the pitch missing for extended periods. He argued that the difficulties Spurs are experiencing are circumstantial rather than structural, and expressed confidence that the underlying work being done on the training ground would ultimately bear fruit.

"People want quick fixes and simple explanations," he said. "But building something that lasts takes time and it takes courage. I'm not here to manage for the short term. I'm here to build something that this club and these supporters can be genuinely proud of."

New Zealand advanced to the semi-finals of the Women's T20 World Cup after a commanding victory over Pakistan in a must-win group stage match that kept their tournament hopes alive and ended their opponents' chances of progression.

The White Ferns posted a competitive total after being put in to bat, with opener Suzie Bates once again proving her worth at the top of the order. Bates struck a fluent half-century, finding the boundary with ease against a Pakistan bowling attack that struggled to maintain consistent lines and lengths in the early stages of the innings. Sophie Devine contributed a steady knock in the middle order as New Zealand finished with a defendable total that ultimately proved more than enough.

Pakistan's chase began brightly, with their openers putting on a promising partnership that briefly raised hopes of a potential upset. However, once New Zealand's spinners were introduced into the attack, the momentum shifted decisively. Lea Tahuhu and Amelia Kerr proved particularly difficult to get away, taking wickets at crucial intervals and strangling the run rate as Pakistan's lower order struggled to keep pace with the required asking rate.

Pakistan were eventually dismissed well short of their target, with the defeat confirming their elimination from the tournament having failed to register a victory across their group stage campaign.

New Zealand, by contrast, will now prepare for a semi-final appearance after navigating what had been an inconsistent group stage of their own. Coach Ben Sawyer expressed relief and satisfaction at the final result, praising the collective effort from his squad.

"We knew what was at stake and the players responded brilliantly," Sawyer said. "There's real belief in this group and we're looking forward to the semi-final."

The result sets up what promises to be an intriguing last-four stage, with New Zealand's opponents to be confirmed following the conclusion of the remaining group matches.

The statistics told a damning story. For all the optimism that accompanied Ruben Amorim's arrival at Old Trafford last month, Saturday's 1-1 draw with Chelsea served as a sobering reminder of just how much work lies ahead for the Portuguese manager as he attempts to rebuild one of football's most storied clubs.

United looked disjointed and laboured for long stretches of a match they were fortunate not to lose, with Chelsea's Nicolas Jackson squandering two gilt-edged chances in the second half that would have condemned the hosts to yet another defeat. Cole Palmer's first-half opener, a characteristic piece of individual brilliance that cut through United's defensive structure with alarming ease, seemed to encapsulate everything that is wrong with this current squad.

Bruno Fernandes's equaliser from the penalty spot offered some relief, but it papered over considerable cracks. United managed just three shots on target across 90 minutes, and their attempts to implement Amorim's preferred 3-4-3 system appeared stilted and uncertain, with players visibly unsure of their positioning and responsibilities when the opposition pressed with any intensity.

Speaking after the final whistle, Amorim was characteristically candid. "We know the situation," the 39-year-old said. "We are working hard every day but you cannot change everything in a few weeks. The players are trying to understand what I want but it takes time and we have to be honest about that."

That honesty, while refreshing, underlines the scale of the challenge. United sit in the lower half of the Premier League table, their squad a patchwork of expensive misadventures and unfulfilled potential accumulated across years of poor recruitment. For Amorim, transforming this group into genuine title contenders feels less like a short-term project and considerably more like an act of footballing archaeology.

Millions of passengers across England will see their bus fares rise by up to £1 from next month, after the government confirmed it would increase the cap on single journeys from £2 to £3, bringing an end to a scheme that was introduced to encourage people back onto public transport following the pandemic.

The fare cap, which was originally set at £2 in January 2023, had been widely praised by commuters and campaigners who said it had made buses a genuinely affordable option for people on lower incomes and those living in areas with limited transport alternatives. Passenger groups warned that the rise represented a 50 per cent increase in the maximum cost of a journey and would price some of the most vulnerable travellers off the network entirely.

The government insisted the revised cap still represented a significant protection for passengers, noting that without any ceiling on fares, some single tickets could cost considerably more. Ministers said the original £2 scheme had been intended as a temporary measure and that sustaining it at that level was no longer financially viable given pressures on public spending.

Bus operators had been lobbying for relief from the cap, arguing that rising fuel costs, driver wages and vehicle maintenance expenses had made it increasingly difficult to run services profitably within the existing limit. Several smaller operators had warned they would be forced to cut routes or reduce frequency if the subsidy arrangement was not revised.

Campaigners from the Campaign for Better Transport said the increase risked reversing gains made in bus passenger numbers over the past two years. "People chose the bus because it was affordable," said a spokesperson for the group. "If that changes, many of them will simply get back in their cars or stop making journeys altogether, and that is bad for congestion, bad for emissions and bad for communities."

Aston Villa have moved swiftly to bolster their squad ahead of the January transfer window closing, completing the signing of former Real Madrid winger Marco Asensio on a permanent deal while also securing the loan arrival of Chelsea defender Axel Disasi.

Asensio, 28, joins Villa following a spell at Paris Saint-Germain, where the Spaniard struggled to hold down a regular starting position despite showing flashes of the form that made him one of the most coveted players in Europe during his time at the Bernabeu. The winger, who contributed significantly to Real Madrid's Champions League triumphs, is expected to bring creativity and experience to Unai Emery's side as they continue to push for European qualification.

Villa head coach Emery, who worked with Asensio during their time together in Spain, is said to have been instrumental in persuading the former international to make the move to Villa Park. Sources close to the club have confirmed the fee is in the region of £15 million, with the deal including performance-related add-ons.

The arrival of Disasi on a loan deal until the end of the season provides further reinforcement at the back, where Villa have been dealing with injury concerns in recent weeks. The French international centre-back has found first-team opportunities limited at Stamford Bridge this season following the considerable investment Chelsea have made in their defensive options. Disasi, 26, made over 30 appearances in all competitions for Chelsea last season and will be eager to rediscover his best form under Emery's guidance.

Villa sporting director Monchi, who has played a crucial role in shaping the club's recruitment strategy since his appointment, is believed to have been working on both deals for several weeks. The double swoop takes Villa's January spending to a significant level as they look to maintain their impressive form in the Premier League.

The man, who is in his 30s, was found with serious injuries to his arms and legs in a car park off Main Street shortly after 22:00 on Saturday. He was taken to hospital, where his condition is described as stable.

Police said he was attacked by a group of men, at least one of whom was armed with a wooden bat with nails driven through it. The attackers are believed to have left the scene on foot towards the Dunluce Road area.

A detective leading the investigation called the assault "a vicious and sustained attack on a man who was left with significant wounds."

"This happened in a public place at a time when people were still out and about in the village," the officer said. "I would ask anyone who was in the area and saw a group of men acting suspiciously, or who has dashcam or doorbell footage, to contact us."

Police have not said what motivated the attack and are keeping an open mind.

Residents of the small County Antrim village, better known for its distillery and as a gateway to the Giant's Causeway, said they were stunned.

"It's just awful," said one woman who lives nearby and did not want to be named. "You don't expect something like that here. This is a quiet place. People walk their dogs through that car park every night."

A local councillor said the community was "shocked and sickened."

"Whoever did this has no place in our village," the councillor said. "Nobody has the right to carry out this kind of brutality, and I would urge anyone with information, however small, to bring it to the police."

The car park was cordoned off for several hours on Sunday morning while forensic officers examined the scene.

Anyone with information can contact police on 101 or pass details anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

The company behind the spacecraft, Pittsburgh-based Astrobotic Technology, confirmed that it lost contact with Peregrine shortly before the lander re-entered Earth's atmosphere over a remote stretch of the South Pacific on Thursday afternoon. Any debris that survived the fiery descent is expected to have fallen harmlessly into the ocean.

The outcome brings a disappointing end to a mission that had been billed as the first American attempt to land softly on the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972, and the first ever by a private company.

Peregrine launched on 8 January aboard the maiden flight of United Launch Alliance's new Vulcan rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The launch itself went smoothly, but within hours of separating from the rocket, the lander suffered what engineers described as a "critical loss of propellant." A leak in its propulsion system made it impossible to reach the Moon and land.

Rather than leave the crippled spacecraft drifting in deep space, where it might eventually pose a hazard to other satellites, Astrobotic's team chose to steer it back towards Earth for a controlled destruction.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, we have learned an enormous amount," the company said in a statement, adding that the flight had proved many of Peregrine's systems worked as designed in the harsh environment of space.

The lander had been carrying 20 payloads, including five scientific instruments from NASA, which paid Astrobotic more than $100m (£79m) under its Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme. The agency hopes such private missions will help pave the way for astronauts to return to the lunar surface later this decade.

Also aboard were more unusual cargoes, including cremated human remains and DNA samples sent by memorial spaceflight firms, an inclusion that had drawn objections from the Navajo Nation, which considers the Moon sacred.

Another US company, Intuitive Machines, is preparing to make its own landing attempt next month.

The Foreign Secretary's visit to New Delhi, coming just weeks after Labour's general election victory, is being seen as a deliberate signal that the new government regards India as a priority partner rather than an afterthought. Officials say Mr Lammy chose India as one of his first major bilateral destinations to underline Labour's ambition to deepen economic, security and technological cooperation with the world's most populous nation.

Central to the discussions is the long-stalled free trade agreement, which has been under negotiation since early 2022. Successive Conservative governments set and missed several deadlines for a deal, with talks snagging on issues including tariffs on Scotch whisky and cars, access for Indian professionals to UK visas, and the treatment of services. Labour has said it is committed to concluding an agreement that works for both sides, and Mr Lammy is expected to press for momentum in the negotiations while stressing that the UK will not rush into a deal at any cost.

Beyond trade, the trip is expected to focus on cooperation in critical and emerging technologies, including semiconductors, artificial intelligence, telecoms and clean energy. Climate finance and the transition away from fossil fuels are also on the agenda, as is collaboration on security in the Indo-Pacific region.

Diplomats acknowledge that the relationship carries sensitivities. Labour's past positions on Kashmir have previously drawn criticism from New Delhi, and the party has worked in recent years to rebuild trust with both the Indian government and British Indian communities, among whom it made notable electoral gains.

Mr Lammy has framed his approach to foreign policy around what he calls "progressive realism," arguing that Britain must engage pragmatically with rising powers in the Global South. Analysts say India, with its fast-growing economy and expanding geopolitical influence, is a natural test of that philosophy, and that early, high-level engagement could help set the tone for the years ahead.

The inquiry heard that Ms Vennells, who led the Post Office from 2012 to 2019, told MPs in 2015 that the organisation had found no evidence of miscarriages of justice linked to its Horizon IT system. She also assured them that it was not possible for branch accounts to be altered remotely without a subpostmaster's knowledge.

Counsel for the inquiry suggested that information available within the Post Office at the time contradicted those assurances. In particular, concerns had been raised internally about bugs in the system and about the ability of staff at Fujitsu, which developed Horizon, to access branch data remotely. Lawyers representing former subpostmasters went further, accusing the former chief executive of knowingly giving Parliament a false picture of the scandal while victims were still fighting to clear their names.

Ms Vennells has previously said she relied on advice from colleagues and external experts and was not aware of the full extent of the system's problems. In earlier evidence to the inquiry, she apologised repeatedly to those affected and became emotional as she acknowledged that she had been too willing to trust what she was told.

More than 900 subpostmasters were prosecuted between 1999 and 2015 on the basis of faulty Horizon data, in what has been described as the most widespread miscarriage of justice in British legal history. Many were sent to prison, made bankrupt or left unable to work, and some have since died without seeing their convictions overturned.

Campaigners watching the proceedings said the evidence reinforced their long-held belief that senior management had been more concerned with protecting the Post Office's reputation than with uncovering the truth.

The inquiry, chaired by retired High Court judge Sir Wyn Williams, is examining who knew what about Horizon's flaws, and when. Its findings could inform any future decisions on criminal or civil action against individuals involved. Ms Vennells returned her CBE earlier this year following public outrage over the scandal.

The guidance, published on Tuesday, recommends that children under the age of 11 should be given only basic phones capable of calls and texts, rather than internet-connected smartphones. For those aged 11 to 13, EE suggests that a smartphone may be appropriate, but only with parental controls switched on and without access to social media apps.

From 13 onwards, the company says, parents might consider allowing social media, provided that accounts are linked to family-sharing tools so that screen time and content can be monitored. Teenagers aged 16 and over should be given more independence, according to the guidance, though EE still encourages families to keep talking openly about how phones are being used.

The move is unusual for a mobile operator, whose business depends in part on selling handsets and data contracts. A spokesperson for the company said it had a responsibility to help families make informed decisions and acknowledged that many parents felt under pressure to hand over a smartphone simply because their child's friends already had one.

The intervention comes amid a growing national debate over children's use of technology. Campaign groups formed by parents have urged families to delay giving children smartphones until at least the start of secondary school. Many schools have introduced restrictions or outright bans on phones during the school day. Ofcom research suggests that a large majority of children own a smartphone by the time they are 12, with ownership common well before that age.

Child safety campaigners welcomed EE's stance but warned that guidance alone would not solve the problem. They argued that technology companies and social media platforms must also do more to make their services safe by design, rather than placing the burden on parents.

Some parents, however, have questioned whether basic phones are realistic when schools, clubs and friendship groups increasingly rely on messaging apps to organise activities.

Manchester United have decided to keep Erik ten Hag as manager after an end-of-season review of the club's football operations concluded that the Dutchman should be given the chance to build on his FA Cup triumph.

The decision ends weeks of uncertainty over the 54-year-old's future. Speculation had grown throughout a turbulent campaign, and it intensified after United finished eighth in the Premier League, their lowest top-flight finish since 1990. The club also suffered 14 league defeats and finished bottom of their Champions League group.

Ten Hag's position was transformed on 25 May, when goals from Alejandro Garnacho and Kobbie Mainoo secured a 2-1 victory over rivals Manchester City at Wembley. The win delivered a second trophy in as many seasons, following the Carabao Cup success of 2023, and secured a place in the Europa League.

The review was led by Sir Jim Ratcliffe's Ineos group, which took control of football operations after completing its purchase of a minority stake earlier this year. Senior figures including Sir Dave Brailsford, incoming chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox were involved in the process. Club sources had confirmed that alternative candidates were considered, with reports linking Thomas Tuchel, Mauricio Pochettino and Ipswich Town's Kieran McKenna with the role.

Ultimately, the hierarchy are understood to have been persuaded by Ten Hag's record of silverware, his work with young players such as Mainoo and Garnacho, and the extensive injury problems that disrupted the squad for much of the season. At times United were without as many as ten first-team players.

Attention will now turn to Ten Hag's contract, which is due to expire in the summer of 2025. Discussions over an extension are expected to begin shortly, as the club prepares for a significant summer transfer window aimed at strengthening a squad that conceded more league goals last season than in any campaign for decades.

Federer, whose rivalry with Nadal defined an era of men's tennis, was among the first to respond. In a post on social media, the Swiss, who retired in 2022 with Nadal at his side, wrote that he had always hoped "this day would never come," and thanked his long-time opponent for the unforgettable memories and achievements in "the game we love."

Djokovic, who faced Nadal 60 times, more than any other pairing in the Open era, said one message was not enough to express the respect he had for the Spaniard and everything he had done for the sport. The Serb described Nadal as a source of motivation that pushed him to new levels and said his legacy would "live forever."

The pair's words were echoed across the sport. Carlos Alcaraz, widely seen as Nadal's heir in Spanish tennis, said he was grateful to have shared the court with his idol, while Andy Murray, who also retired this year, paid tribute to a rival he had battled since their junior days.

Nadal, 38, confirmed his decision in a video message, saying the past two years had been "very difficult" as he struggled with a series of injuries, including a hip problem that kept him out for most of 2023. He will bow out at the Davis Cup Finals in Malaga in November, representing Spain in front of a home crowd.

The left-hander leaves the game with 22 Grand Slam singles titles, including a record 14 at the French Open, where he lost only four matches in nearly two decades. He also won Olympic gold in singles at Beijing 2008 and in doubles at Rio 2016, and helped Spain lift the Davis Cup five times.

"It is a decision that took me time to make," Nadal said. "But in this life everything has a beginning and an end."

The family said they had been left with "more questions than answers" after the hearing concluded, more than two years after the three-year-old was struck while walking with her mother.

Pearl had been on the pavement when an unoccupied vehicle rolled down a sloping street and mounted the kerb. Paramedics and an air ambulance crew treated her at the scene, but she died in hospital later that day.

In a statement released through their solicitor, her parents said they had been "utterly let down" by the agencies they had trusted to establish what happened to their daughter.

"From the very first day, we were promised a thorough investigation," they said. "Instead we have watched delay after delay, been given conflicting information, and have had to fight for answers that should have been offered to us freely. Pearl deserved better than this, and so does every family who goes through what we have."

They described their daughter as "a bright, funny, fearless little girl who filled every room with noise and joy," adding that the house had been "unbearably quiet" since her death.

The couple said they were particularly frustrated that key evidence, including the vehicle's mechanical condition and whether the handbrake had been properly applied, had not been fully examined until many months after the collision.

A spokesperson for the force involved said officers "fully understand the family's distress" and that the investigation had been "complex and carried out with care." They added that a review of how the case had been handled was under way and that the force would "reflect on any lessons that can be learned."

The family is now calling for a change in the law to make it a specific offence to leave a vehicle in a state that allows it to roll away. They said they would continue campaigning "so that no other parent has to stand where we are standing today."

Nga wai hono i te po Paki, 27, was named the new Māori monarch on Thursday at Tūrangawaewae Marae in Ngāruawāhia, hours before her father, King Tūheitia, was laid to rest on the sacred Taupiri mountain.

The decision was made by a council of tribal leaders on the final day of a six-day tangihanga, or funeral ceremony, that drew tens of thousands of mourners to the Waikato region of New Zealand's North Island. Her selection surprised some observers, who had expected one of Tūheitia's two older sons to succeed him.

In a ceremony steeped in tradition, she was blessed with the same Bible used to anoint the first Māori king, Pōtatau Te Wherowhero, in 1858. She sat on her father's carved wooden throne as chants and haka rang out across the marae. Ngā wai hono i te po is the second woman to hold the title. Her grandmother, Dame Te Atairangikaahu, reigned for four decades until her death in 2006.

After the coronation, Tūheitia's casket was carried by a flotilla of waka, or traditional canoes, along the Waikato River to the foot of Taupiri, where he was buried alongside his ancestors in a private ceremony. Tūheitia, who had reigned for 18 years, died last week aged 69, days after undergoing heart surgery.

The Kīngitanga, or Māori King Movement, was established in the 19th century to unite iwi under a single sovereign and to resist the loss of land to British colonisers. Although the monarch has no legal or constitutional power, the role carries considerable cultural and political weight.

The new queen takes the throne at a time of tension between many Māori and New Zealand's centre-right coalition government, whose policies on Māori language, health and the Treaty of Waitangi have sparked protests. Earlier this year her father convened a national hui, or gathering, attended by thousands, to call for Māori unity in response.

Liverpool's injury-ravaged squad looked set to drop points in their title race until Darwin Nunez rose to head home Alexis Mac Allister's cross deep into stoppage time, sending the away end at the City Ground into delirium.

The Uruguay striker, only recently back in contention after a spell on the sidelines, had come off the bench in the second half as Jurgen Klopp searched for a breakthrough against a resolute Forest side. With the clock showing 99 minutes, Nunez found space at the back post and directed his header past Matz Sels to snatch all three points.

Klopp, who had watched his makeshift side huff and puff for long periods, raced onto the pitch at the final whistle before turning to the travelling supporters and pumping his fists in celebration.

The victory, achieved without several first-choice players, moved Liverpool four points clear at the top of the Premier League table, at least until their rivals play.

Forest, however, were left fuming over the sequence of play leading to the goal. Play had been halted moments earlier for an injury, and the hosts felt the restart should have favoured them rather than Liverpool. Nuno Espirito Santo's side were visibly furious at the final whistle, with players and staff surrounding referee Paul Tierney as tempers flared on the touchline.

For much of the afternoon, it had seemed Forest would earn a deserved point in their fight against relegation. They defended deep and in numbers, frustrating Liverpool's young and inexperienced line-up, and carried a genuine threat on the counter-attack. Caoimhin Kelleher was called into action on several occasions to keep the scores level.

Liverpool's frustration grew as chances came and went, with the visitors failing to test Sels with any regularity before the interval.

But once again this season, Klopp's side showed their capacity to find a way, producing a late moment of drama that may yet prove decisive in the title run-in.

The decision follows the death of a 14-year-old boy who was stabbed outside a school in the capital, Tirana, in November. Police said the fight began after an argument between pupils on social media, and that a fellow student had been arrested. Videos about the dispute, some of them appearing to back the attack, later spread across several platforms. The killing caused alarm among parents and teachers across the country.

Announcing the measure after meeting educators and parents' groups, Prime Minister Edi Rama said the platform would be shut down for a year from early 2025. He argued that the problem lay not with young people but with the platform itself. Rama described TikTok as a "thug of the neighbourhood" that was holding children hostage.

Rama also contrasted the app with Douyin, the version available in China, which he said promotes educational content to young users and limits their screen time. He said Albania would use the year to introduce new safety programmes in schools, and to train parents to monitor their children's online activity.

TikTok responded by saying it was seeking "urgent clarity" from the Albanian government. The company said it had found no evidence that either the victim or the attacker had accounts on the platform. It added that many of the videos linked to the incident had been posted on other apps, not TikTok.

The ban has drawn criticism from opposition politicians and some civil society groups. They warned that it sets a troubling precedent for freedom of expression, coming months before parliamentary elections. Some business owners who rely on the app to reach customers also voiced concern about the economic impact.

Albania joins a growing number of countries that have restricted the app, though most other bans have been limited to government devices or prompted by security concerns rather than child safety.

At a state university in the Midwest, a graduate student from South Asia says she has stopped attending evening seminars. She now carries her passport, visa documents and enrollment letter in her backpack at all times, and she has memorized the phone number of an immigration lawyer.

"Every morning I check the news before I check my email," said the student, who asked not to be named for fear of drawing attention to her visa status. "I haven't done anything wrong. But I don't know anymore if that matters."

Her unease is shared by many of the hundreds of thousands of international students enrolled at American colleges and universities. In recent weeks, reports of student visas being revoked and students being detained have spread rapidly through group chats and campus forums. Some cases involve participation in political protests. Others involve minor legal infractions that students say were resolved years ago.

University administrators have struggled to respond. Several institutions have issued guidance advising international students to reconsider travel abroad, even during academic breaks, out of concern they may not be allowed back into the country. Some international student offices say they have learned of revoked visas only after checking federal databases, not through direct notification.

"We are hearing from students who are terrified," said an adviser at a large public university on the East Coast. "They want to know whether they should finish the semester, whether they should go home, whether they should stop posting online. Often we don't have clear answers to give them."

Faculty members have also raised concerns. Some research labs depend heavily on international doctoral candidates, and professors worry the climate could deter future applicants.

Immigration attorneys say demand for consultations has surged. Many are urging students to keep copies of their records and to know their rights if they are questioned by authorities.

The filing, lodged in Texas on Monday, comes just a day after the Canadian rapper submitted a similar petition in New York, as his long-running feud with Lamar moves from the recording studio to the courtroom.

In the latest documents, Drake's lawyers accuse Universal Music Group (UMG), which represents both artists, of conspiring to manipulate the success of Not Like Us. They allege that the label paid, or arranged for third parties to pay, radio giant iHeartRadio to promote the track, a practice known as "payola" that is illegal in the United States if the payments are not disclosed to listeners.

The petition also claims that the song, which became one of the defining hits of the year, contains defamatory material. Not Like Us includes lyrics accusing Drake of predatory behaviour towards minors, an allegation the rapper has consistently and strongly denied.

Neither petition is a lawsuit in itself. Both are pre-action filings, which allow a party to gather evidence and question potential defendants before deciding whether to bring a full case. Lamar is not named in either document.

The New York petition, filed by Drake's company Frozen Moments LLC, alleges that UMG and Spotify used "bots" to artificially inflate streams of the track. It further claims the streaming service was offered reduced licensing rates in exchange for promoting the song, suggestions that have been flatly rejected.

UMG has dismissed the claims as offensive and untrue, insisting that it follows ethical marketing practices and that fans decide which music they want to hear. Spotify and iHeartRadio have not publicly commented on the specific allegations.

Not Like Us, released in May at the height of the rappers' public dispute, topped the Billboard Hot 100 and has since received several Grammy nominations, including for record and song of the year.

Legal experts have suggested that the filings face significant hurdles, noting that proving deliberate manipulation of streaming figures or radio play can be difficult.

Federal investigators said Thursday that they no longer believe anyone else helped plan or carry out the New Orleans attack, reversing an earlier assessment that the driver may have had accomplices.

Christopher Raia, deputy assistant director of the FBI's Counterterrorism Division, told reporters that a review of surveillance footage, interviews and evidence from the suspect's devices pointed to a single attacker. Several people seen on video near improvised explosive devices planted in the French Quarter had been identified and were not considered involved, officials said.

The suspect, Shamsud-Din Jabbar, a 42-year-old U.S. Army veteran from Texas, drove a rented pickup truck into crowds celebrating the new year on Bourbon Street early Wednesday, killing 14 people and injuring dozens more before he was shot dead in a gunfight with police. An Islamic State flag was found in the truck.

Investigators said Jabbar posted several videos to social media in the hours before the attack in which he expressed support for the Islamic State. In one, officials said, he claimed to have joined the group before the summer and described earlier plans to harm his family. Agents are still working to determine how and when he was radicalized, and whether he had any contact with the group or simply drew inspiration from its propaganda.

Authorities also disclosed that Jabbar had visited New Orleans at least twice in recent months, and that he appeared to have used a pair of camera-equipped smart glasses to record parts of the French Quarter during a trip in the fall.

Officials said they had found no definitive link between the New Orleans attack and the explosion of a Tesla Cybertruck outside a Las Vegas hotel hours later, though both vehicles had been rented through the same app and both drivers had served in the military.

The FBI urged anyone with photos or video from the area to come forward as the investigation continues.

For years, Pablo Virgilio David was one of the most prominent voices in the Philippines condemning the bloody anti-drug campaign waged under former President Rodrigo Duterte. As bishop of Kalookan, a diocese north of Manila that includes some of the capital region's poorest neighborhoods, David saw the toll firsthand. Thousands of people, many of them young men from impoverished communities, were killed in police operations and by unidentified gunmen. He opened church doors to grieving families, helped document killings and spoke out from the pulpit when few others in public life would.

The criticism made him a target. Duterte publicly lashed out at the Catholic hierarchy, singling out outspoken clergy with insults. In 2019, David was among a group of church figures named in an inciting-to-sedition complaint filed by police, a case that was later dismissed. He has said he received death threats during this period.

Through it all, David has described the support he felt from Rome as a source of strength. Pope Francis, who made care for the marginalized a hallmark of his papacy, elevated him to the College of Cardinals in December 2024. The appointment was widely read in the Philippines as an affirmation of the bishop's stance, though the Vatican did not frame it in political terms.

Now 66, David is among the cardinals eligible to vote for Francis's successor. He arrives at the Sistine Chapel as one of the younger members of the conclave and as a representative of a country where roughly eight in ten people identify as Catholic, one of the largest Catholic populations in the world.

His elevation came only months before a dramatic turn at home. In March 2025, Duterte was arrested and flown to The Hague to face charges at the International Criminal Court over the drug war killings. For families David had ministered to, it was a moment many had long doubted would ever come.

US Secretary of State Antony Blinken has said the toll the war in Gaza is taking on children is "far too high," in some of his sharpest remarks yet on the human cost of Israel's military campaign.

Speaking to reporters during his latest visit to the region, Mr Blinken said Washington continued to support Israel's right to defend itself after the 7 October attacks, but stressed that how it does so matters. "Far too many Palestinians have been killed, far too many have suffered," he said, adding that the images of injured and displaced children were something "none of us can ignore."

According to the Hamas-run health ministry in Gaza, thousands of children are among those killed since the conflict began, and UN agencies say many more have been wounded, orphaned or forced from their homes. The UN children's agency, Unicef, has warned that Gaza has become one of the most dangerous places in the world to be a child, with shortages of clean water, food and medical care threatening those who have survived the bombardment.

Mr Blinken said he had raised the issue directly with Israeli leaders, urging them to take "every possible step" to protect civilians and to allow a greater flow of humanitarian aid into the territory. He said the US was also pressing for longer pauses in the fighting to enable the delivery of supplies and the release of hostages still held in Gaza.

Israeli officials say they are targeting Hamas fighters and infrastructure, and accuse the group of embedding itself among the civilian population, putting non-combatants in harm's way.

Aid organisations, however, say current measures fall well short of what is needed. Several have renewed calls for a full ceasefire, arguing that only a sustained halt to hostilities can prevent the humanitarian crisis from deepening further as winter approaches.

The decision brings a brutal end to Lawson's tenure at the senior team after just two grands prix. The New Zealander struggled badly in Australia and China, qualifying near the back of the grid at both events and failing to score a point. Tsunoda will now partner four-time world champion Max Verstappen, while Lawson returns to sister team Racing Bulls alongside rookie Isack Hadjar.

The timing gives the swap an added dimension. Suzuka is Tsunoda's home circuit, and the 24-year-old will make his debut for Red Bull in front of a Japanese crowd that has followed his career closely since he arrived in Formula 1 in 2021. The move also comes in the final season of Red Bull's partnership with Honda, which has long backed Tsunoda's development.

In announcing the change, team principal Christian Horner said the decision had been made early in the season because of how difficult the opening rounds had been. He described Lawson as a talented young driver who still had the team's support, and said the priority was giving him the chance to rebuild his confidence in a more familiar environment at Racing Bulls, where he impressed during his part-season stint in 2024.

Tsunoda had been widely seen as the more experienced candidate when Red Bull chose Lawson to replace Sergio Pérez over the winter, and he has made a strong start to the year with Racing Bulls. His promotion is likely to intensify scrutiny of the RB21, which Verstappen has openly acknowledged is not yet as competitive as rivals McLaren.

For Lawson, the demotion is a painful setback but not necessarily the end of his ambitions. Red Bull has a history of moving drivers between its two teams, and Alex Albon and Pierre Gasly both went on to rebuild their reputations after similar switches.

Lucy Bronze believes England's ability to change their approach mid-match will be key when they face world champions Spain in the Nations League on Friday.

The Lionesses' right-back, who spent two seasons at Barcelona, said the squad had grown more comfortable switching formations and tactics under head coach Sarina Wiegman.

"I think we're one of the most adaptive teams in the world now," Bronze said. "We can play a back three, we can play a back four, we can press high or sit in and hurt teams on the counter. Against a side like Spain, you have to be ready for anything because they'll find the gaps if you're rigid."

England have faced Spain several times since losing to them in the 2023 World Cup final in Sydney, a defeat that still lingers for many of the players who started that day.

Bronze admitted that the rivalry had taken on extra meaning but insisted the focus was on the present rather than the past.

"Of course people will talk about the final, and we think about it too," she said. "But this is a different tournament and a different moment. We've learned a lot about them and about ourselves. The games have been tight, and that tells you how close the two teams are."

Wiegman has used the Nations League campaign to experiment with personnel, handing opportunities to younger players while managing the workload of senior figures. Bronze said the rotation had strengthened the group rather than unsettled it.

"Everyone knows their role, even when it changes," she added. "The coaches give us clear information, and we trust each other to carry it out."

Spain, who boast Ballon d'Or winner Aitana Bonmatí in midfield, are expected to dominate possession. Bronze said England would need patience as well as flexibility.

"You won't have the ball for long spells," she said. "It's about staying calm, staying organised and taking your chances when they come."

In a small apartment on the outskirts of Tehran, the curtains are drawn well before sunset. A dozen people sit cross-legged on a Persian rug, a single candle flickering beside a plate of painted eggs. When they sing, they keep their voices low.

"We have learned to worship in whispers," says Maryam, a woman in her thirties who asked that her real name not be used. "Easter is about the resurrection, about hope. But for us, it is also about being careful."

Maryam converted from Islam to Christianity nearly a decade ago, a decision that in Iran can carry severe consequences. While the country's ancient Armenian and Assyrian Christian communities are officially recognised and permitted to worship in their own churches, services there are typically held in their own languages, and converts from a Muslim background are not welcome to attend. Many converts have instead turned to informal "house churches", gatherings the authorities regard as illegal.

Rights groups say members of these groups have faced raids, arrests and lengthy prison sentences, often on charges of "acting against national security" or "propaganda against the state". Some have been forced to leave the country altogether.

For those who remain, celebrating Christianity's most important festival requires planning. Members arrive at staggered times so as not to draw the attention of neighbours. Phones are sometimes left switched off or outside the room. Hymns are sung softly, or not at all.

"There is always a moment when someone knocks on the door of the building, and everyone goes quiet," says Reza, who leads a small fellowship in another city. "Most of the time it is just a delivery. But you never forget that it could be something else."

Despite the risks, he says, the number of people seeking out such gatherings has not diminished.

"People come because they are searching," he says. "And on Easter, of all days, we cannot turn them away."

The handwritten notice, posted in Hebrew at a rental kiosk on the Pischa mountain above the resort, told customers that because of "various very annoying incidents," including the theft of a sledge, the business would no longer hire out sports equipment to Jews. Photographs of the sign spread rapidly on social media over the weekend and drew condemnation from Jewish organisations in Switzerland and abroad.

The Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities said it had filed a criminal complaint under the country's anti-racism laws, which prohibit refusing a service to a person on the basis of race, ethnicity or religion. Officials from the federation described the notice as a blatant act of discrimination and said that singling out an entire group for the alleged behaviour of a few individuals was textbook antisemitism.

Local tourism officials moved quickly to distance the region from the incident. Representatives of Davos Klosters said they had contacted the operator, and the sign was removed shortly afterwards. In a statement, the tourism body stressed that guests of every background were welcome in the region and that it did not tolerate discrimination of any kind.

Israel's foreign ministry also weighed in, calling the episode shameful and urging Swiss authorities to take firm action.

The case has reignited a long-running debate in Graubünden, the eastern canton where Davos lies, about tensions between some residents and Orthodox Jewish holidaymakers, who visit the Alpine resorts in large numbers each summer and winter. In 2017, a hotel in nearby Arosa provoked outrage by posting a notice asking Jewish guests to shower before using its swimming pool.

Community leaders said that incident and this latest one reflected a worrying climate. Jewish groups in Switzerland have reported a sharp rise in antisemitic incidents since the October 7 attacks on Israel and the war in Gaza that followed, with many recorded online but a growing number occurring in public spaces.

Under the terms of the agreement, Barclays will take over Tesco Bank's credit card, personal loan and savings operations, adding around £8bn of customer lending and roughly £7bn of deposits to its balance sheet. The supermarket chain will keep its insurance, ATM and travel money businesses, which will be folded back into its retail operations once the sale completes.

The two companies have also agreed a long-term partnership, under which Barclays will continue to offer banking products under the Tesco Bank brand and Clubcard holders will still be able to earn rewards points on their spending. Customers have been told they do not need to take any action and that their accounts will carry on as normal while the transfer takes place.

Tesco expects to receive about £700m in cash from the deal, including a dividend from the bank before completion, and has said it plans to return £250m of that to shareholders through a share buyback. Chief executive Ken Murphy described the sale as a way to sharpen the group's focus on its core grocery business, while keeping the benefits of the bank for its Clubcard members.

For Barclays, the acquisition fits a strategy, set out at its investor update, of growing its UK retail bank and reducing its reliance on its more volatile investment banking arm. The lender's chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, has pledged to shift more of the group's capital towards its domestic consumer business, and the Tesco deal brings in several million new customers at a stroke.

The transaction is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to complete in the second half of the year. Tesco Bank employs about 2,800 people, many of them at its headquarters in Edinburgh and offices in Glasgow and Newcastle, and the companies said a large number of staff would be expected to move across to Barclays as part of the deal.

A former senior manager at the Countess of Chester Hospital has told the Thirlwall Inquiry that she "genuinely believed" Lucy Letby was innocent at the time doctors first raised concerns about the nurse.

Giving evidence at Liverpool Town Hall, the witness said she had found it "inconceivable" that a member of staff could deliberately harm babies in her care, and that the hospital's leadership had been focused on looking for other explanations for the rise in deaths on the neonatal unit.

"I could not get my head around it," she told the inquiry. "Nothing I had seen of her suggested someone capable of that. I accept now that I was wrong."

Letby, 34, is serving 15 whole-life orders after being convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others between June 2015 and June 2016. She maintains her innocence.

The inquiry, chaired by Lady Justice Thirlwall, is examining how the hospital responded to concerns raised by consultant paediatricians, who repeatedly warned managers about a link between Letby and a number of unexpected collapses.

The witness was asked why senior consultants had been told to apologise to the nurse in early 2017 after a grievance she brought was upheld. She said the decision had been made "in good faith" on the information available, but admitted it had caused "deep distress" to the doctors involved.

Counsel to the inquiry put it to her that managers had treated the consultants' concerns as a personnel dispute rather than a patient safety issue. She said she "understood why it looks that way", but denied there had been any attempt to protect the hospital's reputation.

Police were not contacted until May 2017, nearly a year after Letby was removed from frontline duties.

The inquiry heard that the witness later wrote to the families of the babies to apologise. Several parents were in the public gallery as she gave evidence.

The hearing continues.

Police Scotland has confirmed it is prepared to send officers to Northern Ireland after several nights of disorder left dozens of officers injured and homes and vehicles damaged.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has made a formal request for mutual aid, the arrangement that allows UK forces to lend each other officers and equipment during major incidents. Officers trained in public order policing, along with specialist vehicles, are understood to be among the resources being considered.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said the force had received the request and was "assessing what support can be provided while ensuring we maintain our own operational commitments across Scotland." Any deployment would be coordinated through the National Police Coordination Centre, which manages mutual aid requests across the UK.

The violence has seen petrol bombs, bricks and fireworks thrown at police lines, and water cannon deployed in an effort to disperse crowds. Senior PSNI officers have described the disorder as "racially motivated thuggery" and warned that those responsible would be identified and brought before the courts. Several arrests have already been made, with more expected as detectives review CCTV and social media footage.

Political leaders across Northern Ireland have condemned the unrest and appealed for calm, while community representatives have urged young people in particular to stay away from the streets.

This would not be the first time Scottish officers have been sent across the Irish Sea. Police Scotland provided support to the PSNI during periods of disorder in previous years, and officers from forces in England and Wales have also been deployed in the past to help manage the marching season.

The Scottish Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, said it would support colleagues in Northern Ireland but stressed that any officers sent must be properly equipped and that Scotland's own policing needs should not be left short as a result.

The portrait, unveiled by the King at Buckingham Palace on Tuesday, is the first completed since his coronation last May. It shows the monarch in the uniform of the Welsh Guards, of which he became Regimental Colonel in 1975, set against a sweeping wash of vivid red that almost engulfs the figure.

Its most striking detail is a butterfly hovering near the King's right shoulder. Yeo said it was intended to symbolise the King's metamorphosis from Prince to monarch during the portrait's creation, as well as his decades of environmental campaigning.

"When I started this project, His Majesty The King was still His Royal Highness The Prince of Wales," Yeo said. "Much like the butterfly I've painted hovering over his shoulder, the subject has transformed, and I hope it captures something of that moment."

The commission dates back to 2020, when it was ordered to mark 50 years of the then Prince of Wales's membership of The Drapers' Company, one of the City of London's historic livery companies. The King first sat for Yeo in June 2021 at Highgrove, and later at Clarence House, with the final sitting in November 2023. The artist supplemented these sessions with drawings and photographs.

Measuring roughly 8.5ft by 6.5ft (2.6m by 2m), the painting will go on public display at the Philip Mould Gallery in London for a month before moving to Drapers' Hall, where it will hang alongside portraits of past monarchs.

Yeo, one of Britain's best-known portrait artists, has previously painted several members of the Royal Family, as well as figures including Sir David Attenborough and Tony Blair. He said the King had initially seemed "mildly surprised" by the bold colour, but appeared to smile approvingly.

The palace has not formally commented on the King's reaction. But Queen Camilla was reported to have told the artist: "Yes, you've got him."

Two people have been detained after a suspicious package was found at Gatwick Airport, prompting the partial evacuation of the South Terminal on Tuesday afternoon.

Sussex Police said officers were called at about 14:20 BST after staff reported an unattended item near the check-in area. A security cordon was put in place and specialist officers, including an explosive ordnance disposal team, were sent to the scene as a precaution.

A man and a woman were later detained in connection with the incident. Police said they were being questioned, but stressed it was too early to say whether any offence had been committed.

"We understand the disruption this has caused to passengers and thank them for their patience while our officers carried out the necessary checks," a police spokesperson said. "The safety of the public is our priority, and we will always take reports of this nature seriously."

Passengers described scenes of confusion as announcements instructed people to leave the building. Some said they had waited outside for more than an hour before being allowed back in.

One traveller, who had been due to fly to Malaga, said: "We were just queuing to drop our bags when security staff started moving everyone back. Nobody really knew what was happening, but people stayed fairly calm."

The airport confirmed that a number of departures had been delayed and advised passengers to check with their airlines before travelling. A Gatwick spokesperson said the North Terminal had not been affected and operations there had continued as normal.

The cordon was lifted shortly after 16:30 BST and the terminal reopened, although knock-on delays were expected to continue into the evening.

Police said inquiries were ongoing and urged anyone with information to come forward. They added that there would be a visible police presence at the airport over the coming days to reassure the public.

The Israeli military said its aircraft had targeted a "Hamas compound" embedded inside the school, located in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, and that the militants killed had taken part in the 7 October attacks on southern Israel. It said it had taken steps before the strike to reduce the risk to civilians, including aerial surveillance, and accused Hamas of operating from within shelters and other civilian sites.

Hospital officials in the nearby town of Deir al-Balah said at least 35 people had been killed, among them women and children, and dozens more injured. The figure could not be independently verified. Footage filmed at the scene showed people searching through rubble in classrooms on the upper floors of the building, while bodies wrapped in blankets were carried to waiting vehicles.

The school is run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA, and had been sheltering thousands of displaced people who fled fighting elsewhere in the territory. The agency's head said the building had been struck without prior warning, describing the attack as part of a pattern of assaults on UN facilities since the war began. He said more than 180 UNRWA buildings had been hit during the conflict, some of them repeatedly.

One man who had been staying at the school with his family told reporters he had been woken by two loud explosions shortly after midnight. "We came here because we were told it was safe," he said. "There is nowhere safe."

Israel has repeatedly accused UNRWA of allowing its facilities to be used by Hamas, allegations the agency denies. Several countries paused funding to UNRWA earlier this year following Israeli claims that some of its staff took part in the 7 October attacks, though many have since resumed payments.

The strike came as Israeli forces pressed ahead with an expanded operation in central Gaza, with residents reporting heavy bombardment overnight in several areas.

Sarah Whitfield, 46, had her breast implants fitted in 2011 after years of feeling self-conscious about her figure. More than a decade later, she noticed that her left breast had become noticeably swollen and tender.

"I thought maybe I'd pulled a muscle at the gym," she said. "It didn't occur to me that it could be anything serious. Nobody had ever mentioned cancer to me when I was signing the consent forms."

After an ultrasound revealed a large build-up of fluid around the implant, doctors drew off a sample for testing. Weeks later, Ms Whitfield was diagnosed with breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), a rare cancer of the immune system that develops in the scar tissue and fluid surrounding an implant.

Experts stress that BIA-ALCL is not a form of breast cancer, and that the overall risk remains low. However, it has been linked predominantly to implants with a textured surface, and estimates of how often it occurs among women with those implants vary widely. Cases typically appear several years after surgery, with persistent swelling, a lump, or pain around the implant being the most common warning signs.

In most cases, the disease is treatable if caught early, usually by surgically removing the implant and the capsule of scar tissue around it. Ms Whitfield underwent surgery in the spring and has since been told there is no sign of the cancer spreading.

"I was lucky," she said. "But I keep thinking about all the women who don't know this is even possible. If something changes, even years later, don't ignore it."

Health regulators advise that women with implants who have no symptoms do not need to have them removed, but should check their breasts regularly and seek medical advice promptly if they notice any unexplained changes.

Ms Whitfield is now campaigning for clearer information to be given to patients before surgery.

Bridget Phillipson said she was "open-minded" about changing the law on physical punishment, signalling for the first time that ministers could consider following Scotland and Wales in outlawing smacking.

Under current legislation in England, parents can use the defence of "reasonable punishment" if accused of assaulting their child, provided the force used does not leave more than a temporary reddening of the skin. The defence was established by the Children Act 2004, which tightened earlier rules but stopped short of an outright ban.

The education secretary was responding to growing pressure from children's charities and medical bodies, which argue that the existing position leaves children with less legal protection from assault than adults. Phillipson stressed that the government had no immediate plans to legislate, but said she would look closely at the evidence, including the experience of the devolved nations.

Scotland became the first part of the UK to remove the reasonable punishment defence in November 2020, and Wales followed in March 2022. Campaigners say neither country has seen the surge in prosecutions of ordinary parents that opponents had predicted. They point instead to a shift in public attitudes and greater awareness of alternative forms of discipline.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health has long called for a change in England, citing research linking physical punishment to poorer mental health and behavioural problems in later life. The children's commissioner for England has also urged ministers to act, describing the current law as outdated.

However, some parents' groups and Conservative MPs have warned against what they see as state interference in family life. They argue that a light smack is distinct from abuse and that criminalising it would divert police and social services from genuinely vulnerable children.

Any change would require primary legislation, and government sources indicated that it was unlikely to be included in the forthcoming children's wellbeing bill.

Ministers have warned that more than £1bn of extra spending on public services could be lost if opposition parties in the Senedd refuse to support the Welsh government's draft budget.

The finance secretary said the additional money, which includes funding for the NHS, schools and local councils, would only reach frontline services if the spending plans were approved before the end of the financial year.

Because Labour holds exactly half of the 60 seats in the Senedd, it needs the backing, or at least the abstention, of at least one opposition member to pass its budget.

"This is not a game of brinkmanship," the finance secretary told members on Tuesday. "If this budget falls, the consequences are real. Councils will be left without the certainty they need to set council tax, health boards will face difficult choices, and the extra investment we have secured will simply not be spent."

Under the rules governing devolved finances, if no budget is agreed, the Welsh government would be limited to spending a proportion of the previous year's allocation, a scenario ministers describe as "a cliff edge" for public services.

Opposition parties have accused the government of using scare tactics. The Welsh Conservatives said the budget failed to address long waiting lists and called for cuts to what they described as wasteful spending.

Plaid Cymru said it was willing to talk, but wanted firm commitments on issues including childcare, free school meals and support for farmers before it would consider abstaining.

A Plaid Cymru spokesperson said: "We will not be handed a blank cheque. If the government wants our cooperation, it has to show it is listening."

Talks between the parties are expected to continue over the coming weeks ahead of a final vote, scheduled for early March.

Local government leaders have urged politicians to reach an agreement quickly, warning that uncertainty was already making it harder to plan for the year ahead.

Lewis Hamilton says he "could not be more excited" after completing his first official day as a Ferrari driver at the team's Maranello headquarters on Monday.

The seven-time world champion, who left Mercedes at the end of last season after 12 years and six of his titles with the Silver Arrows, arrived at the Italian team's base early in the morning to begin what he has described as the "next chapter" of his career.

Hamilton later shared a photograph of himself standing beside a classic Ferrari F40 outside the house once used by company founder Enzo Ferrari, an image that quickly spread across social media and drew enthusiastic responses from the team's famously passionate supporters, the tifosi.

"There are some days in your life that you know will be special, and today is one of those days," Hamilton said in a statement. "I'm looking forward to writing the next chapter of history with this iconic team."

The 40-year-old spent the day meeting staff, touring the factory and holding discussions with team principal Fred Vasseur and senior engineers. He is also expected to take to the track at Ferrari's Fiorano test circuit later this week to gain early familiarity with the team's procedures before pre-season testing begins in Bahrain.

Hamilton's move, first announced in February last year, ranks among the most high-profile driver transfers in the sport's history. He joins Charles Leclerc, who has been with Ferrari since 2019, in what many observers consider the strongest line-up on the grid.

Ferrari finished just 14 points behind McLaren in last season's constructors' championship. The team will hope Hamilton's experience can help it end a drivers' title drought stretching back to Kimi Raikkonen's triumph in 2007.

Vasseur said the team was "proud" to welcome a driver of Hamilton's calibre and believed his work ethic would push everyone at Maranello forward.

The new season begins in Melbourne in March.

England know that a routine victory will not be enough at Twickenham on Saturday. With the championship table tightening and points difference likely to decide the title, the hosts have spoken openly this week about the need not only to beat Italy but to do so with the attacking ambition that has too often eluded them.

The head coach has made four changes to the side that edged past Wales a fortnight ago, with a reshuffled back line designed to inject pace and width. The decision to start a playmaking full-back alongside a recalled fly-half signals a clear intent: England want to move the ball, stretch a disciplined Italian defence and turn pressure into tries rather than penalties.

"We've talked a lot about control, and that still matters," the attack coach told reporters at the team's training base. "But there's a point where control becomes caution. The players want to express themselves, and the supporters deserve to see that."

Italy, however, arrive with little inclination to play the role of willing opponents. Once the tournament's whipping boys, the Azzurri have grown into a side capable of troubling anyone, built on a fierce back-row and a willingness to counter-attack from deep. Their narrow defeat to France earlier in the championship showed how dangerous they can be when given space.

The visiting captain was quick to dismiss any suggestion that his team would simply be there to make up the numbers. "Everyone talks about England's bonus point," he said. "We are thinking about winning."

For England, the margin for error is slim. Defeat would end their title hopes, and even a narrow win could leave them reliant on results elsewhere on the final weekend. A sell-out crowd is expected, and patience may be in short supply if the first half becomes another arm-wrestle. The message from inside the camp is simple: entertain, and the results will follow.

The Education Secretary, who also serves as Minister for Women and Equalities, said the Supreme Court's ruling had provided "clarity" and that organisations should now follow the law as set out by the judges.

Asked during a broadcast interview whether trans women should use women's toilets, Ms Phillipson said facilities should be used "based on biological sex", adding that the government expected public bodies and employers to act in line with the judgment.

Her comments follow last month's unanimous decision by the UK's highest court that the terms "woman" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex. The ruling was brought by campaign group For Women Scotland, which had challenged the Scottish government's guidance on gender representation on public boards.

Since then, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) has issued interim guidance stating that trans women should not be permitted to use women's toilets and changing rooms in workplaces and services open to the public. It added that trans people should not be left without access to any facilities, and suggested that, where possible, mixed-sex or single-occupancy options could be provided.

Ms Phillipson said she recognised that the period since the ruling had been "deeply worrying" for many trans people, and insisted they remained protected from discrimination under the law on the basis of gender reassignment.

"Trans people deserve to be treated with dignity and respect," she said. "But the court has been clear, and we will make sure the law is followed."

Campaigners for transgender rights criticised the remarks, warning that the guidance risked excluding trans people from public life and leaving them uncertain about where they could safely go. Several Labour backbenchers have also expressed concern about how the ruling is being implemented.

Gender-critical groups welcomed the clarification, though some Conservative politicians accused ministers of having been slow to respond to the judgment.

The EHRC is expected to publish an updated statutory code of practice for services later this year, following a public consultation.

The prime minister's official spokesman told reporters on Monday morning that all government departments had now agreed their budgets, bringing to an end weeks of tense negotiations between the Treasury and several senior cabinet ministers.

"The spending review is settled," the spokesman said. "Every department has reached agreement with the Treasury, and the Chancellor will set out the full details to Parliament on Wednesday as planned."

The announcement follows reports of protracted wrangling over the weekend, with the Home Office and the Department for Housing understood to have been among the last to sign off on their settlements. Ministers in both departments were said to have pushed back against proposed limits on day-to-day spending, warning that further restraint could put pressure on policing numbers and housebuilding targets.

Asked whether any minister had threatened to resign over the outcome, the spokesman said he would not comment on "private discussions", adding that the cabinet was "united behind a plan that delivers on the government's priorities while maintaining fiscal discipline".

The review will set departmental budgets for the next three years of day-to-day spending and four years of capital investment. The Treasury has signalled that the NHS and defence will receive the most generous increases, leaving other unprotected departments facing real-terms squeezes once inflation is taken into account.
