Economists have cautioned that the settlement leaves little room for manoeuvre. The Institute for Fiscal Studies said last week that some departments could see their budgets fall in real terms, raising questions about whether public services can meet rising demand.

Opposition parties seized on the reports of disagreement. A shadow minister said the delays showed a government "at war with itself" and accused ministers of "papering over the cracks".

Treasury sources insisted the process had been "robust but constructive", and said final figures would demonstrate investment in growth, infrastructure and frontline services.

Anna Henderson claimed Great Britain's first medal of the Paris Games with a superb ride to take silver in the women's individual time trial, while Josh Tarling narrowly missed out on the podium in the men's event.

Henderson, 25, coped impressively with treacherous conditions on a rain-soaked 32.4km course through the streets of the French capital. Several riders crashed on the slick roads, and the Briton rode with a careful aggression that kept her upright and in contention.

Australia's Grace Brown, the newly crowned world champion's closest rival in recent seasons, was in a class of her own, setting a blistering pace to win gold. But Henderson held her nerve to edge out American Chloe Dygert, who recovered from a crash to take bronze.

"I can't quite believe it," said an emotional Henderson after crossing the finish line on the Pont Alexandre III. "I just wanted to give everything and not have any regrets. The conditions were so tricky, and I was just trying to stay on my bike and keep the power down. To come away with a silver medal is a dream."

The Visma-Lease a Bike rider was not considered among the favourites before the race, making her performance all the more remarkable for a British team who had hoped for a strong start on the opening day of competition.

There was disappointment, however, for 20-year-old Tarling, who had been tipped as an outside medal contender in the men's race. The Welshman, who rides for Ineos Grenadiers, produced a strong effort but could not match the pace of the leading trio.

Belgium's Remco Evenepoel delivered a dominant performance to take gold, finishing ahead of Italy's Filippo Ganna and his compatriot Wout van Aert.

Tarling, one of the brightest young talents in the sport, will take encouragement from his performance on his Olympic debut, with many expecting him to challenge for medals at future Games.

The scale of the defeat at the Wankhede Stadium was stark. India's 150-run victory sealed a 4-1 series win, and it gave Brendon McCullum a sobering introduction to life as England's all-format head coach.

For the first time on this tour, the gulf between the sides was not just visible but cavernous. Abhishek Sharma's 135 from 54 balls was the second-highest score by an India batter in men's T20 internationals, and England had no answers. They were bludgeoned to all corners as the left-hander cleared the ropes 13 times. Mark Wood, Jofra Archer and Brydon Carse were all pummelled, and the tactical plans that had looked sound in the dressing room disintegrated within the first six overs.

England's reply lasted barely half the allotted overs. Phil Salt's defiant half-century offered brief resistance, but once he fell the innings collapsed to 97 all out. It was a familiar pattern from the series: bright starts undone by reckless shot selection against high-class spin.

McCullum was appointed to bring the aggressive philosophy that transformed the Test side into England's white-ball teams. Yet this series has exposed a key difference. In the shorter formats, every team plays with aggression. Intent alone is no longer an advantage. What separates the best sides is the ability to adapt, to read conditions and to absorb pressure when the opposition seizes control.

India did exactly that across five matches. Their spinners, led by Varun Chakravarthy, repeatedly strangled England's middle order. Their batters, by contrast, punished every error.

With three one-day internationals to come before the Champions Trophy, time is short. Jos Buttler's side must find balance quickly, particularly in their bowling attack, which leaked runs alarmingly whenever plans went awry.

McCullum has rebuilt a team before. This challenge, however, may prove considerably steeper.

Southampton's Premier League fixture was called off on Saturday afternoon after a major fire broke out at an industrial site less than a mile from St Mary's Stadium, sending a thick plume of black smoke across the city.

Crews from Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service were called to the blaze shortly after 11:00 GMT. At its height, more than 15 fire engines and around 80 firefighters were tackling the flames, supported by an aerial ladder platform and a specialist hazardous materials unit.

Police set up a wide cordon around the area, closing several roads near the stadium and the Northam Bridge. Residents in nearby streets were advised to keep windows and doors shut because of the smoke, and some homes closest to the site were evacuated as a precaution.

In a statement, the club said the decision to postpone the match had been taken "following advice from the emergency services and Southampton City Council's safety advisory group." It added: "The safety of supporters, staff and the wider community is our absolute priority. We understand the disappointment this will cause, particularly to away fans who have already travelled, and we thank everyone for their patience."

Supporters already gathering outside the ground were asked to leave the area calmly. Many described seeing flames rising above warehouse roofs as they walked from the city centre.

A fire service spokesperson said there were no reports of injuries but warned that crews were likely to remain at the scene "well into the evening and possibly overnight" as they worked to damp down hotspots. The cause of the fire is not yet known and an investigation will begin once the site is safe.

The club said tickets would remain valid for the rearranged fixture, with a new date to be confirmed in due course.

Peter Sullivan, who has spent 38 years behind bars, had his conviction for the murder of Diane Sindall overturned at the Court of Appeal after new DNA evidence pointed to another, as yet unidentified, man.

Ms Sindall, a 21-year-old florist who also worked shifts as a barmaid, was attacked in Bebington, Wirral, in August 1986 as she walked home after her van ran out of fuel. She was sexually assaulted and beaten, and her body was found the following morning. She had been due to marry later that year.

Mr Sullivan, now in his late 60s, was convicted in 1987 and given a life sentence. He has always maintained his innocence. His case was referred back to the court by the Criminal Cases Review Commission after scientists, re-examining samples preserved from the original investigation, produced a DNA profile that did not match him.

The Crown Prosecution Service did not oppose the appeal. Quashing the conviction, the judges said the fresh scientific evidence undermined the safety of the verdict, and they declined to order a retrial.

Mr Sullivan followed the hearing by video link from prison. His legal team said he was overwhelmed by the decision and that the years he had lost could never be returned to him. His family, who campaigned for his release for decades, wept in the public gallery as the ruling was delivered.

His case is now thought to be the longest-running miscarriage of justice involving a living person in British legal history.

Merseyside Police said the investigation into Ms Sindall's death remained open and that the new DNA profile had been checked against the national database without producing a match. Officers have urged anyone with information, however small, to come forward.

The force added that its thoughts remained with Ms Sindall's family, who have been told that the person responsible for her death has never been brought to justice.

Professor Michelle Francl, a chemist at Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania, says a tiny pinch of salt, too little to taste, can make a cup of tea noticeably less bitter. The suggestion, published in her book *Steeped: The Chemistry of Tea*, has sparked indignation among British tea drinkers.

Francl explains that sodium ions interfere with the receptors on the tongue that detect bitterness, masking the harsh notes that can develop when tea is brewed too long or with very hot water. The idea is not entirely new, she notes. Salt appears in references to tea preparation in medieval Chinese manuscripts, and salted tea remains common in parts of Central Asia and the Himalayas.

Her book covers more than salt. Drawing on hundreds of research papers, Francl recommends warming the pot or cup beforehand, using freshly boiled water, and pouring tea into the cup before adding milk, which she says helps prevent the milk proteins from clumping. She also suggests a splash of lemon juice to break up the unappetising film that can form on the surface of black tea, particularly in hard-water areas.

The advice drew a swift and largely incredulous response in the United Kingdom, where tea etiquette is a matter of fierce national debate. Social media users called the idea everything from "unnatural" to an outright provocation.

The row escalated far enough that the US Embassy in London issued a tongue-in-cheek statement distancing Washington from the professor's recommendations. It insisted that adding salt to Britain's national drink was not official United States policy, adding that it would continue to make tea "the proper way", by microwaving it. That remark provoked a fresh wave of outrage.

Francl, for her part, has said she hoped to start a conversation about the science of an everyday ritual, and that she never expected to cause an international incident.

Shweta Sharma, who had lived in the US and Hong Kong for years before returning to India, says she opened an account with the bank's branch in Delhi in 2016 and over the following years transferred much of her savings into it from abroad. On the advice of a relationship manager at the branch, she says, she placed the money in fixed deposits, expecting it to grow steadily over time.

But Ms Sharma alleges that the official was quietly draining the account. She says the employee forged her signatures, opened fixed deposits in her name without her knowledge, broke them prematurely and moved the funds elsewhere. She also accuses the employee of creating a fake email address and changing the phone number linked to the account, so that she would not receive alerts about the withdrawals. All the while, she says, she was shown statements suggesting her savings were intact.

"I trusted the bank completely," Ms Sharma told reporters. "I never imagined that the person who was supposed to look after my money would be the one taking it."

She says she discovered the alleged fraud only when another employee of the branch showed her the account's actual statements. By then, she claims, around 160 million rupees ($1.9m; £1.5m) had disappeared. That figure includes the interest she says her deposits should have earned.

Ms Sharma has filed a complaint with the police, who say they have opened a case and are examining the bank's records.

In a statement, ICICI Bank said it had begun an internal investigation as soon as it learned of the matter and was cooperating fully with the authorities. The lender said it had "zero tolerance" for fraud and would take appropriate action once the facts were established.

The case has drawn wide attention on social media, with many customers asking how such transactions could have gone unnoticed for so long.

If you haven't yet heard of Chappell Roan, chances are you've heard her. Her songs have been soundtracking TikTok videos, pride parties and late-night karaoke sessions for months, and her name is quickly becoming impossible to avoid.

Born Kayleigh Rose Amstutz and raised in Willard, Missouri, the 26-year-old singer took her stage name from her late grandfather, Dennis Chappell, and his favorite song, the old cowboy ballad "The Strawberry Roan." That blend of small-town roots and big-city glamour runs through everything she does. Her music is campy, sincere, horny and heartfelt, often all within a single chorus.

Roan's path to stardom wasn't straightforward. She signed with a major label as a teenager, only to be dropped in 2020, the same year she released "Pink Pony Club," a shimmering ode to a Los Angeles gay bar that has since become a fan favorite. She kept writing, working day jobs and collaborating with producer Dan Nigro, best known for his work with Olivia Rodrigo.

That partnership produced her 2023 debut album, "The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess," a glittering, synth-soaked record about queer awakening, heartbreak and growing up. Tracks like "Femininomenon," "Casual" and the cheerleader-chant anthem "Hot to Go!" showcase her knack for pairing silly, sing-along hooks with surprisingly vulnerable lyrics.

Her live shows have become events in their own right. Roan draws heavily on drag culture, performing in elaborate costumes and encouraging fans to dress up according to a theme for each concert. Opening slots on Rodrigo's "Guts" world tour introduced her to arena-sized crowds, and a buzzy Coachella set cemented her status as one of the year's breakout acts.

Then came "Good Luck, Babe!", a soaring, '80s-tinged single that became her biggest hit to date. It's the sound of an artist who spent years waiting in the wings, finally stepping into the spotlight, and refusing to tone anything down.

For the thousands who had made the journey, the final whistle brought a familiar silence. Scotland's campaign is over once again, ended at the group stage by a defeat that left supporters staring at the pitch long after the players had trudged off.

Outside the stadium, the bagpipes that had serenaded the city all week fell quiet. Groups of fans in kilts and replica shirts sat on kerbs, some still clutching flags, others simply shaking their heads. The mood was not angry so much as weary, the resignation of people who have seen this story play out before.

"You come here believing," said Graham Mcintyre, 54, from Kilmarnock, who has followed the national team abroad for more than three decades. "That's the whole point. If you didn't believe, you'd stay at home. But it hurts every single time."

The result means Scotland have still never progressed beyond the first round of a major tournament, a record stretching back across generations. Hopes had been high after a qualifying campaign that saw the side beat stronger opposition and climb the world rankings. But on the biggest stage, the team struggled to create chances and was undone by defensive lapses at crucial moments.

The manager, speaking afterwards, admitted his players had "fallen short" and apologised to the travelling support. "They've been magnificent," he said. "They deserved more from us."

If the football disappointed, the fans themselves won plaudits once more. Local police praised their behaviour, and residents spoke warmly of the singing, dancing and impromptu ceilidhs that had filled squares and bars throughout the week.

For many, attention now turns to the long journey home and the inevitable question of whether to do it all again.

"Of course we will," said Mcintyre's daughter, Eilidh, 23, folding a Saltire into her rucksack. "That's what being Scottish is. You get your heart broken, and then you book the next trip."

Ms Harvey, who has been widely identified online as the real-life inspiration for the character Martha, made the claim during a televised interview with Piers Morgan. She said the series had defamed her and that she intended to take legal action against both the streaming giant and Mr Gadd, who wrote and stars in the drama.

Baby Reindeer, which became one of Netflix's most-watched shows after its release in April, follows a struggling comedian, Donny Dunn, who is relentlessly pursued by a woman he meets while working in a London pub. Each episode opens with the words "This is a true story", and Mr Gadd has said the show is based on his own experiences of being stalked.

In the interview, Ms Harvey disputed central elements of the drama. She denied that she had stalked Mr Gadd and rejected the suggestion that she had sent him tens of thousands of emails, saying she may have exchanged only a handful of messages with him. She also said she had never been convicted of a crime or jailed, as the character Martha is in the series. She described the portrayal as hurtful and said she had received threats since internet users began trying to track down the people depicted in the show.

Mr Gadd had previously urged viewers not to speculate about the identities of real people connected to the story, saying that was not the point of the series.

Netflix has faced growing scrutiny over how it fictionalised real events while describing the programme as true. MPs on the Culture, Media and Sport Committee have questioned the company about what steps were taken to protect the identities of those involved.

Netflix did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Ms Harvey's remarks. Media lawyers said that any case would be likely to hinge on whether viewers could reasonably identify her from the character, and on how far the "true story" label could be treated as a statement of fact.

On a sweltering afternoon in Dhaka, a group of university students in white shirts stood at a busy intersection, waving cars and rickshaws through with improvised batons. Just days earlier, many of them had been dodging tear gas and live fire on these same streets. Now, with police stations deserted and many officers fearing reprisals, they had taken it upon themselves to keep the city moving.

"Nobody told us to do this," said one 21-year-old engineering student, wiping sweat from her forehead. "But if we want a new Bangladesh, we have to build it ourselves, starting with the traffic."

Across the capital, similar scenes have unfolded. Young volunteers have swept up debris from torched buildings, painted murals on walls once covered in political slogans, and formed neighbourhood groups to guard temples and homes after reports of attacks on minority communities and on supporters of the ousted Awami League.

The movement began in July as a protest against a quota system that reserved a large share of government jobs for descendants of independence-war veterans, a scheme critics said favoured allies of the ruling party. But a violent crackdown, which left hundreds dead, transformed the demonstrations into a nationwide uprising against Sheikh Hasina's 15-year rule. On 5 August, as crowds converged on her official residence, she fled by helicopter to India.

Days later, Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus was sworn in as head of an interim government, with two student leaders among his advisers, an unprecedented role for a generation that until recently had little say in the country's politics.

Yet the euphoria is tempered by uncertainty. Many students speak of rooting out corruption, reforming the judiciary and holding free elections, but few agree on how quickly that can happen, or who should lead it.

"We removed one person," said a political science student outside Dhaka University. "Removing a system is much harder. That is the real fight now."

The FBI has launched an appeal to trace relatives of everyone killed in the Lockerbie bombing, as it prepares for the trial of the man accused of building the bomb that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103.

All 259 people on board the Boeing 747 were killed when it exploded over the Scottish town on 21 December 1988. Another 11 residents of Lockerbie died when wreckage fell on their homes. It remains the deadliest terrorist attack ever carried out in the UK.

Libyan national Abu Agila Mohammad Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi is awaiting trial in Washington DC. He denies charges including destruction of an aircraft resulting in death. He was taken into US custody in December 2022, more than three decades after the attack, and has pleaded not guilty.

Under US law, victims of federal crimes and their families have specific rights, including the right to be notified of court proceedings, to attend hearings and, in some circumstances, to be heard. The FBI's victim services division has said it wants to ensure that anyone entitled to those rights is aware of the case and can choose whether to take part.

Investigators acknowledge that tracing every family is a significant challenge. The victims came from 21 countries, and many relatives have moved, changed their names or died in the years since. Some younger family members may never have been contacted by authorities at all.

Families who wish to register are being asked to contact the FBI directly, and information is also being shared through victims' support groups in the UK and the US.

The case marks the first time a suspect in the bombing has faced trial on American soil. Abdelbaset al-Megrahi, the only person ever convicted over the attack, was found guilty in 2001 by Scottish judges sitting at a special court in the Netherlands. He died in Libya in 2012, still protesting his innocence.

Tottenham manager Ange Postecoglou says he is "in a fight" to turn around his side's fortunes but insists he will not abandon the attacking philosophy that has defined his time in north London.

Spurs have struggled for consistency in recent weeks, and pressure has mounted on the Australian amid criticism of his side's high defensive line and relentless approach, which some argue has left them exposed.

Speaking at his pre-match news conference on Thursday, Postecoglou was defiant.

"I'm in a fight, there's no doubt about that," he said. "But when I'm in a fight, I don't go and hide in the corner. I double down. That's what I've always done throughout my career, and I'm not going to change now."

The 59-year-old acknowledged that results had not been good enough and accepted responsibility for the team's position, but rejected suggestions that a more cautious style would solve their problems.

"People say, 'Just be a bit more pragmatic, just sit back a bit.' I understand why people say that when things aren't going well," he said. "But I know what got us success in the past, and I know what will get us success in the future. If I start compromising now, then I'm just another manager trying to survive week to week, and that's not who I am."

Injuries have compounded Tottenham's difficulties, with several key players unavailable, forcing Postecoglou to rely on younger members of the squad and players operating out of position.

He refused to use the absences as an excuse, however, saying the squad had to "find a way" regardless of who was on the pitch.

"The players have been outstanding in terms of their effort and commitment," he added. "They're hurting just as much as the supporters are. Our job now is to stick together, keep believing in what we're doing, and make sure we come out the other side stronger."

A 26-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after three women were killed at a house in Bushey, Hertfordshire.

Kyle Clifford was detained on Wednesday afternoon following a manhunt that stretched across Hertfordshire and north London. Officers found him in Lavender Hill Cemetery in Enfield. He was injured and was taken to hospital for treatment, where he remains under police supervision.

The victims have been named as Carol Hunt, 61, and her daughters Hannah, 28, and Louise, 25. Carol Hunt was the wife of the broadcaster racing commentator John Hunt. Emergency services were called to the property in Ashlyn Close shortly before 10pm on Tuesday. The three women were found with serious injuries and pronounced dead at the scene. Police believe a crossbow was among the weapons used.

Hertfordshire Police said the attack was being treated as targeted and that officers were not looking for anyone else in connection with the deaths. They urged the public not to speculate while the investigation continues. The force had earlier released Clifford's name and photograph and warned people not to approach him if they saw him.

Neighbours described the street as quiet and close-knit. Many said they were shocked to wake to police cordons and forensic tents outside the family home. Floral tributes began to appear near the scene on Wednesday as officers carried out house-to-house inquiries.

The case has been referred to the Independent Office for Police Conduct, a standard step where there has been prior police contact with those involved. Specialist officers are supporting the Hunt family, who have asked for privacy as they come to terms with their loss.

Police have appealed for anyone with information, dashcam footage or doorbell camera recordings from the Bushey and Enfield areas to come forward.

Bus passengers in England will pay up to £3 for a single journey from January, after the government confirmed that the current £2 cap on fares will rise by 50%.

The £2 cap, introduced in January 2023 to help with the cost of living and encourage people back onto public transport after the pandemic, had been due to expire at the end of December. Ministers said the higher cap would remain in place until the end of 2025, at a cost of about £150m.

The Department for Transport said the previous government had not set aside money to continue the scheme beyond this year, and that without intervention many fares would have returned to their previous levels. On some longer rural routes, single tickets had cost more than £10 before the cap was introduced.

Officials argued that the new limit would still protect passengers from steep price rises, particularly in areas where fares had been highest. They added that funding would continue for councils to improve services and reliability.

However, campaigners warned the increase would hit those who rely most heavily on buses, including younger people, older passengers who do not qualify for free travel, and people on low incomes without access to a car. Some groups said the change risked reversing the rise in passenger numbers seen since the cap began, at a time when operators are still struggling to recover from the pandemic.

Opposition politicians criticised the move as a tax on working people, saying commuters making two journeys a day could face hundreds of pounds in extra costs over a year.

Not every passenger will be affected. Several mayoral authorities, including Greater Manchester, have said they will keep their own £2 caps, funded through local budgets, meaning fares will vary depending on where in England people live.

New Zealand booked their place in the semi-finals with a commanding 54-run victory over Pakistan in Dubai, a result that also ended India's hopes of progressing from Group A.

Sophie Devine's side were held to a modest 110-6 after being put in on a sluggish pitch, with Suzie Bates top-scoring with a patient 28. But their bowlers made light work of the defence, dismissing Pakistan for just 56 inside 12 overs.

Pakistan's chase never gathered momentum. Wickets fell steadily in the powerplay as New Zealand's seamers exploited the extra bounce, and the spinners then tightened the grip through the middle overs. Amelia Kerr was the pick of the attack, taking 3-14 to continue her fine tournament, while the fielders backed her up with sharp catches.

The contrast in the field was stark. Pakistan put down a string of chances during New Zealand's innings, and Devine admitted afterwards that her side had been given "a few lives" that made the difference on a difficult surface.

"We knew 110 was probably a par score, maybe a bit above, on that wicket," she said. "The girls were outstanding with the ball. To restrict a side to that total shows how far this group has come over the past few weeks."

Pakistan captain Fatima Sana conceded her team had let the opportunity slip. "We bowled well to keep them to 110, but you can't drop that many catches in a World Cup and expect to win," she said. "We will learn from it."

The result means New Zealand finish second in the group behind unbeaten Australia, setting up a semi-final against the winners of Group B in Sharjah later this week.

For India, who had needed Pakistan to win to stay in contention on net run rate, it was a disappointing end to a campaign that began with high expectations.

Ruud van Nistelrooy's second match as interim manager ended in a familiar stalemate, but the more pressing story at Old Trafford was the man not yet in the dugout. Ruben Amorim, who arrives from Sporting Lisbon later this month, will have plenty of footage to study from this 1-1 draw with Chelsea. Little of it will make for comfortable viewing.

For long spells United looked like a side without a clear identity, a team of capable individuals operating without a shared idea of how to hurt opponents. They pressed in bursts rather than as a unit, and when they won the ball back, attacks too often stalled in midfield as players searched for options that were not there. Chelsea, more assured in possession, were content to probe and wait.

The breakthrough came from a moment of chaos rather than design. Rasmus Højlund was brought down by Robert Sánchez, and Bruno Fernandes converted the penalty with his customary composure. The lead lasted barely four minutes. Moisés Caicedo met a loose ball with a thunderous volley that left André Onana with no chance, and United's fragility at defending second balls was exposed once more.

That sequence summed up the scale of Amorim's challenge. His Sporting side were built on a back three, relentless coordination and wing-backs who could cover the length of the pitch. United's squad, assembled across several managerial eras with conflicting philosophies, does not obviously suit that system. Some of the full-backs are better defending than driving forward, and the midfield lacks the legs to protect a back line when the press is bypassed.

There were encouraging signs. The effort was there, and the crowd responded to a team that at least competed. But effort alone will not lift United back toward the Champions League places. Amorim inherits a club craving clarity, and he will need time, patience and probably reinforcements to provide it.

The Pittsburgh-based company Astrobotic said it had steered the crippled spacecraft into Earth's atmosphere on Thursday, where it is believed to have burned up over a remote stretch of the South Pacific. A tracking station in Canberra, Australia, confirmed loss of signal with the lander at about 21:00 GMT, indicating the craft had begun its fiery descent.

Peregrine had been in trouble almost from the moment it separated from its Vulcan rocket after launching from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on 8 January. Engineers soon discovered a propellant leak, which left the lander struggling to keep its solar panels pointed at the Sun and ended any hope of a touchdown on the lunar surface.

Astrobotic believes a faulty valve allowed high-pressure helium to rush into an oxidiser tank, causing it to rupture. Despite the damage, the team managed to stabilise the craft and keep it operating for more than 10 days, far longer than first expected. During that time it travelled out to the distance of the Moon's orbit before swinging back towards Earth.

The company said it chose to dispose of the lander deliberately rather than risk leaving it adrift, where it might become a hazard to other spacecraft. The decision was taken in consultation with NASA and the US government.

NASA had paid Astrobotic about $108m to carry five scientific instruments to the Moon, as part of a programme that pays private firms to deliver its cargo. Several of the payloads were switched on during the flight and returned data, including measurements of the radiation environment in deep space.

Had it succeeded, Peregrine would have been the first American spacecraft to make a soft landing on the Moon since Apollo 17 in 1972, and the first commercial lander to do so.

That opportunity now passes to another US company, Houston-based Intuitive Machines, which is due to launch its own lander next month. Astrobotic says it will apply the lessons learned to its larger Griffin lander, scheduled to fly later.

Aston Villa have completed the loan signing of Marco Asensio from Paris Saint-Germain, adding further attacking quality to Unai Emery's squad as the club enters a demanding final stretch of the season on multiple fronts.

The Spain international, who has struggled for regular minutes in the French capital this term, joins on a deal running until the end of the campaign. The 29-year-old brings considerable experience at the highest level, having won multiple La Liga and Champions League titles during his time at Real Madrid before moving to PSG in 2023.

Asensio's versatility is expected to appeal to Emery, who has long favoured players capable of operating across the front line. The left-footed forward can play on the right wing, through the middle or as an attacking midfielder, and his arrival offers Villa another creative option following the departure of Jhon Durán earlier in the window.

Villa have also reached an agreement with Chelsea to take defender Axel Disasi on loan for the remainder of the season. The France international has found opportunities increasingly limited at Stamford Bridge under Enzo Maresca, and he is expected to undergo a medical before the deal is finalised.

Disasi's addition would address a clear need at the back. With Diego Carlos having left for Fenerbahçe and injuries testing Villa's defensive depth, Emery has been keen to bring in a centre-back who can step in immediately. The 26-year-old, who joined Chelsea from Monaco in 2023, can also operate at right-back, giving the Villa manager welcome flexibility.

The moves cap a busy deadline period for the Midlands club, who are balancing a push for European qualification in the Premier League with their continued involvement in the Champions League and FA Cup. Club officials have worked to strengthen the squad while remaining mindful of the Premier League's profit and sustainability rules, making short-term loan arrangements a particularly attractive option.

Pearl Black, aged 22 months, was walking with her father and younger brother in Heolgerrig, Merthyr Tydfil, in August 2017 when an unoccupied Range Rover rolled off a driveway and down a hill. The vehicle crossed the road and struck a garden wall, which collapsed on top of her. She was taken to hospital but could not be saved.

Her parents, Paul and Gemma Black, said they had been left "utterly let down" by the justice system after being told that no one would face prosecution over their daughter's death.

The Crown Prosecution Service concluded that charges could not be brought under road traffic legislation because the car had begun its journey on private land rather than on a public road. Prosecutors also decided there was insufficient evidence to support any alternative charge.

The family said they could not understand how the place where the car had been parked could make such a difference when Pearl was killed on a public street. They said the decision had compounded their grief and left them feeling that their daughter's life had counted for nothing in the eyes of the law.

Mr and Mrs Black are now calling for the legislation to be changed so that drivers can be held responsible for vehicles left on private property which go on to cause death or serious injury elsewhere. They said they did not want another family to go through the same experience.

Their campaign has won the backing of their local MP, who has raised the case in Parliament and described the situation as a loophole that needs to be closed.

A CPS spokesman said it had every sympathy with Pearl's family and had met them to explain its reasoning in detail, but added that prosecutors were bound to apply the law as it stands.

The Department for Transport said it was aware of the case and would consider the issues it raised.

Darwin Nunez marked his return from injury with a dramatic 99th-minute header as Liverpool snatched victory at Nottingham Forest to move four points clear at the top of the Premier League.

The Uruguayan striker, who missed last weekend's Carabao Cup final win over Chelsea with a muscle problem, came off the bench after an hour and rose to glance Alexis Mac Allister's cross beyond Matz Sels with almost the last touch of the game.

It was a cruel blow for Forest, who had defended resolutely and created the better chances for long periods, but the manner of the goal left the home side furious.

Referee Paul Tierney had stopped play moments earlier for a head injury to Ibrahima Konate while Forest were in possession, yet restarted with a drop ball to Liverpool goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher. The visitors went up the other end and eventually forced the winner, sparking angry protests from Forest's players and staff at the final whistle.

Jurgen Klopp's side, still without Mohamed Salah, Alisson and Trent Alexander-Arnold among a lengthy list of absentees, had struggled to find their rhythm at the City Ground.

Forest should have been ahead before the break when Anthony Elanga raced clear, only for Kelleher to save with his legs. The hosts continued to threaten on the counter-attack in the second half.

Liverpool gradually increased the pressure after the introduction of Nunez and Dominik Szoboszlai, who was also making his comeback from injury, but they looked set to drop points until the Uruguayan's late intervention sent the travelling supporters into raptures.

The result piles the pressure on Manchester City, who host Manchester United in Sunday's derby, while Nuno Espirito Santo's Forest remain just four points above the relegation zone.

"It is hard to take," said Nuno. "The players worked so hard and deserved something from the game."

The decision follows an extensive end-of-season review carried out by the club's board, led by minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his Ineos team, who took control of football operations earlier this year.

Ten Hag's future had been the subject of intense speculation after United finished eighth in the Premier League, their lowest placing since the competition began in 1992. They lost 14 league matches, ended the campaign with a negative goal difference, and were eliminated from the Champions League after finishing bottom of their group.

However, the Dutchman finished the season by guiding his side to a 2-1 victory over rivals Manchester City in the FA Cup final at Wembley. That secured his second trophy in two years, following the Carabao Cup success in 2023, and earned the club a place in next season's Europa League.

It is understood that United spoke to representatives of several potential replacements during the review, with Thomas Tuchel, Roberto De Zerbi and Mauricio Pochettino among those linked with the role. Ultimately, the club's hierarchy concluded that Ten Hag remained the best candidate to take the team forward.

The 54-year-old, who joined from Ajax in the summer of 2022, has one year remaining on his current contract, with the club holding an option for a further 12 months. Talks are now expected to take place over an extension to that deal.

Speaking after the cup final, Ten Hag had made clear that if United no longer wanted him, he would go elsewhere to win trophies, pointing to the record he had built throughout his career. He also highlighted the injury problems that disrupted his squad for much of the season, particularly in defence.

Supporters had shown their backing for the manager at Wembley, and the players were reported to be largely supportive of him staying.

Attention is now expected to turn to the summer transfer window, with United keen to strengthen in several positions before the new season.

Novak Djokovic and Roger Federer led the tributes to Rafael Nadal after the 22-time Grand Slam champion announced he will retire from professional tennis at the end of the season.

The 38-year-old Spaniard, who has been troubled by injuries over the past two years, confirmed in a video message on Thursday that next month's Davis Cup Finals in Malaga will be his last event.

Federer, who retired in 2022 with Nadal alongside him at the Laver Cup, wrote on social media: "What a career, Rafa! I always hoped this day would never come.

"Thank you for the unforgettable memories and all your incredible achievements in the game we love. It's been an absolute honour!"

Djokovic, who faced Nadal a record 60 times, said a single post was "not enough to express the respect I have for you and what you have done for our sport".

"You have inspired millions of children to start playing tennis and I think that's probably the greatest achievement anyone can wish for," the Serb added.

"Your tenacity, dedication, fighting spirit is going to be taught for decades. Your legacy will live forever."

Nadal won a record 14 French Open titles, losing just four matches at Roland Garros in almost two decades, and spent 209 weeks as world number one. Together with Federer and Djokovic he formed the 'Big Three' that dominated the men's game for the best part of 20 years.

World number one Jannik Sinner, speaking at the Shanghai Masters, described the announcement as "tough news for all the tennis world, and not only the tennis world".

Carlos Alcaraz, who partnered his compatriot in the doubles at the Paris Olympics this summer, said the news was difficult to accept, having grown up idolising Nadal.

In his announcement, Nadal said the last couple of years had been especially difficult. "I don't think I have been able to play without limitations," he said. "It is obviously a difficult decision, one that has taken me some time to make."

Residents of the County Antrim village have spoken of their disbelief after a man was found nailed to a fence in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The victim, who is in his 20s, was discovered in the Dundarave car park with nails driven through both of his hands. He was taken to hospital, where his injuries were described as serious and potentially life-changing.

Police said a van was also set alight in the car park and graffiti was daubed on the walls of a nearby public toilet block. Detectives have described the incident as a "sinister attack" and say they are keeping an open mind about the motive.

One woman, who has lived in Bushmills for more than 30 years, said the news had left neighbours shaken.

"It's just awful. You don't expect to wake up and hear something like that has happened a few hundred yards from your front door," she said. "This is a quiet place. People come here from all over the world for the distillery and the Causeway, and now this is what we're known for."

A local shop owner said the attack was the only topic of conversation among customers on Monday morning.

"Everybody is horrified. Whoever did this has no place in this community," he said. "Nobody knows what was behind it, but nothing could justify it."

A local councillor said those responsible had shown "a level of brutality that is hard to comprehend" and urged anyone with information to come forward.

"Somebody knows who did this, and they need to tell the police what they know," the councillor said.

The car park, which is regularly used by tourists and coach parties, remained partially cordoned off for much of Sunday while forensic officers examined the scene.

Police have appealed for witnesses, and for anyone with dashcam or CCTV footage from the area between Saturday night and Sunday morning, to contact them.

The foreign secretary arrived in New Delhi less than three weeks after Labour's election victory, making good on a pledge he made in opposition to visit India within his first month in office. He was due to meet prime minister Narendra Modi and external affairs minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, with trade, technology and climate co-operation at the top of the agenda.

Central to the visit is the long-delayed free trade agreement, which has been under negotiation since January 2022. Successive Conservative governments failed to conclude the deal, most notably when Boris Johnson's promise to have it "done by Diwali" that year came and went. Lammy has previously criticised the Tories for over-promising and under-delivering on India, and officials said the new government wanted to restart talks as soon as possible.

"Our free trade agreement negotiation is the floor not the ceiling of our ambitions to unlock our shared potential and deliver growth, from Bengaluru to Birmingham," Lammy said ahead of the trip. He described India as "the emerging superpower of the 21st century", with 1.4bn people and one of the fastest-growing economies in the world.

Significant obstacles remain. New Delhi has pushed for more visas for Indian professionals and students, a politically sensitive demand for a government that has promised to bring down net migration. Britain, meanwhile, is seeking lower tariffs on exports such as Scotch whisky and cars, as well as greater access for its legal and financial services firms.

Analysts said the timing of the visit was itself a signal. Labour's relationship with India soured under Jeremy Corbyn, particularly after a 2019 party conference motion on Kashmir angered New Delhi and alienated many British Indian voters. Sir Keir Starmer has worked to repair that damage, and sending his foreign secretary so early is intended to show that the party regards the relationship as a strategic priority rather than an afterthought.

The mobile network, one of the largest in the UK, said children under 11 should instead be given "limited capability" devices, such as feature phones that allow calls and text messages but offer no access to social media or the wider internet.

The guidance, issued before the start of the new school year, is thought to be the first of its kind from a British mobile operator. It comes amid growing concern among parents, teachers and politicians about how smartphones affect children's wellbeing, attention and safety.

For children aged 11 to 13, EE advises that a smartphone should have parental controls switched on and be paired with a family-sharing app, with access to social media restricted. For those aged 13 to 16, it says smartphones are appropriate, but parents should still use controls to limit access to unsuitable sites, content and platforms.

Mat Sears, EE's corporate affairs director, said the increasing complexity of smartphones could be challenging for parents and carers, and that the company wanted to help them make the best choices for their children through their formative years.

Research published by Ofcom earlier this year found that about a quarter of children aged five to seven in the UK now own a smartphone. By the time they move to secondary school, the overwhelming majority have one. The regulator also found that many children use social media apps well before the minimum age of 13.

The announcement follows the rapid growth of the grassroots campaign Smartphone Free Childhood, in which tens of thousands of parents have pledged to delay giving their children smartphones. MPs on the Commons education committee have also urged the government to consider tougher restrictions, including a possible ban on smartphones for under-16s.

Campaigners welcomed EE's move but said responsibility could not rest with families alone. They called on technology companies and ministers to do more to make devices and online platforms safe for young users.

The new monarch, Ngā Wai hono i te pō, 27, was anointed on Thursday morning at Tūrangawaewae Marae in Ngāruawāhia, the seat of the Kiingitanga, or Māori King movement, on New Zealand's North Island. She is the youngest child and only daughter of Kiingi Tuheitia Pootatau Te Wherowhero VII, who died last week aged 69 while recovering from heart surgery, just days after celebrations marking the 18th anniversary of his coronation.

Her selection by a council of tribal leaders was announced to thousands of mourners who had gathered for the final day of the king's tangihanga, or funeral rites. She was ushered onto the marae to chants and cheers and seated on a carved wooden throne beside her father's coffin. Archbishop Don Tamihere anointed her with the same Bible used to crown the first Māori king in 1858.

She becomes the eighth Māori monarch and only the second queen. The first was her grandmother, Te Arikinui Dame Te Atairangikaahu, who reigned for four decades until her death in 2006.

After the ceremony, the king's coffin was carried to the Waikato River and borne by a flotilla of waka, or traditional canoes, to Taupiri Mountain, which is sacred to the Waikato-Tainui people. Rugby players and local men hauled the casket up the steep slope to its summit, where he was laid to rest alongside his ancestors.

The Kiingitanga was founded in 1858 to unite Māori tribes in resisting the loss of land to British colonisation and to preserve Māori culture. The role carries no legal power and is largely ceremonial, but it holds considerable symbolic weight.

Ngā Wai hono i te pō, who holds a master's degree in Māori cultural studies and teaches kapa haka, the traditional performing arts, takes the throne at a tense moment. Earlier this year her father convened a rare national gathering of Māori in response to government policies that critics say would roll back Indigenous rights.

The filing, lodged in a Texas court on Monday, accuses Universal Music Group (UMG) of defamation, claiming the label could have stopped the release of a song that "falsely" accused the Canadian star of being a sex offender.

Lawyers for Drake, whose full name is Aubrey Drake Graham, allege that UMG "funnelled payments" to the radio giant iHeartRadio as part of a "pay-to-play scheme" to boost the track's airplay. The petition seeks depositions from executives at both companies before any full lawsuit is brought.

It comes a day after a separate action in New York, in which the rapper accused UMG and Spotify of conspiring to artificially inflate the popularity of Not Like Us through the use of bots and discounted licensing rates.

Lamar, who is not named as a respondent in either filing, released the track in May at the height of a bitter feud between the two artists. Its lyrics brand Drake a "certified pedophile", an allegation he has strenuously denied.

The song went on to top the US charts, break streaming records and earn several Grammy nominations, including record and song of the year.

According to the Texas filing, UMG "knew that the song itself, as well as its accompanying album art and music video, attacked the character of another one of UMG's most prominent artists" yet "chose to do the opposite" of blocking it. The label, it adds, "designed, financed and then executed a plan to turn Not Like Us into a viral mega-hit".

Both Drake and Lamar are signed to divisions of Universal: Drake through Republic Records and Lamar through Interscope.

UMG has rejected the claims. "The suggestion that UMG would do anything to undermine any of its artists is offensive and untrue," a spokesperson said. "We employ the highest ethical practices in our marketing and promotional campaigns.

"No amount of contrived and absurd legal arguments in this pre-action submission can mask the fact that fans choose the music they want to hear."

iHeartRadio has not yet commented publicly on the allegations.

The former chief executive of the Post Office, Paula Vennells, broke down in tears as she was accused of giving a false statement to MPs about the prosecution of post office operators.

Giving evidence to the Horizon IT inquiry, Vennells was questioned about a meeting with parliamentarians in 2012. At that meeting she said every prosecution involving the Horizon system had been found in favour of the Post Office.

Jason Beer KC, counsel to the inquiry, told her the claim was untrue. He listed several post office operators who had been acquitted by juries after blaming the faulty accounting software for shortfalls at their branches, among them Suzanne Palmer, Maureen McKelvey and Nichola Arch.

Asked why she had told MPs that every prosecution had been successful, Vennells paused to compose herself before replying: "I fully accept now that the Post Office knew that. Personally, I didn't know that, and I'm incredibly sorry that it happened to those people and to so many others."

She said she had relied on information given to her by colleagues, and insisted she had not set out to mislead anyone. Beer suggested the statement had been used to reassure politicians who were raising concerns on behalf of constituents, at a time when doubts about the reliability of Horizon were mounting.

Vennells, who led the organisation from 2012 to 2019, began her evidence with an apology to those affected by the scandal. She told the hearing she had been "too trusting" of those around her.

More than 900 post office operators were prosecuted between 1999 and 2015 after the Fujitsu-built Horizon system made it appear that money was missing from their branches. Some were jailed and many more were left bankrupt.

Former post office operators watching from the public gallery reacted with audible scepticism at points during her testimony. The inquiry, chaired by Sir Wyn Williams, continues.

Albania's prime minister, Edi Rama, has announced that the government will shut down TikTok for one year, weeks after a 14-year-old schoolboy was stabbed to death by a fellow pupil in the capital, Tirana.

The ban is expected to come into force early in 2025. It follows a series of meetings Rama held with parents' groups and teachers across the country after the killing in November. Local media reported that the stabbing came after arguments between the two boys on social media, and videos later emerged on TikTok of young people voicing support for the killing.

"For one year, we'll be completely shutting it down for everyone. There will be no TikTok in Albania," Rama said on Saturday.

The prime minister has singled out the video-sharing platform in particular, blaming it for fuelling violence among young people both inside and outside school. "The problem today is not our children, the problem today is us, the problem today is our society, the problem today is TikTok and all the others that are taking our children hostage," he said.

TikTok said it was seeking "urgent clarity" from the Albanian government. The company said it had found no evidence that either the suspect or the victim held TikTok accounts, and that multiple reports indicated videos leading up to the incident had been posted on another platform.

Opposition politicians criticised the decision, accusing the government of curbing freedom of expression in the run-up to parliamentary elections due next year.

Rama said the government would use the year to observe how the company and other countries respond before deciding whether to allow the platform to resume operating in Albania.

The move comes amid growing international concern over the effect of social media on children. Australia approved a ban on social media for under-16s in November, while several European countries, including France, Germany and Belgium, have introduced restrictions on its use by minors.

The FBI said on Thursday that it no longer believes anyone else was involved in the New Year's Day attack on Bourbon Street, reversing its earlier assessment that the driver may have had accomplices.

"We do not assess at this point that anyone else is involved in this attack except for Shamsud-Din Jabbar," Christopher Raia, deputy assistant director of the bureau's counterterrorism division, told reporters in New Orleans. He described the attack as "premeditated and an evil act" and said Jabbar was "100% inspired by ISIS."

Jabbar, a 42-year-old US Army veteran from Texas, drove a rented pickup truck into crowds of revellers in the city's French Quarter in the early hours of Wednesday, killing 14 people and injuring dozens more. He died in an exchange of gunfire with police, during which two officers were wounded.

Investigators had initially said they did not believe Jabbar was "solely responsible", raising fears that others connected to the attack remained at large. Raia said that after reviewing hundreds of tips, surveillance footage and Jabbar's phone records, agents had concluded that he placed two improvised explosive devices found in coolers near the scene himself. Both were made safe.

According to the FBI, Jabbar rented the truck in Houston on 30 December and drove to New Orleans the following evening. During the journey he posted five videos to Facebook in which he pledged support for the Islamic State group. In one, Raia said, Jabbar explained that he had originally planned to harm his family and friends but feared that news coverage would not focus on the "war between the believers and the disbelievers." A black IS flag was recovered from the rear of the vehicle.

Raia added that investigators had so far found "no definitive link" between the New Orleans attack and the explosion of a Tesla Cybertruck outside a Trump hotel in Las Vegas later the same day.

Red Bull announced on Thursday that Lawson will return to sister team Racing Bulls after just two grands prix alongside Max Verstappen, with Tsunoda moving in the opposite direction in time for his home race at Suzuka on 4-6 April.

The 23-year-old New Zealander, promoted in December to replace Sergio Perez, endured a bruising start to the season. He qualified 18th in Australia before crashing out in wet conditions, then lined up last for both the sprint and the grand prix in China, where he was classified 12th only after three cars ahead of him were disqualified.

Team principal Christian Horner described the switch as "a purely sporting decision".

"It has been difficult to see Liam struggle with the RB21 at the first two races and as a result we have collectively taken the decision to make an early switch," Horner said.

"We came into the 2025 season with two ambitions, to retain the world drivers' championship and to reclaim the world constructors' title. We acknowledge there is a lot of work to be done with the RB21 and Yuki's experience will prove highly beneficial in helping to develop the current car."

Horner added that the team had "a duty of care to protect and develop Liam", saying it made sense "to act quickly" so he could continue his career in "an environment and a team he knows very well".

Tsunoda, 24, is in his fifth season in Formula One, all of it spent with Red Bull's junior outfit, and was overlooked for the senior seat over the winter despite outperforming Lawson during their six races as team-mates last year. He will become the first Japanese driver to race for Red Bull, doing so in front of his home crowd and at a circuit owned by engine partner Honda.

Lawson will partner French rookie Isack Hadjar at Racing Bulls for the remainder of the campaign.

England defender Lucy Bronze says the Lionesses are "one of the most adaptive teams" in international football as they prepare to face world champions Spain in a decisive Nations League match in Barcelona on Tuesday.

Sarina Wiegman's side must win at the RCDE Stadium to top their group and reach the semi-finals, while a draw would be enough for Spain to progress.

England beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley in February and warmed up for the trip with a 6-0 thrashing of Portugal on Friday.

"I think we're one of the most adaptive teams in international football at the moment," said Bronze, who spent two seasons at Barcelona before joining Chelsea last summer.

"We've got players who can play in a number of different positions and we've shown we can change the way we play depending on who we're up against. Not many teams can say that.

"Spain have a very clear way of playing and they're very good at it. Everybody knows what they're going to do, but stopping it is the difficult part. We managed it at Wembley and we know we will have to be at our very best to do it again."

The match is England's last competitive fixture before they begin the defence of their European title in Switzerland next month, where they have been drawn in a group alongside France, the Netherlands and Wales.

Bronze, 33, believes a meeting with the side who beat them in the 2023 World Cup final is ideal preparation.

"These are the games you want to play in," she added. "It's a must-win, away from home, against the world champions. You can't really ask for a better test going into a major tournament.

"We've had ups and downs over the past year, but I think the performance against Portugal showed what this team is capable of when everything clicks."

Wiegman is expected to name her Euro 2025 squad on Thursday.

Speaking at a news conference in Tel Aviv after meeting Israeli leaders, Mr Blinken said the daily toll on civilians in Gaza, "particularly children, is far too high". He urged Israel to do more to protect non-combatants and to allow more aid into the territory.

The US secretary of state said he had pressed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the need to avoid further civilian harm. He stressed that Washington continued to support Israel's right to prevent a repeat of the 7 October attacks.

"We know that facing an enemy that embeds itself among civilians, who hides in and fires from schools and hospitals, makes this incredibly challenging," he said. "But the daily toll on civilians in Gaza, particularly children, is far too high."

More than 23,000 people, many of them women and children, have been killed in Gaza since the war began, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. Israel launched its offensive after Hamas gunmen killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel and took some 240 others hostage.

Mr Blinken said displaced Palestinians must be allowed to return to their homes "as soon as conditions allow" and must not be pressed to leave Gaza. He added that an agreement had been reached for a United Nations mission to assess conditions in the north of the territory, where much of the infrastructure has been destroyed.

He also said Israel must stop taking steps that undermine the ability of Palestinians to govern themselves, and repeated US support for a future Palestinian state alongside Israel.

Mr Blinken, on his fourth visit to the region since the conflict began, said countries he had visited in recent days were prepared to help rebuild and stabilise Gaza. He said this would require a clear path towards Palestinian statehood.

He dismissed as "meritless" a case brought by South Africa at the International Court of Justice accusing Israel of genocide.

Dr Susan Gilby, who joined the Countess of Chester Hospital as medical director in August 2018, told the Thirlwall Inquiry that the then chief executive Tony Chambers had made his views clear in their earliest conversations.

She said Mr Chambers told her that he believed the police investigation, which had led to Letby's first arrest a month earlier, would find no evidence of wrongdoing by the nurse. He instead suggested the rise in deaths on the neonatal unit was linked to poor clinical care and the unit's leadership, she said.

Dr Gilby told the hearing at Liverpool Town Hall that she was given the impression that the consultants who had raised the alarm were regarded as the problem, and that Mr Chambers had spoken of referring some of them to the General Medical Council.

She said she was surprised by how firmly he held this view, given that detectives were still gathering evidence.

When she later reviewed documents held in the executive offices, Dr Gilby said she was shocked by what she found. She said it appeared to her that the doctors' concerns had not been properly listened to.

Letby, 34, is serving 15 whole-life orders after being convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others between June 2015 and June 2016.

Consultants on the unit had repeatedly raised concerns about the nurse's presence at a series of unexplained collapses and deaths, but she was not removed from frontline duties until July 2016. Police were not called in until the following year.

Dr Gilby, who went on to succeed Mr Chambers as chief executive after he stepped down in September 2018, said the paediatricians had been deeply affected by how they were treated.

Mr Chambers is due to give his own evidence to the inquiry at a later date.

The inquiry, chaired by Lady Justice Thirlwall, is examining how Letby was able to commit her crimes and how the hospital's management responded to concerns raised by staff. It continues.

At Tufts University, near Boston, students say the mood changed overnight after video circulated of Rumeysa Ozturk, a Turkish doctoral student, being stopped on a suburban street by masked, plainclothes officers and led away to an unmarked car. Ozturk, who had co-written an opinion piece in the student newspaper about the war in Gaza, was taken to a detention centre in Louisiana, more than 1,500 miles away.

"Everyone has watched that video," said one graduate student from South Asia, who asked not to be named for fear of losing his visa. "You see it and think, that could be me walking to dinner."

Her case followed the arrest of Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia University graduate and legal permanent resident who was a prominent figure in pro-Palestinian protests on campus. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the government has revoked at least 300 student visas. "Every time I find one of these lunatics, I take away their visas," he told reporters.

The administration says it is acting against people who support terrorist groups or threaten US foreign policy interests. Lawyers for the students say their clients have been targeted for protected political speech, and that some have had their visas cancelled over minor infractions or for no stated reason at all.

On campuses across the country, the effect has been chilling. International students described deleting social media accounts, avoiding demonstrations and carrying immigration documents wherever they go. Several said they had cancelled trips home, fearing they would not be allowed back in.

Universities, some facing threats to their federal funding, have urged foreign students to stay in contact with advisers and to think carefully before travelling abroad. Faculty members have begun organising legal information sessions and, in some cases, offering to accompany students to class.

"I came here because I believed I could speak freely," said a master's student from the Middle East. "Now I just keep my head down and count the months until graduation."

On Sunday morning, Maryam will draw the curtains of her apartment in a suburb of Tehran, turn the television up loud enough to mask the sound of voices, and wait for the knock at the door. Seven people are expected, arriving one or two at a time so as not to attract the neighbours' attention. Phones will be switched off and left in another room.

"We sing very quietly, almost whispering," says the 34-year-old, whose name has been changed for her safety. "But it is still Easter. It is still the happiest day of our year."

Maryam was raised in a Muslim family and converted to Christianity eight years ago. In Iran, that decision carries considerable risk. While the constitution recognises the country's historic Armenian and Assyrian Christian communities, who are permitted to worship in their own churches, services in Persian are effectively banned and converts from Islam have no legal recognition.

Instead, they gather in so-called house churches, small informal groups that meet in private homes and frequently change location. Rights groups say members are regularly arrested in raids, often around Christmas and Easter, and charged with offences such as "acting against national security" or "propaganda against the system". Some have received prison sentences of up to ten years.

Iranian officials insist that no one is prosecuted for their beliefs and describe house churches as illegal networks with foreign backing.

Reza, another convert who fled to Turkey after being interrogated in 2021, remembers the fear vividly. "Every time the doorbell rang during prayer, everyone would freeze," he says. "You hide your Bible. You look at each other and wonder if this is the day."

Even so, he says, the gatherings continued. One year his group shared a single loaf of bread and a cup of grape juice around a kitchen table.

"We could not have a church, bells or candles," he says. "But nobody could take the meaning away."

Before Pope Francis made him a cardinal in December, Pablo Virgilio David was best known in the Philippines as "Bishop Ambo," the soft-spoken biblical scholar who refused to stay silent as bodies piled up in the alleys of his diocese.

Kalookan, the diocese he has led since 2016, takes in some of metropolitan Manila's poorest and most densely packed neighborhoods. They became a front line in the anti-drug campaign of then-President Rodrigo Duterte, in which thousands of mostly poor suspects were killed by police and unidentified gunmen. Among the dead was Kian delos Santos, a 17-year-old whose 2017 killing by police officers was captured in part on security cameras and stirred rare public outrage.

David denounced the killings from the pulpit, opened church doors to witnesses, and set up programs for the widows and orphans left behind, as well as community-based rehabilitation for drug users. Duterte responded with fury, accusing the bishop in public speeches of stealing church donations and suggesting he was himself involved in drugs. David received death threats, and in 2019 police filed a sedition complaint against him and several other clergymen and opposition figures. The case against him was later dropped.

Through it all, David has said, he drew strength from Francis. During a visit by Filipino bishops to the Vatican in 2019, the pope took him aside, told him he knew what was happening in his diocese and assured him of his prayers, according to David's account of the meeting.

Now 66 and president of the Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines, David enters the Sistine Chapel this week as one of three Filipino electors. His adversary's fortunes, meanwhile, have reversed: Duterte was arrested in March and flown to The Hague, where he faces charges of crimes against humanity before the International Criminal Court.

The portrait, unveiled by the King himself at Buckingham Palace on Tuesday, shows the monarch in the uniform of the Welsh Guards, of which he was made Regimental Colonel in 1975. Sword in hand, he emerges from a backdrop of vivid red brushstrokes, with a butterfly hovering just above his shoulder.

Measuring roughly 8ft 6in by 6ft 6in, the oil on canvas was commissioned in 2020 by the Drapers' Company to mark the then Prince of Wales's 50 years as a member of the livery company in 2022.

Yeo, who has previously painted Sir Tony Blair, Sir David Attenborough and Malala Yousafzai, had four sittings with the King. The first took place at Highgrove in June 2021 and the last at Clarence House in November 2023. He also worked from drawings and photographs.

"When I started this project, His Majesty The King was still His Royal Highness The Prince of Wales, and much like the butterfly I've painted hovering over his shoulder, this portrait has evolved as the subject's role in our public life has transformed," the artist said.

He added that he had tried to capture the life experiences etched into his sitter's face, and to reference the traditions of royal portraiture in a way that reflects a 21st Century monarchy.

Queen Camilla, whom Yeo painted in 2014, is said to have looked at the finished work and told the artist: "Yes, you've got him."

The King, who returned to public duties last month following his cancer diagnosis, was seen to pull back the covering with a slight look of surprise before smiling at the result.

The painting will go on public display at the Philip Mould Gallery in London from 16 May until 14 June. It will then hang at Drapers' Hall in the City of London from the end of August, alongside the company's collection of royal portraits.

Police in the canton of Graubünden have opened an investigation after a sign appeared at a ski rental shop above Davos saying that sports equipment would no longer be rented to Jewish customers.

The notice, written in Hebrew, was posted at the mountain station restaurant on the Pischa, a small ski area popular with families. It said that following a series of "very annoying incidents", including the theft of a sledge, the business would no longer rent items such as sledges, airboards and snowshoes to "our Jewish brothers".

A photograph of the sign spread quickly on social media, prompting outrage in Switzerland and abroad. The Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities (SIG) said it would file a legal complaint, arguing that the notice breached the country's anti-discrimination law.

Its secretary general, Jonathan Kreutner, described the sign as shocking and said that an entire group of guests was being collectively stigmatised because of their appearance and origin.

The operators of the restaurant initially defended the decision, telling Swiss media that it had nothing to do with religion and that they no longer wanted the daily hassle of equipment being left on the slopes or returned damaged. They later removed the sign and apologised, saying it had been badly worded.

Davos, best known internationally as host of the annual World Economic Forum, has long been a favoured holiday destination for Orthodox Jewish visitors, with several thousand arriving each year. But relations have at times been strained. Last summer, the local tourism director complained that some guests failed to respect local customs, and a joint project with the SIG aimed at easing tensions was brought to an end.

The incident also revived memories of a 2017 case in nearby Arosa, where a hotel asked Jewish guests to shower before using its pool.

Jewish groups say antisemitic incidents in Switzerland have risen sharply since the Hamas attacks on Israel on 7 October.

The deal will see Barclays take on Tesco Bank's credit cards, unsecured personal loans and savings accounts, covering roughly £8.3bn of lending and £6.7bn of customer deposits. Around 2,800 staff, many of them based in Edinburgh, Glasgow and Newcastle, are expected to transfer to Barclays once the sale completes, which the companies anticipate will happen in the second half of the year, subject to regulatory approval.

Tesco will keep hold of its insurance business, cash machines, travel money service and gift cards, which it described as "capital-light" activities with a strong connection to its stores. The supermarket said these retained operations serve several million customers and would continue to generate steady profits.

As part of the agreement, the two companies will enter a ten-year partnership under which Barclays will continue to market banking products under the Tesco brand, paying the retailer a royalty fee expected to be worth about £50m a year. Customers have been told they do not need to take any action and that there will be no immediate change to their accounts or to the way they collect Clubcard points.

Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy said the sale would allow the group to concentrate on its core retail business while still offering financial services to shoppers through an established banking partner. Barclays boss C.S. Venkatakrishnan said the acquisition supported the lender's ambition to grow its presence in UK consumer banking.

Tesco expects to receive about £1bn in cash from the transaction once a special dividend from the bank is included, and plans to return the majority of that sum to shareholders through a share buyback.

Tesco Bank was launched in 1997 as a joint venture with Royal Bank of Scotland, before the supermarket took full ownership in 2008. Rival Sainsbury's has also announced plans to wind down its own banking arm, as grocers retreat from a sector facing higher funding costs and tighter regulation.

Local journalists said an Israeli warplane fired two missiles at classrooms on the top floor of the school in the densely populated Nuseirat refugee camp, in central Gaza, in the early hours of Thursday. Hundreds of displaced people were believed to be sleeping inside at the time.

Israel's military said it had "conducted a precise strike on a Hamas compound" embedded in the school and that it had killed many of the 20 to 30 fighters it believed were operating there. A spokesman said steps had been taken beforehand to reduce the risk of harming civilians, including aerial surveillance and the use of additional intelligence.

Gaza's Hamas-run Government Media Office rejected the claim and accused Israel of carrying out a "horrific massacre". It put the death toll at 40, saying women and children were among the dead. Officials at the nearby al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital in Deir al-Balah, where casualties were taken, said they had received at least 35 bodies.

Videos shared on social media showed shattered classrooms, with mattresses and belongings scattered among the rubble, and rows of bodies wrapped in white shrouds and blankets in the hospital courtyard. Residents described being woken by the blasts and searching for relatives in the dark.

The head of the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (Unrwa), Philippe Lazzarini, said the school had been sheltering about 6,000 displaced people when it was hit "without prior warning". He said the agency was unable to verify claims that armed groups had been inside, but stressed that attacking, targeting or using UN buildings for military purposes showed a blatant disregard for international humanitarian law.

Unrwa says it shares the co-ordinates of all its facilities with the Israeli military and other parties to the conflict.

The strike came as Israeli forces stepped up operations in central Gaza, and as mediators continued to press both sides to accept a ceasefire and hostage release deal.

A large part of the airport's South Terminal was evacuated on Friday morning after security staff found what police described as a "suspected prohibited item" in a piece of luggage.

Sussex Police said officers were called to the terminal at about 08:20 GMT and a security cordon was put in place as a precaution. An explosive ordnance disposal team was sent to the scene.

Two people who were detained while enquiries were carried out have since been allowed to continue their journeys, the force said.

"Officers have made the package safe and the airport has been handed back to its operator," a police spokesperson said. "We would like to thank the public and airport staff for their patience while the incident was ongoing."

Thousands of passengers were left standing outside in cold weather for several hours, with many handed foil blankets and bottles of water by airport staff. Some travellers described abandoning taxis and walking along the approach road with their suitcases after traffic came to a standstill.

One passenger, who had been due to fly to Spain with her family, said there had been "very little information" in the early stages. "We were just told to leave the building straight away. Nobody knew what was happening," she said.
