Train services were also affected, with rail operators confirming that trains did not call at the airport station for much of the morning. Buses were laid on to take passengers to nearby stations.

A Gatwick spokesperson said the terminal reopened in the afternoon but warned that delays and cancellations were likely to continue for the rest of the day.

"Safety and security of our passengers and staff remains our top priority," the spokesperson said. "We are working hard to get operations back to normal and would advise passengers to check with their airline for the latest information."

The North Terminal was not affected and continued to operate as normal throughout.

Anna Henderson delivered the ride of her career on the rain-soaked streets of Paris to claim silver in the women's individual time trial, Team GB's second medal of the Games.

The 25-year-old from Hemel Hempstead, a former junior ski racer who only took up cycling seriously after injury, finished one minute 31 seconds behind Australia's Grace Brown, who dominated the 32.4km course from Les Invalides to the Pont Alexandre III. Henderson edged out the American world champion Chloe Dygert by less than a second. Dygert had been the pre-race favourite but crashed on one of the many slippery corners that caught out riders throughout the afternoon.

Henderson's medal is all the more remarkable given the disruption to her season. She broke her collarbone twice in the early months of the year and faced a race against time to prove her fitness for selection. On Saturday she rode with composure where others faltered, staying upright through the treacherous bends and holding her pace over the closing kilometres as Dygert closed in.

There was heartbreak, however, for Josh Tarling in the men's event. The 20-year-old Welshman, considered a genuine contender for gold, suffered a front-wheel puncture early in his ride and was forced into a bike change that cost him precious seconds. He fought back to finish fourth, just over two seconds short of the bronze medal won by Belgium's Wout van Aert.

Van Aert's compatriot Remco Evenepoel took gold, adding the Olympic title to the world crown he won in 2023, with Italy's Filippo Ganna taking silver around 15 seconds back.

Tarling, a European champion and world bronze medallist against the clock, was visibly distraught at the finish, knowing that without the mechanical problem a podium place would almost certainly have been his. He will have another chance in the road race next weekend, and at 20 has time firmly on his side.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed it had submitted a formal request for support under mutual aid arrangements, which allow forces across the UK to share officers and resources at times of exceptional demand.

It follows several consecutive nights of disorder in which petrol bombs, masonry and fireworks were thrown at police lines, and a number of homes and businesses were damaged. Dozens of officers have been injured since the violence began, and several arrests have been made.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said the force was assessing the request and would decide soon how many officers could be released. "We are in close contact with our colleagues in the PSNI and are working through what support we can provide, while ensuring that policing in Scotland's communities is maintained," the spokesperson said.

It is understood that any officers deployed would be drawn from specialist public order units, and that they would travel by ferry from Cairnryan with their own vehicles and equipment.

However, the body representing rank-and-file officers warned that the force was already stretched. The Scottish Police Federation said its members would always be willing to help colleagues in need, but questioned whether sufficient numbers could be spared without affecting cover at home.

"Our members are regularly having rest days cancelled and working extended shifts as it is," a federation representative said. "Any deployment has to come with proper guarantees around welfare, accommodation and the safety of those being sent."

The Scottish government said operational decisions were a matter for the chief constable, but added that ministers were being kept informed of developments.

Mutual aid has been used on a number of occasions in recent years, including during major events such as the COP26 climate summit in Glasgow, when thousands of officers from forces across the UK were drafted in to assist Police Scotland.

Political leaders in Northern Ireland have jointly appealed for calm, with further protests expected in the coming days.

The 46-year-old mother of two said she first noticed swelling in her left breast last spring, almost nine years after having implants fitted following the birth of her second child.

"I assumed I'd pulled a muscle at the gym," she said. "It never crossed my mind that it could be connected to the implants, and certainly not that it could be cancer."

After an ultrasound scan revealed a build-up of fluid around the implant, tests confirmed she had breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL). This is a rare cancer of the immune system, not a form of breast cancer, which develops in the scar tissue and fluid surrounding an implant.

The condition has been linked mainly to implants with a textured surface. Symptoms typically appear years after surgery and can include persistent swelling, a lump in the breast or armpit, and pain. When caught early, it is usually treated successfully by removing the implant and the capsule of scar tissue around it, though some patients also need chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

She underwent surgery in the autumn and has since been told there is no sign the disease has spread. But she says she was never warned of the risk when she had her original operation.

"If I had been told there was even a small chance of this, I would have asked a lot more questions," she said. "I'm not trying to frighten anyone. I just want women to know what to look out for, because I very nearly ignored it."

Health regulators stress that the illness remains uncommon and do not recommend that women without symptoms have their implants removed. However, they advise anyone who notices changes around their implants, particularly sudden swelling, to see their GP or surgeon promptly.

Surgeons' groups say patients considering implants should now be told about BIA-ALCL as part of the consent process, alongside more familiar risks such as rupture and infection.

Speaking on Sunday, the education secretary said she was "open-minded" about changing the law but stressed that the government had no immediate plans to legislate.

She said she wanted to hear from experts, including those working with children and families, about how a ban would operate in practice, and that ministers would look closely at the evidence from other parts of the UK before reaching a view.

Her comments follow renewed calls from the children's commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, who has urged ministers to give children the same protection from assault as adults.

Under the Children Act 2004, it is unlawful in England to hit a child, except where it amounts to "reasonable punishment". Whether a smack is judged reasonable depends on the circumstances, including the child's age and the force used.

Scotland became the first part of the UK to remove that defence in November 2020, and Wales followed in March 2022. In both nations, physical punishment of children is now illegal in all settings. The defence remains available to parents in England and Northern Ireland.

Children's charities have long argued that the current law is confusing for parents and professionals alike. The NSPCC has said there is mounting evidence that physical punishment harms children's mental health and wellbeing, and that the law should be clear that it is never acceptable.

Leading doctors have also backed a change. The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health has described the existing legislation as "unjust and dangerously vague", saying it makes it harder for professionals to identify children at risk.

Opponents of a ban say it would criminalise loving parents and intrude on family life, and that existing laws already protect children from abuse. The previous Conservative government repeatedly rejected calls for change, saying parents should be trusted to discipline their children.

A government spokesperson said that any form of violence towards a child was unacceptable.

Labour holds exactly half of the 60 seats in the Senedd, meaning ministers need at least one opposition politician to vote with them, or to abstain, for their spending plans to pass.

The finance secretary, Mark Drakeford, said failure to reach a deal would have "very real consequences" for hospitals, schools and councils across Wales.

"If the budget does not pass, we do not get the full benefit of the money that is on the table," he said. "More than £1bn that could be going to the front line would be put at risk. I don't think anybody who cares about public services could look their constituents in the eye and say that was a price worth paying."

Under the rules governing devolved finances, if a budget is not approved before the start of the financial year in April, the Welsh government is automatically limited to spending a proportion of the previous year's allocation.

Drakeford said he was "open to conversations" with any party willing to engage seriously, but he would not be drawn on what concessions might be on offer.

Plaid Cymru, which ended its co-operation agreement with Labour earlier this year, said the draft plans fell "far short" of what Wales needed. A spokesperson said: "Labour cannot expect other parties to simply wave through a budget that fails to deliver fair funding for Wales. It is for the government to make its case, not to issue threats."

The Welsh Conservatives said they would vote against the proposals. "This is a budget that rewards failure," the party's finance spokesman said. "After 25 years of Labour running Wales, waiting lists are the longest in the UK, and more of the same will not fix that."

Attention is now likely to turn to the Senedd's sole Liberal Democrat, Jane Dodds, whose vote could prove decisive. She said she would "listen carefully", but wanted to see more support for childcare and social care before committing either way.

A final vote on the budget is expected in March.

The prime minister's official spokesperson confirmed on Monday that the final departmental budgets had been agreed, ending weeks of tense negotiations between the Treasury and cabinet ministers over how much each would have to spend in the coming years.

"The spending review is settled," the spokesperson told reporters. "We will be focused on investing in Britain's renewal so that all working people are better off."

The Home Office was the last department to reach agreement, with talks understood to have continued late into the weekend amid concerns about police funding. Senior officers had warned publicly that without a significant increase in resources, forces would struggle to meet the government's pledges on neighbourhood policing and on halving violence against women and girls.

Downing Street declined to say whether the home secretary had secured the uplift she had been seeking, insisting that the details would be set out by the chancellor in the Commons on Wednesday. Asked whether any minister had threatened to resign during the process, the spokesperson said only that discussions had been "constructive throughout".

The housing department is thought to have reached its own settlement on Sunday evening, after a dispute over the size of the affordable homes budget.

The review will set day-to-day budgets for the next three years and capital investment plans for the next four. While health and defence are expected to receive real-terms increases, economists have warned that the arithmetic leaves little room for other areas, with some unprotected departments facing a squeeze.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies said last week that the chancellor faced "unavoidably tough choices", adding that generous settlements for the NHS and the armed forces would mean cuts elsewhere unless taxes rose again in the autumn.

Opposition parties accused ministers of presiding over chaos. A Conservative spokesperson said the last-minute wrangling showed a government "making it up as it goes along", while the Liberal Democrats called for guarantees that social care would not be overlooked.

The numbers alone make for grim reading. India's 247-9 was built on Abhishek Sharma's astonishing 135 from 54 balls, an innings containing 13 sixes and a century reached in just 37 deliveries. England's reply lasted only 10.3 overs. Bowled out for 97, they slumped to a 150-run loss, their heaviest defeat by runs in T20 internationals, and a 4-1 series scoreline that flattered nobody in the touring dressing room.

Only Phil Salt, with a defiant 55 from 23 balls, offered any resistance. Once he fell, the rest folded with barely a whimper, the last seven wickets tumbling in a blur of mistimed slogs and misread spin. That, more than the fireworks from Abhishek, will trouble McCullum most. Across the five matches England's batters never came to terms with Varun Chakravarthy, who finished with 14 wickets and the player of the series award, and their struggles against the turning ball have become too consistent to dismiss as a blip.

McCullum's arrival as white-ball coach was meant to bring the freedom and clarity that transformed the Test side. Instead, the early evidence suggests a team caught between aggression and recklessness. Captain Jos Buttler insisted afterwards that his players would not abandon their approach, but he conceded they had been "outplayed" by a side operating at a different level.

There is little time to regroup. The three-match one-day series begins in Nagpur on Thursday, with the Champions Trophy in Pakistan following later this month. Joe Root's return should lend the middle order some much-needed calm against spin, yet the questions extend beyond one player. England's fast bowlers, Jofra Archer and Mark Wood among them, were taken apart in the powerplay at the Wankhede, and the reliance on raw pace looked one-dimensional on a true surface.

McCullum has never been one for panic. But the scale of the task facing him is now impossible to ignore.

Mr Sullivan, now 68, was convicted in 1987 of killing 21-year-old Diane Sindall, who was beaten to death and sexually assaulted as she walked home from a pub shift in Bebington, Merseyside, in August 1986.

He has spent 38 years in prison, in what is thought to be the longest-running miscarriage of justice involving a living prisoner in the UK.

Three senior judges at the Court of Appeal quashed the conviction after hearing that new tests on samples preserved from the scene had revealed a DNA profile that did not belong to Mr Sullivan. The Crown Prosecution Service did not oppose the appeal, telling the court there was no credible basis on which the conviction could be upheld.

Lord Justice Holroyde said: "In the light of that evidence, it is impossible to regard the appellant's conviction as safe."

Mr Sullivan, who watched the hearing via video link from HMP Wakefield, held his hand to his mouth and appeared to weep as the decision was read out.

In a statement read by his solicitor Sarah Myatt outside court, he said: "I am not angry, I am not bitter. What happened to me was very wrong, but it does not detract from the fact that what happened to Diane was a heinous and most terrible loss of life."

Miss Sindall, a florist who was engaged to be married, had been working behind a bar to save for her wedding. Her van ran out of petrol on the way home and she is believed to have been walking to a garage when she was attacked.

Merseyside Police said the hunt for her killer had been reopened. The force said the newly identified DNA did not match anyone on the national database, and that more than 260 men had so far been screened and eliminated from the inquiry.

Mr Sullivan's sister, Kim Smith, said nobody had won. "They've lost their daughter, they are not going to get her back," she said of the Sindall family.

Lewis Hamilton says he "could not be more excited" about the year ahead as he begins his career as a Ferrari driver.

The seven-time world champion's contract with the Italian team formally began at the start of January, bringing to an end a 12-season spell at Mercedes that yielded six drivers' titles and made him the most successful driver in the sport's history.

Hamilton, who turned 40 this month, announced his decision to leave Mercedes before the start of last season, a move that stunned the paddock. He replaces Carlos Sainz, who has joined Williams, and will line up alongside Charles Leclerc in one of the most eagerly anticipated driver pairings in years.

The Briton has spoken of fulfilling a childhood ambition by racing in red. He arrives at Maranello with the team in arguably its strongest position for some time. Ferrari finished second in last year's constructors' championship, just 14 points behind McLaren, and won five races.

But the scale of the challenge is considerable. Ferrari have not won a drivers' title since Kimi Raikkonen triumphed in 2007, and their last constructors' crown came the following year. Hamilton, meanwhile, endured a difficult final season at Mercedes. Although he ended a win drought of more than two years with an emotional victory at Silverstone, he was regularly out-qualified by team-mate George Russell.

Hamilton is expected to spend the coming weeks getting to know his new engineers and the team's working methods, with time in the simulator and a run in an older car at Ferrari's Fiorano test track planned before official pre-season testing in Bahrain.

Team principal Frederic Vasseur, who ran Hamilton in the junior categories, has said he has no doubts about the driver's motivation or ability to adapt.

The new season begins in Australia on 14-16 March, when Hamilton will resume his pursuit of a record eighth world title.

Asked on the broadcaster's Today programme which facilities a trans woman should use, the education secretary, who also serves as minister for women and equalities, said the Supreme Court's judgment had settled the matter. "The ruling was clear that provisions and services should be accessed on the basis of biological sex," she said.

Pressed on whether that meant a trans woman should use the men's toilets, Phillipson said that was the position set out by the ruling. She added that many businesses, large and small, would want to ensure they had appropriate provision in place, and noted that a growing number had already moved towards unisex facilities or self-contained cubicles that anyone can use.

Her comments follow last week's unanimous decision by the UK's highest court that the terms "woman" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex. The case was brought by the campaign group For Women Scotland against the Scottish government. Delivering the judgment, Lord Hodge cautioned that it should not be read as a triumph for one group at the expense of another, and stressed that trans people remain protected from discrimination under the characteristic of gender reassignment.

Phillipson said the government welcomed the clarity the ruling provided, and that ministers would work with the Equality and Human Rights Commission, which is expected to publish an updated statutory code of practice for service providers in the coming months. The commission's chair, Baroness Falkner, has described the judgment as "enormously consequential" and suggested trans people should advocate for additional "third space" facilities.

Trans rights campaigners have reacted with alarm, warning that the decision could leave trans people excluded from public life or at risk of harassment when using facilities that do not match their appearance. Gender-critical groups, meanwhile, have urged ministers to ensure public bodies, including the NHS, update their policies without delay.

Michelle Francl, a professor of chemistry at Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania, says a pinch of salt is the secret to a better brew. The sodium ions, she explains, block the receptors on the tongue that detect bitterness, particularly when tea has been stewed for too long.

The claim appears in her new book, Steeped: The Chemistry of Tea, published by the Royal Society of Chemistry. It draws on her analysis of research papers and ancient texts spanning more than a thousand years. The idea is not entirely new: an eighth-century Chinese manuscript mentions adding salt to tea.

Francl stresses that the amount should be so small it cannot be tasted. She also recommends using loose leaves rather than teabags, pre-warming the mug or pot, and using a short, stout mug, which keeps the tea hotter because it has less surface area. Warmed milk, she says, should be added after the tea is poured to reduce the chance of curdling. A small squeeze of lemon juice can remove the "scum" that sometimes forms on the surface.

Her advice has caused a stir in Britain, where an estimated 100 million cups of tea are drunk every day. It was enough to prompt a tongue-in-cheek intervention from the US embassy in London.

In a statement posted on social media, the embassy said the suggestion had landed the two countries' special relationship "in hot water". It assured "the good people of the UK that the unthinkable notion of adding salt to Britain's national drink is not official United States policy. And never will be."

It then added: "The US embassy will continue to make tea in the proper way – by microwaving it."

Francl said she had not meant to cause a diplomatic incident. She has been fielding messages since the story broke and admitted she had not expected quite so strong a reaction.

The blaze broke out in industrial units on Marine Parade, close to St Mary's Stadium, on Wednesday afternoon, sending a thick plume of black smoke across the city that could be seen for miles.

Southampton's Championship fixture against Preston North End, which had been due to kick off at 19:30 GMT, was called off several hours beforehand on safety grounds. The club said the decision had been taken following discussions with the emergency services and the city's safety advisory group.

"The safety of supporters, staff and players is our priority," a club statement said. "We apologise for any inconvenience caused and will confirm a new date for the match in due course." Tickets will remain valid for the rearranged game.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service said a large number of firefighters had been sent to the scene from across the county, with crews using aerial ladder platforms and jets to tackle the flames. A spokesperson said the fire had taken hold in several units and crews were expected to remain there throughout the night.

People living and working nearby were urged to keep their windows and doors shut because of the smoke, and the public were asked to stay away from the area.

Police closed a number of surrounding roads, causing long delays for traffic during the evening rush hour. Rail services were also disrupted, with lines running close to the site shut while firefighters worked.

Witnesses described hearing a series of loud bangs as the fire spread. One man who works nearby said: "The smoke just kept getting thicker and darker. Within minutes you could see flames coming through the roof."

There have been no reports of any injuries.

Preston North End said fans who had already set off on the journey of more than 250 miles should turn back.

The cause of the fire is not yet known and an investigation will begin once the site is declared safe.

Shveta Sharma says she transferred money from her US account to ICICI Bank expecting it to be invested in fixed deposits. Instead, she alleges, a bank official "created fake accounts, forged my signature, took out debit cards and cheque books in my name" to withdraw money from her account.

"He gave me fake statements, created a fake email ID in my name and manipulated my mobile number in the bank records so I would not get any withdrawal notifications," she told the broadcaster.

A spokesman for the bank admitted that "there has been a fraud", but said ICICI, a leading private bank with assets running into trillions of rupees, has a reputation to protect and that the guilty would be punished.

Ms Sharma and her husband, who returned to India in 2016 after decades living in the US and Hong Kong, met the banker through a friend. With interest rates on deposits in the US very low, he advised her to move her money to India, where fixed deposits were offering returns of 5.5% to 6%.

On his advice, she visited a branch in Gurugram, near Delhi, and opened an account, into which she began transferring funds from her US account in 2019.

"Over a four-year period, from September 2019 to December 2023, we deposited our entire life savings of about 135m rupees in the bank," she said, adding that with interest earned, the amount should have grown to more than 160m rupees.

She says she never suspected anything was wrong, as the branch manager regularly sent her receipts and statements.

The alleged fraud came to light in January, when a new employee at the bank offered her better returns on her money. It was then that she discovered all her fixed deposits had vanished.

The bank says the manager has been suspended pending an investigation, and that a complaint has been filed with the Economic Offences Wing of Delhi police.

England know that only a bonus-point victory is likely to be enough at Twickenham on Saturday if they are to stay in contention for the Six Nations title.

Defeat by Wales in Cardiff a fortnight ago ended their Grand Slam ambitions and handed the initiative to Warren Gatland's side, who remain unbeaten with two rounds to play. England must now win their remaining fixtures against Italy and Scotland, ideally with maximum points, and hope the Welsh slip up.

Head coach Eddie Jones has responded by selecting one of the most powerful backlines England have fielded in recent years. Ben Te'o comes into the midfield alongside Manu Tuilagi, while 21-year-old Bath wing Joe Cokanasiga is handed his first Six Nations start. Up front, Ellis Genge is preferred at loose-head prop and Brad Shields takes over on the blind-side flank.

Jones insisted the changes were made with Italy's strengths in mind rather than as a reaction to the loss at the Principality Stadium, where England led at half-time but were outplayed after the interval. He said his players had trained with real intensity over the past fortnight and were determined to give the home crowd something to shout about.

Italy arrive in south-west London on a run of 20 successive defeats in the championship, a sequence stretching back to 2015, and they have never beaten England in 24 previous attempts. However, Conor O'Shea's team caused problems for Ireland in Rome last time out, leading at the break before fading in the final quarter.

The visitors are boosted by the return of their talismanic captain Sergio Parisse, who missed that game with concussion. The number eight will be making what is expected to be his final Six Nations appearance at Twickenham.

England captain Owen Farrell said the squad was focused on its own performance rather than the permutations in the table, adding that Italy had earned respect with the way they had played in this year's tournament.

Raised in Willard, Missouri, a small town where church attendance was expected and queerness was rarely discussed, Kayleigh Rose Amstutz spent her teenage years posting cover songs to YouTube and dreaming of somewhere bigger. Her stage name is a tribute to her late grandfather, Dennis Chappell, whose favorite song was the cowboy ballad "The Strawberry Roan."

Success did not come quickly. Signed to Atlantic Records at 17, she was dropped in 2020, just months after releasing "Pink Pony Club," a glittering ode to a West Hollywood gay bar that would later become her calling card. She moved back home and worked at a drive-through to pay the bills. For a while, it looked as if her pop career had ended before it began.

Instead, she regrouped with producer Dan Nigro, best known for his work with Olivia Rodrigo, and built the campy, theatrical world of her 2023 debut album, "The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess." The record swings from cheerleader chants ("HOT TO GO!") to heartbreak ballads ("Casual") to flirtatious glam-rock ("Red Wine Supernova"). Its lyrics are frank, funny and unabashedly queer.

Her live shows have become the stuff of fan legend. Each tour stop has a costume theme, local drag queens serve as opening acts, and Roan herself appears in towering wigs, smeared white face paint and rhinestones, a look she credits to drag culture. Audiences learn the "HOT TO GO!" choreography as readily as an earlier generation learned the "Y.M.C.A."

An opening slot on Rodrigo's Guts World Tour introduced her to arena crowds, and a buzzy Coachella set this spring did the rest. Her latest single, "Good Luck, Babe!," a soaring synth-pop kiss-off, has given her a first real chart hit.

What sets Roan apart is her commitment to the bit. In an era of understated, whisper-voiced pop, she is loud and ridiculous, and she is sincere about it.

Fiona Harvey, the Scottish woman who says she is the inspiration for the stalker character Martha in the hit Netflix series Baby Reindeer, has said she intends to take legal action against the streaming service and the show's creator, Richard Gadd.

In an interview with Piers Morgan on his YouTube show Piers Morgan Uncensored, Harvey described the drama as "a work of fiction" and denied stalking the comedian. She told Morgan that she had instructed lawyers and was considering her options.

The seven-part series, which opens with the claim that it is a true story, is based on Gadd's account of being harassed over several years by a woman he met while working in a London pub. In the show, Martha, played by Jessica Gunning, sends the character based on Gadd 41,000 emails, hundreds of hours of voicemail messages and more than 100 pages of letters. She is ultimately convicted and jailed.

Harvey disputed that account. She said she had sent Gadd only a handful of emails, a small number of tweets and a single letter, and insisted she had never been convicted of any offence or served a prison sentence. She also said she had not watched the series.

She said she had been forced to speak publicly after internet sleuths identified her as the supposed real-life Martha, and that she had since received death threats and abuse online.

Gadd has previously urged viewers not to speculate about the real identities of the people depicted in the series, saying that was not the point of the show.

Netflix has defended its handling of the programme. Giving evidence to MPs, the company's policy chief, Benjamin King, said the streamer and the producers had taken "every reasonable precaution" to disguise the real identities of those involved while preserving the truth of Gadd's story.

Baby Reindeer has become one of Netflix's most watched shows of the year, attracting tens of millions of views worldwide since its release in April.

By the time the Hungarian players had finished celebrating in front of their own supporters, the kilted thousands at the other end of the Stuttgart Arena had fallen silent. Kevin Csoboth's goal, struck in the 100th minute of a match Scotland had to win, did more than end a football match. It closed a fortnight in which an estimated 200,000 Scots had turned German city squares into a travelling ceilidh.

They had sung in the rain in Munich, even after a 5-1 thrashing by the hosts on opening night. They had drunk Cologne's old town dry, by some local accounts, and been praised by police and publicans alike for their good humour. What they had not done, once again, was watch their team reach the knockout stage of a major tournament. That remains a feat beyond every Scotland side in history.

"We came for a party and we got one, but you can't keep telling yourself that's enough," said Craig Mulholland, 44, from Paisley, folding a saltire into his rucksack outside the ground. "One shot on target all night. We deserved nothing, and nothing's what we're going home with."

Others were angrier, pointing to the penalty Scotland were denied when Stuart Armstrong went down in the box late in the second half. But few were prepared to pretend that one decision explained a campaign that yielded a single point and two goals, one of them scored by an opponent.

At the main station on Monday morning, the bagpipes were back in their cases. Fans queued bleary-eyed for trains to Frankfurt and flights home, swapping scarves with Hungarians and handshakes with the locals who had hosted them.

"The Germans have been brilliant to us," said Eilidh Fraser, a nurse from Inverness, who had taken unpaid leave to follow the team. "I just wish we'd given them something to remember besides the singing."

The FBI has launched a fresh appeal to trace everyone affected by the Lockerbie bombing as US prosecutors prepare for the trial of a Libyan man accused of making the device that destroyed Pan Am Flight 103.

The Boeing 747 was flying from London to New York when it exploded over the Dumfries and Galloway town on 21 December 1988. All 259 passengers and crew were killed, along with 11 people on the ground. It remains the deadliest terror attack ever carried out on British soil.

Abu Agila Mas'ud Kheir Al-Marimi, known as Masud, has been in US custody since December 2022. He denies building the bomb that brought down the aircraft and is due to stand trial before a federal court in Washington DC.

US authorities say they want to hear not only from the relatives of those who died, but from anyone who suffered direct harm as a result of the attack. That could include people who were living in Lockerbie at the time, as well as police officers, military personnel and volunteers who took part in the search and recovery operation.

The move follows legislation passed by the US Congress that allows victims of the bombing to follow court proceedings remotely, wherever in the world they live. Those who believe they may be eligible are being asked to complete an online form, and the information gathered will help the court decide who should be given access.

Investigators acknowledge that, after more than three decades, many of those affected have moved away, and some may never have been formally recorded as victims.

Only one man has ever been convicted over the bombing. Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was found guilty by a panel of Scottish judges sitting at a special court in the Netherlands in 2001. He was released on compassionate grounds in 2009 and died in Libya three years later.

New Zealand reached the semi-finals of the Women's T20 World Cup for the first time since 2016 with a crushing 54-run victory over Pakistan in Dubai, a result that also eliminated India from the tournament.

After choosing to bat, the White Ferns were restricted to 110-6 on a sluggish surface, with Suzie Bates top-scoring with 28. Left-arm spinner Nashra Sandhu was the pick of the Pakistan attack, taking 3-18. The total might have been considerably smaller had Pakistan held their chances, but they put down eight catches in a ragged fielding display.

Those misses proved costly. Pakistan needed to reach their target in 10.4 overs to leapfrog both New Zealand and India on net run-rate and claim the second qualifying spot in Group A, which forced their batters to attack from the outset. The approach backfired badly, as wickets tumbled in the powerplay and the chase never gained momentum.

Captain Fatima Sana offered brief resistance with 21, but she found little support. Pakistan were dismissed for 56 in 11.4 overs.

Leg-spinner Amelia Kerr again led the way for New Zealand with 3-14, taking her to the top of the tournament's wicket-taking charts, while off-spinner Eden Carson claimed 2-7 to do the early damage.

The result means New Zealand join defending champions Australia in progressing from Group A. India had been relying on a narrow Pakistan win to sneak through after their defeat by Australia on Sunday, and they now head home early.

"We knew it was going to be tough work out there, and we were a bit disappointed with the bat, but we knew if we bowled well it would be hard to chase," said New Zealand captain Sophie Devine.

"We haven't been in a semi-final for a long time, so I'm incredibly proud of this group."

On the streets of Dhaka, where only days ago police fired tear gas and live rounds at crowds of demonstrators, students in high-visibility vests now direct traffic at busy intersections. Others sweep broken glass from the pavements or paint over the scorch marks left on walls during weeks of unrest.

"We brought down a dictator. Now we have to show we can build something better," says Rafiq, a 22-year-old economics student at Dhaka University, pausing from waving rickshaws through a junction near Shahbagh. "People died for this. We can't waste it."

The protests began in early July as a campaign against quotas in government jobs, but swelled into a nationwide uprising after a deadly crackdown by security forces. Hundreds of people were killed, many of them young. On 5 August, as thousands marched on her official residence, Sheikh Hasina resigned and fled to India by helicopter, ending 15 years of increasingly autocratic rule.

For many of those who took part, the moment still feels unreal. "I grew up knowing only one prime minister," says Nusrat, 20, who joined the marches after a classmate was shot. "We were afraid to post anything critical on Facebook. Now we are talking openly about what kind of country we want."

What they want, the students say, goes far beyond a change of leader. They speak of independent courts, an end to enforced disappearances, a police force that serves the public rather than a party, and elections that people can trust.

The appointment of Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus to lead an interim government, a choice put forward by student leaders themselves, has fuelled their optimism. But there are worries too. Reports of attacks on minority communities and on supporters of the former ruling party have alarmed many, and police have been largely absent from their posts.

"The hard part starts now," Rafiq says. "Removing her took a month. Fixing the system will take years."

A 26-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of three counts of murder after a mother and her two daughters were killed in a crossbow attack at their home in Hertfordshire.

Kyle Clifford was found injured in the Lavender Hill Cemetery area of Enfield, north London, on Wednesday afternoon after a manhunt involving armed officers, search teams and police helicopters. Hertfordshire Constabulary said he remained in hospital in a serious condition and had not yet been questioned by detectives. The force confirmed that no shots were fired by police.

Carol Hunt, 61, and her daughters Hannah, 28, and Louise, 25, were found with serious injuries at a property in Ashlyn Close, Bushey, shortly before 7pm on Tuesday. Despite the efforts of paramedics, all three died at the scene. They were the wife and daughters of the broadcaster racing commentator John Hunt.

Police said the attack was believed to have been targeted and that a crossbow had been used, although they added that other weapons may also have been involved. A crossbow has since been recovered as part of the investigation.

Detectives from the Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire Major Crime Unit are leading the inquiry. Officers said the suspect was known to the victims, and it is understood he was a former partner of one of the daughters. Clifford, from Enfield, is reported to have served briefly in the British Army before leaving in 2022.

Residents of the quiet cul-de-sac described hearing screams on Tuesday evening before emergency vehicles, including an air ambulance, arrived in the street. A cordon remained in place on Thursday as forensic teams continued their work, and floral tributes were left nearby.

The killings have prompted renewed debate over the regulation of crossbows, which can be bought without a licence by anyone over 18. The Home Office said the home secretary would urgently consider the findings of a recent review into whether tighter controls are needed.

For long stretches at Old Trafford, it was hard to tell what kind of side Amorim will inherit when he formally takes charge on November 11. United were diligent rather than dangerous under interim boss Ruud van Nistelrooy, content to sit in a compact shape and wait for Chelsea to make a mistake. The first half passed with barely a chance of note, and the home crowd grew restless at a side still struggling to build attacks with any conviction.

When the breakthrough came, it owed more to opportunism than design. Casemiro's ball over the top released Rasmus Hojlund, who was brought down by the onrushing Robert Sanchez, and Bruno Fernandes sent the goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot with 20 minutes remaining. A team with greater assurance might have seen the game out from there. United held their lead for just four minutes, a half-cleared corner dropping to Moises Caicedo on the edge of the area for the midfielder to steer a low volley beyond Andre Onana.

That inability to manage key moments has plagued United throughout a campaign that cost Erik ten Hag his job, and the draw left them 13th in the Premier League, having scored fewer goals than all but a handful of top-flight sides. Alejandro Garnacho wasted two presentable openings, while Lisandro Martinez was perhaps fortunate to escape with only a yellow card for a late, high challenge on Cole Palmer.

Amorim built his reputation at Sporting Lisbon on a well-drilled 3-4-3 system, with aggressive wing-backs and a clear pattern of play. Little in this squad suggests an easy fit. There are doubts over who can fill the wide roles, whether the midfield has the legs for the pressing he demands, and where the goals will come from.

Van Nistelrooy has restored some spirit and organisation in his brief spell at the helm, but the Portuguese will arrive in Manchester knowing that a few days on the training ground will not close the gap to the top four.

Aston Villa have completed the signing of Marco Asensio on loan from Paris Saint-Germain until the end of the season, while the club have also reached an agreement with Chelsea to take defender Axel Disasi on a temporary basis.

Asensio, 29, becomes the second high-profile attacking arrival at Villa Park in the space of 48 hours, following Marcus Rashford's loan switch from Manchester United. The Spain international had fallen down the pecking order under Luis Enrique in Paris and was keen to secure regular football for the second half of the campaign. It is understood Villa will cover the bulk of his wages, and the deal does not include an option to buy.

The former Real Madrid forward, who won three Champions League titles during his time at the Bernabeu, gives Unai Emery another versatile option across the front line after the sale of Jhon Duran to Al-Nassr and the departure of Emi Buendia on loan to Bayer Leverkusen.

Disasi, meanwhile, is expected to undergo a medical before the paperwork is finalised. The 26-year-old France centre-back had also attracted interest from Tottenham Hotspur, who had agreed terms with Chelsea, but the player made clear his preference was a move to the Midlands. Villa are understood to be paying a loan fee in addition to covering his salary.

Emery has been eager to strengthen his defence after Diego Carlos joined Fenerbahce last month, with injuries to Pau Torres, Ezri Konsa and Tyrone Mings leaving him short of options at the back.

The late business caps a busy window for Villa, who have also brought in Donyell Malen from Borussia Dortmund and Andres Garcia from Levante as they look to push for a top-four finish and prepare for the last 16 of the Champions League.

Both Asensio and Disasi could be in contention to make their debuts this weekend, subject to registration.

Ange Postecoglou says he is "in a fight" to turn Tottenham's season around, but insists he will not abandon the attacking approach that has drawn growing scrutiny.

Spurs sit in the bottom half of the Premier League after a damaging run of results, and a lengthy injury list has stripped the Australian of several first-choice defenders. Sunday's home defeat to Chelsea, in which his side surrendered a two-goal lead, prompted fresh questions over whether the head coach should adopt a more pragmatic style.

Postecoglou was unmoved when asked if the situation called for compromise.

"I'm in a fight, there's no doubt about that," he said. "But I've been in fights before, and I've never got through them by becoming something I'm not. If anything, this is the time you double down on what you believe in. That's what I intend to do."

The 59-year-old acknowledged the frustration among supporters, some of whom voiced their anger at the final whistle at the weekend, but said changing course now would undermine the work done since his arrival from Celtic in the summer of 2023.

"I understand people are disappointed, and so are we. Nobody is hurting more than the people in that dressing room," he added. "But if I start tearing things up every time we hit a rough patch, we end up nowhere. The players believe in what we're doing, and I believe in them."

Tottenham have been without goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario and centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven for much of the past month, forcing Postecoglou to field makeshift back lines and lean heavily on younger members of the squad.

He refused to use the absences as an excuse, however. "Every club has injuries. It's my responsibility to find solutions, and I'm not going to shy away from that," he said.

Spurs return to action in the Europa League on Thursday before a busy festive schedule that could define their campaign.

The £2 cap on single fares, which covers most bus journeys in England outside London, was introduced by the previous Conservative government in January 2023 to help passengers with the cost of living. It had been due to expire at the end of December.

Speaking in Birmingham ahead of the Budget, Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer confirmed the cap would instead rise to £3 and remain in place until the end of 2025. He said the previous government had only funded the scheme until the end of this year, and that he knew how much the cap mattered, particularly in rural communities where people rely heavily on buses.

The Department for Transport said that without continued support, fares on some routes could have risen sharply, with passengers on certain rural services facing single tickets costing more than £10. Under the new arrangement, fares that currently sit between £2 and £3 will only be allowed to rise in line with inflation.

But the decision has drawn criticism from campaigners and opposition parties, who argue it will hit those on the lowest incomes hardest. Someone commuting five days a week on a single bus each way would pay an extra £10 a week, or around £40 a month.

Environmental groups said the increase made little sense at a time when ministers want to encourage people out of their cars. The Conservatives, who had pledged in their election manifesto to keep the £2 cap for the duration of the Parliament, accused Labour of clobbering working people.

Not all passengers will be affected. In London, where transport is devolved, single bus fares remain at £1.75. Some regional mayors, including Greater Manchester's Andy Burnham, have indicated they intend to hold fares at £2 in their areas using local funding.

Bus operators broadly welcomed the announcement, saying it avoided a "cliff edge" return to commercial fares in January, though they warned some passengers would still struggle with the higher cost.
